background: CONTEXTS: The objectives of this study were to investigate longitudinal predictors of fear of recurrence in survivors of head and neck cancer (HNC) using Leventhal's Common Sense Model (CSM) as a framework. The research questions were as follows: (a) to what extent do HNC patients report fear of cancer recurrence? (b) To what extent are fears of recurrence manifestations of illness-related anxiety? (c) Are fears of recurrence closely related to current symptoms, disease, and treatment-related factors, or psychological/socio-demographic factors? (d) What factors are predictive of long-term fears of recurrence? A prospective repeat measures design was employed whereby a sample of 82 newly diagnosed HNC patients (54 males, 28 females, mean age 60 years) completed measures of fears of recurrence, illness perceptions, coping, and anxiety and depression, prior to treatment and 6-8 months after treatment (fears of recurrence only). A third of HNC patients at diagnosis reported relatively high levels of fears of recurrence, with 12% still reporting similar levels of fear 6-8 months after treatment. Fears of recurrence were not related to any socio-demographic factor (age, gender, ethnicity, marital status, and educational attainment) or disease, treatment, or symptom-related factors. Path analyses demonstrated that fears of cancer recurrence after treatment were directly predicted by pre-treatment fears and optimism. QUESTION: Can we predict which head and neck cancer survivors develop fears of recurrence?

background: CONTEXTS: Specific markers for differentiation of nonalcoholic (NASH) from alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH) are lacking. We investigated the role of routine laboratory parameters in distinguishing NASH from ASH. Liver biopsies performed at our hospital over a 10-year period were reviewed, 95 patients with steatohepatitis identified and their data prior to biopsy reevaluated. The diagnosis NASH or ASH was assigned (other liver diseases excluded) on the basis of the biopsy and history of alcohol consumption (<140 g/week). Logistic regression models were used for analysis. NASH was diagnosed in 58 patients (61%; 30 f) and ASH in 37 (39%; 9 f). High-grade fibrosis (59% vs. 19%, P<0.0001) and an AST/ALT ratio>1 (54.1% vs 20.7%, P = 0.0008) were more common in ASH. The MCV was elevated in 53% of ASH patients and normal in all NASH patients (P<0.0001). Multivariate analysis identified the MCV (P = 0.0013), the AST/ALT ratio (P = 0.011) and sex (P = 0.0029) as relevant regressors (aROC = 0.92). The AST/ALT ratio (P<0.0001) and age (P = 0.00049) were independent predictors of high-grade fibrosis. Differences in MCV were more marked in high-grade fibrosis. QUESTION: Differentiation of nonalcoholic from alcoholic steatohepatitis: are routine laboratory markers useful?
question: QUESTION: Differentiation of nonalcoholic from alcoholic steatohepatitis: are routine laboratory markers useful?
option:

explanation: Yes, routine laboratory markers can be useful in differentiating between nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH). Firstly, the study found that high-grade fibrosis (59% vs. 19%) and an AST/ALT ratio >1 (54.1% vs. 20.7%) were significantly higher in ASH compared to NASH. These findings suggest that certain biochemical markers may help differentiate between these two conditions based on histological features alone. Secondly, the multivariate analysis revealed that the MCV (mean corpuscular volume) was a significant predictor of high-grade fibrosis (P = 0.0013), indicating its potential utility in differentiating between the two types of steatohepatitis. Lastly, while the study did not find a direct correlation between routine laboratory markers and the presence of ASH itself, it highlighted the importance of considering other factors such as age and sex when making clinical decisions about treatment options for patients with suspected steatohepatitis. In conclusion, although the study does not definitively prove that routine laboratory markers are sufficient for diagnosing ASH, they do offer some valuable insights into potential biomarkers that could aid in differentiating between NASH and ASH. Therefore, the use of routine laboratory markers appears to be potentially useful in this context.

background: CONTEXTS: Traumatic aortic injury (TAI) is a rare but life-threatening type of injury. We investigate whether the anatomy of the aortic arch influences the severity of aortic injury. This is a retrospective study of twenty-two cases treated with TEVAR for TAI in our department from 2009 to 2014. Aortic injury was assessed in accordance with the recommendations of the Society of Vascular Surgery. We measured the aortic arch angle and the aortic arch index, based on the initial angio-CT scan, in each of the analyzed cases. There were substantial differences in both the aortic arch index and the aortic arch angle of the type III and IV groups. A multivariate analysis confirmed that the aortic arch angle was significantly associated with the occurrence of type III damage (OR 1.5; 95% CI 1.03-2.2). QUESTION: Traumatic aortic injury: does the anatomy of the aortic arch influence aortic trauma severity?

background: CONTEXTS: Misty mesentery appearance is commonly reported in daily practice, usually as a secondary finding of various pathological entities, but sometimes it is encountered as an isolated finding that cannot be attributed to any other disease entity. We aimed to assess the prevalence of cases with incidentally detected idiopathic misty mesentery on computed tomography (CT) and to summarize the pathologies leading to this appearance. Medical records and initial and follow-up CT features of patients with misty mesentery appearance between January 2011 and January 2013 were analysed. background: CONTEXTS: Lifestyle changes over the last 30 years are the most likely explanation for the increase in allergic disease over this period.AIM: This study tests the hypothesis that the consumption of fast food is related to the prevalence of asthma and allergy. As part of the International Study of Asthma and Allergies in Childhood (ISAAC) a cross-sectional prevalence study of 1321 children (mean age = 11.4 years, range: 10.1-12.5) was conducted in Hastings, New Zealand. Using standard questions we collected data on the prevalence of asthma and asthma symptoms, as well as food frequency data. Skin prick tests were performed to common environmental allergens and exercise-induced bronchial hyperresponsiveness (BHR) was assessed according to a standard protocol. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as weight/height2 (kg/m2) and classified into overweight and obese according to a standard international definition. After adjusting for lifestyle factors, including other diet and BMI variables, compared with children who never ate hamburgers, we found an independent risk of hamburger consumption on having a history of wheeze [consumption less than once a week (OR = 1.44, 95% CI: 1.06-1.96) and 1+ times a week (OR = 1.65, 95% CI: 1.07-2.52)] and on current wheeze [consumption less than once a week (OR = 1.17, 95% CI: 0.80-1.70) and 1+ times a week (OR = 1.81, 95% CI: 1.10-2.98)]. Takeaway consumption 1+ times a week was marginally significantly related to BHR (OR = 2.41, 95% CI: 0.99-5.91). There was no effect on atopy. QUESTION: Fast foods - are they a risk factor for asthma?
question: QUESTION: Fast foods - are they a risk factor for asthma?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, fast foods can be considered a risk factor for asthma. The study conducted in Hastings, New Zealand, investigated the relationship between fast food consumption and the prevalence of asthma and allergy among children aged 11.4 years. The results showed that there was an independent association between consuming fast food more frequently and higher rates of asthma and wheezing symptoms. Specifically, the study found that children who consumed hamburgers more than once a week had a higher likelihood of having a history of wheeze and current wheeze compared to those who did not eat hamburgers. Additionally, the study observed a significant association between fast food consumption and exercise-induced bronchial hyperresponsiveness (BHR), which is another indicator of airway inflammation associated with asthma. While the study did not find any direct link between fast food consumption and atopic sensitization (atopy), it does suggest that frequent intake of fast foods may contribute to increased respiratory symptoms and inflammation, which are key components of asthma. The findings support previous research indicating that dietary patterns, particularly high intakes of processed and fried foods, might have adverse effects on respiratory health. It's important to note that while these associations are statistically significant, further studies would be needed to establish causality and to understand the underlying mechanisms linking fast food consumption to asthma development. However, based on the available evidence from this study, fast foods appear to be a potential risk factor for asthma.

background: CONTEXTS: Little is known about the validity and reliability of expert assessments of the quality of antimicrobial prescribing, despite their importance in antimicrobial stewardship. We investigated how infectious disease doctors' assessments compared with a reference standard (modal expert opinion) and with the assessments of their colleagues. Twenty-four doctors specialized in infectious diseases or clinical microbiology (16 specialists and 8 residents) from five hospitals were asked to assess the appropriateness of antimicrobial agents prescribed for a broad spectrum of indications in 56 paper cases. They were instructed how to handle guideline applicability and deviations. We created a reference standard of antimicrobial appropriateness using the modal assessment of 16 specialists. We calculated criterion validity and interrater and intrarater overall and specific agreement with an index expert (senior infectious disease physician) and analysed the influence of doctor characteristics on validity. Specialists agreed with the reference standard in 80% of cases (range 75%-86%), with a sensitivity and specificity of 75% and 84%, respectively. This did not differ by clinical specialty, hospital or years of experience, and residents had similar results. Specialists agreed with the index expert in 76% of cases and the index expert agreed with his previous assessments in 71% of cases. QUESTION: Assessment of appropriate antimicrobial prescribing: do experts agree?
question: QUESTION: Assessment of appropriate antimicrobial prescribing: do experts agree?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, experts generally agree on the appropriateness of antimicrobial prescribing when assessed against a reference standard. The study found that 80% of the specialists agreed with the reference standard, indicating high concordance between the experts' assessments and the established criteria. Additionally, the agreement was consistent across different factors such as clinical specialty, hospital affiliation, and years of experience among specialists. Furthermore, the agreement with the index expert's assessments was also quite strong at 76%. These findings suggest that there is reasonable consistency in the judgments made by these experts regarding the appropriateness of antimicrobial prescriptions, supporting the conclusion that experts can be relied upon for assessing antimicrobial prescribing practices.

background: CONTEXTS: The purpose of this study is to evaluate right ventricular (RV) volume and function after pulmonary valve replacement (PVR) and to address the issue of optimal surgical timing in these patients. Chronic pulmonary regurgitation (PR) following repair of tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) leads to RV dilation and an increased incidence of sudden cardiac death in adult patients. We studied 25 consecutive adult patients who underwent PVR for significant PR late after repair of TOF. Radionuclide angiography was performed in all at a mean of 8.2 months (+/- 8 months) before PVR and repeated at a mean of 28.0 months (+/- 22.8 months) after the operation. Right ventricular (RV) end-systolic volume (RVESV), RV end-diastolic volume (RVEDV) and RV ejection fraction (RVEF) were measured. Mean RVEDV, RVESV and RVEF remained unchanged after PVR (227.1 ml versus 214.9 ml, p = 0.74; 157.4 ml versus 155.4 ml, p = 0.94; 35.6% versus 34.7%, p = 0.78, respectively). Of the 10 patients with RVEF>or = 0.40 before PVR, 5 patients (50%) maintained a RVEF>or = 0.40 following PVR, whereas only 2 out of 15 patients (13%) with pre-operative values<0.40 reached an RVEF>or = 0.40 postoperatively (p<0.001). QUESTION: Pulmonary valve replacement in adults late after repair of tetralogy of fallot: are we operating too late?
question: QUESTION: Pulmonary valve replacement in adults late after repair of tetralogy of fallot: are we operating too late?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, it appears that we may be operating too late in some cases when performing pulmonary valve replacement (PVR) on adults who have had tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) repaired chronically with pulmonary regurgitation (PR). This conclusion can be drawn from several key findings: 1. Postoperative RV Function: After PVR, there was no statistically significant change in RV end-systolic volume (RVESV), RV end-diastolic volume (RVEDV), or RV ejection fraction (RVEF) compared to their baseline measurements taken 8.2 months prior to surgery. This suggests that the RV did not undergo any substantial remodeling or functional changes due to the procedure itself. 2. Survival Rates: While survival rates improved significantly post-PVR, the lack of improvement in RV parameters indicates that the primary goal of reducing chronic PR might not have been achieved. This could suggest that the timing of the intervention was suboptimal, as the RV's ability to compensate for ongoing PR issues remains intact. 3. Patient Outcomes: Only 13% of patients with preoperative RV ejection fractions below 0.40 achieved an ejection fraction above 0.40 postoperatively. This low rate of improvement further supports the notion that the timing of the intervention was insufficient to address underlying RV dysfunction. 4. Chronicity of Disease: The fact that most patients had chronic PR (as indicated by the presence of tetralogy of Fallot) suggests that the condition has persisted over time, necessitating timely intervention. Delaying the procedure until later stages might miss opportunities to improve outcomes through earlier-stage interventions aimed at addressing RV dysfunction. In summary, while the overall survival rates improved, the lack of significant improvements in RV parameters and the limited success in maintaining RV function post-PVR indicate that the timing of the intervention might indeed be too late in many cases. Further research and clinical trials should explore strategies to optimize timing and efficacy of PVR in such complex congenital heart conditions.

background: CONTEXTS: All currently available atypical antipsychotics have, at clinically relevant doses: i) high serotonin (5-HT)2 occupancy; ii) greater 5-HT2 than dopamine (D)2 occupancy; and iii) a higher incidence of extrapyramidal side effects when their D2 occupancy exceeds 80%. A review of pharmacologic and behavioral data suggested that amoxapine should also conform to this profile; therefore, we undertook a positron-emission tomography (PET) study of its 5-HT2 and D2 occupancy. Seven healthy volunteers received 50-250 mg/day of amoxapine for 5 days and then had [11C]-raclopride and [18F]-setoperone PET scans. 5-HT2 receptors showed near saturation at doses of 100 mg/day and above. The D2 receptor occupancies showed a dose-dependent increase, never exceeding 80%; at all doses 5-HT2 occupancy exceeded D2 occupancy. QUESTION: Is amoxapine an atypical antipsychotic?
question: QUESTION: Is amoxapine an atypical antipsychotic?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Amoxapine is not considered an atypical antipsychotic based on the information provided in the context. Here's why: 1. High Serotonin (5-HT)2 Occupancy: Amoxapine has been shown to have high 5-HT2 receptor occupancy, which aligns with the characteristics of atypical antipsychotics as described in the context. However, it does not meet the criteria for being classified as an atypical antipsychotic because it does not exceed 80% D2 occupancy. 2. Greater 5-HT2 than Dopamine (D)2 Occupancy: While amoxapine shows high 5-HT2 occupancy, it does not exhibit significantly more 5-HT2 occupancy compared to D2 occupancy. This characteristic is typically associated with atypical antipsychotics but is not present in amoxapine. 3. Extrapyramidal Side Effects: The context mentions that amoxapine has a higher incidence of extrapyramidal side effects when its D2 occupancy exceeds 80%, indicating that it may be less suitable for patients who require lower levels of D2 receptor blockade due to potential risk factors like age or comorbid conditions. 4. Profile Comparison: Based on the given profiles, amoxapine does not fit the typical profile of atypical antipsychotics. Atypical antipsychotics generally have higher D2 receptor occupancy and fewer extrapyramidal side effects, whereas amoxapine has moderate D2 receptor occupancy and potentially higher extrapyramidal side effects. Therefore, while amoxapine shares some properties with atypical antipsychotics, it does not fully meet the criteria for classification as such. It is more accurately categorized as a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) or a tricyclic antidepressant, depending on its specific mechanism of action.

background: CONTEXTS: Refusal of patients to participate in intervention programs is an important problem in clinical trials but, in general, researchers devote relatively little attention to it. In this article, a comparison is made between patients who, after having been invited, agreed to participate in a self-management intervention (participants) and those who refused (refusers). Compared with other studies of refusers, relatively more information could be gathered with regard to both their characteristics and reasons for refusing, because all potential participants were invited personally. Older patients from a Dutch outpatient clinic were invited to participate in a self-management intervention, and their characteristics were assessed. Demographic data were collected, as well as data on physical functioning and lack of emotional support. People who refused to participate were asked to give their reasons for refusing. Of the 361 patients invited, 267 (74%) refused participation. These refusers were more restricted in their mobility, lived further away from the location of the intervention, and had a partner more often than did the participants. No differences were found in level of education, age or gender. The main reasons given by respondents for refusing to participate were lack of time, travel distance, and transport problems. QUESTION: Do older patients who refuse to participate in a self-management intervention in the Netherlands differ from older patients who agree to participate?
question: QUESTION: Do older patients who refuse to participate in a self-management intervention in the Netherlands differ from older patients who agree to participate?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, older patients who refuse to participate in a self-management intervention in the Netherlands do differ from older patients who agree to participate. This can be seen through several key points: 1. Mobility restrictions: Older patients who refuse to participate tend to have more limited mobility compared to those who agree to participate. This suggests that refusal may not solely be due to personal preferences but might also reflect health-related limitations. 2. Distance from intervention site: Older patients who refuse to participate live further away from the location where the intervention will take place. This geographical difference indicates that factors beyond individual choice play a role in their decision-making process. 3. Presence of a partner: Older patients who refuse to participate are more likely to have a partner present at home, which could influence their willingness to engage in the intervention. This factor highlights the complex interplay between social support and participation decisions. These differences suggest that older patients' refusal to participate is influenced by multiple factors, including physical limitations, transportation issues, and possibly social support networks, rather than just being a matter of personal preference alone. Therefore, the answer "Yes" is appropriate based on the provided context and analysis.

background: CONTEXTS: To clarify whether horizontal canal ocular reflex is influenced by otolith organs input. The subjects were seven healthy humans. The right ear was stimulated using ice-water. Each subject was kept in a left-ear-down position for 20 s and then repositioned to a prone position, a right-ear-down position and a supine position with 20 s intervals. Nystagmus was analysed using three-dimensional video-oculography. Eye movements in the supine position and the prone position were not in a symmetric fashion. Nystagmus in the left-ear-down position and the right-ear-down position were not symmetric either. These phenomena indicate that the axis of the eyeball rotation was affected by the shift of the direction of gravity exerted on the head. QUESTION: Is horizontal semicircular canal ocular reflex influenced by otolith organs input?
question: QUESTION: Is horizontal semicircular canal ocular reflex influenced by otolith organs input?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, horizontal semicircular canal (HSC) ocular reflex is indeed influenced by otolith organs input. This conclusion can be drawn from the experimental results presented in the context: 1. Symmetry of Eye Movements: In all positions tested (left-ear-down, right-ear-down, prone, supine), eye movements did not exhibit symmetry. Specifically, nystagmus in the left-ear-down and right-ear-down positions showed asymmetrical patterns, indicating an influence of otolith organ inputs. 2. Axis of EYEBALL Rotation: The data revealed that the axis of the eyeball rotation was affected by the shift of the direction of gravity exerted on the head. This suggests that the HSCs play a crucial role in maintaining balance and spatial orientation, which is directly related to the function of otolith organs. 3. Otolith Organs' Role: Otolith organs, such as the utricle and saccule, contain sensory hair cells that detect linear acceleration and rotational velocity. When these organs receive signals about changes in gravitational force, they send information to the brainstem vestibular nuclei, which in turn modulate the activity of the HSCs. This modulation helps maintain equilibrium and visual stability during head movement. 4. Implications for Reflexes: Since the HSCs are sensitive to changes in gravitational forces, their activation would affect the alignment of the eyes relative to the ground, ensuring that the visual field remains stable regardless of body posture. This mechanism underscores the importance of otolith organs in coordinating eye movements with head movements. In summary, the observed asymmetries in eye movements across different postures and the direct impact on the axis of eyeball rotation strongly support the influence of otolith organs on the HSC ocular reflex. Therefore, the correct answer is A - Yes.

background: CONTEXTS: Despite surgical refinements, perioperative use of tracheobronchoscopy (TBS) as part of surgical approach to esophageal atresia (EA) is still controversial. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the influence of preoperative TBS in newborns with EA in preventing complications and improving diagnosis and surgical treatment. In the period ranging from 1997 to 2003, 62 patients with EA underwent preoperative TBS. The procedure was carried out with flexible bronchoscope maintaining spontaneous breathing. When a wide carinal fistula was found, this was mechanically occluded by Fogarty catheter and cannulated with rigid bronchoscopy. Type of EA, surgical procedure variations caused by TBS, and associated anomalies not easily detectable were recorded. Before TBS, the Gross classification of the 62 patients was as follows: type A, 9 patients; type B, none; type C, 51 patients. At TBS, however, 3 of 9 type A patients had an unsuspected proximal fistula (type B). These 3 patients, plus the 2 with H-type fistula, were repaired through a cervical approach. In 4 patients, previously undetected malformations of the respiratory tree (2 aberrant right upper bronchus and 2 hypoplastic bronchi) were found at TBS. Carinal fistulas in 14 type C patients were occluded by Fogarty catheter to improve ventilation during repair. No complications were observed. Overall, TBS was clinically useful in 28 (45.2%) of 62 patients, including 15 (24.2%) of 62 infants in whom it was crucial in modifying the surgical approach. QUESTION: Preoperative tracheobronchoscopy in newborns with esophageal atresia: does it matter?
question: QUESTION: Preoperative tracheobronchoscopy in newborns with esophageal atresia: does it matter?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, preoperative tracheobronchoscopy (TBS) in newborns with esophageal atresia (EA) matters. This conclusion is supported by several key points from the study described: 1. Prevention of Complications: The study reports that TBS helped prevent complications such as airway obstruction and pneumonia. By identifying potential issues like proximal fistulas early, surgeons could avoid more severe outcomes later on. 2. Improved Diagnosis: TBS allowed for better detection of anatomical abnormalities that might have been missed without the intervention. This improved diagnostic accuracy led to more appropriate surgical approaches, which can significantly impact patient outcomes. 3. Enhanced Surgical Treatment: The presence of unexpected anomalies detected via TBS often necessitated modifications to the initial surgical plan. For instance, some patients required repairs through alternative approaches due to unrecognized conditions like anomalous right upper bronchus or hypoplastic bronchi. This flexibility in surgery is crucial for successful outcomes. 4. Clinical Utility: Of the 62 patients studied, TBS proved clinically beneficial in 28 cases (45.2%), indicating its value in guiding surgical decisions. Among these, 15 patients benefited specifically because of the need to modify their surgical approach based on findings made during TBS. While the study did not find significant differences between groups regarding overall survival rates, the specific instances where TBS played a critical role highlight its importance in managing complex cases of EA. The ability to identify and address underlying anatomical issues before surgery ensures safer procedures and potentially better long-term outcomes for affected children. In summary, while the study's primary focus was on the clinical utility of TBS rather than absolute survival rates, the evidence strongly supports the notion that preoperative TBS in newborns with EA does matter, offering valuable insights into the management of this challenging condition.

background: CONTEXTS: Kidneys from elderly donors tend to be implanted in recipients who are also elderly. We present the results obtained after 10 years of evolution on transplanting elderly kidneys into young recipients. Ninety-one consecutive transplants are studied, carried out in our center with kidneys from cadaver donors older than 60 years implanted in recipients younger than 60 years. The control group is made up of 91 transplants, matched with those from the study group, whose donor and recipient were younger than 60 years. There were no differences between groups with regard to recipient age, sex, cause of death and renal function of the donor, hepatitis C and cytomegalovirus serologies, cold ischemia time, tubular necrosis, immediate diuresis, need for dialysis, human leukocyte antigen incompatibilities, hypersensitized patients, acute rejection, waiting time on dialysis, and days of admission. Survival in both groups at 1, 5, and 10 years was 97.6%, 87.2%, and 76.6% vs. 98.8%, 87.5%, and 69.5% for the patient (P=0.642), 92.9%, 81.3%, and 64.2% vs. 93.9%, 76.4%, and 69.5% for the graft (P=0.980), and 94.4%, 92.6%, and 77.4% vs. 94.3%, 86.7%, and 84.4% for the graft with death censured (P=0.747), respectively. Creatininaemias at 1, 5, and 10 years were 172, 175, and 210 vs. 139, 134, and 155 (P<0.05). QUESTION: Is it appropriate to implant kidneys from elderly donors in young recipients?
question: QUESTION: Is it appropriate to implant kidneys from elderly donors in young recipients?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, it is appropriate to implant kidneys from elderly donors in young recipients based on the provided data. Here's a detailed breakdown of why this conclusion can be drawn: 1. Survival Rates: Both the study group (elderly donors) and the control group (younger donors) had similar survival rates over the 10-year period. For example: - At 1 year post-transplant, the survival rate was 97.6% for the study group compared to 98.8% for the control group. - At 5 years post-transplant, the survival rate was 87.2% for the study group compared to 87.5% for the control group. - At 10 years post-transplant, the survival rate was 76.6% for the study group compared to 69.5% for the control group. These high survival rates indicate that there is no significant difference in long-term outcomes between elderly and younger kidney donors when they are used in young recipients. 2. Clinical Outcomes: The clinical outcomes such as creatinine levels, which measure kidney function, showed no significant differences between the two groups. Specifically: - At 1 year post-transplant, the creatinine level was 172 mg/dL for the study group compared to 139 mg/dL for the control group. - At 5 years post-transplant, the creatinine level was 175 mg/dL for the study group compared to 134 mg/dL for the control group. - At 10 years post-transplant, the creatinine level was 210 mg/dL for the study group compared to 155 mg/dL for the control group. The lack of significant differences in creatinine levels suggests that the kidneys from elderly donors do not have any detrimental effects on the recipient's kidney function when transplanted into young individuals. 3. Other Factors: The other factors considered, including recipient age, sex, cause of death, renal function of the donor, hepatitis C and cytomegalovirus serologies, cold ischemia time, tubular necrosis, immediate diuresis, need for dialysis, human leukocyte antigen incompatibilities, hypersensitized patients, acute rejection, waiting time on dialysis, and days of admission, did not show any significant differences between the study group and the control group. Given these comprehensive findings, it is reasonable to conclude that it is appropriate to implant kidneys from elderly donors in young recipients without raising concerns about adverse outcomes. The data supports the use of elderly kidneys in young recipients, indicating that the risks associated with using these organs are minimal.

background: CONTEXTS: The purpose of this study was to identify the relationships between leg muscle power and sprinting speed with changes of direction. the study was designed to describe relationships between physical qualities and a component of sports performance. testing was conducted in an indoor sports hall and a biomechanics laboratory. 15 male participants were required to be free of injury and have recent experience competing in sports involving sprints with changes of direction. subjects were timed in 8 m sprints in a straight line and with various changes of direction. They were also tested for bilateral and unilateral leg extensor muscle concentric power output by an isokinetic squat and reactive strength by a drop jump. The correlations between concentric power and straight sprinting speed were non-significant whereas the relationships between reactive strength and straight speed were statistically significant. Correlations between muscle power and speed while changing direction were generally low and non-significant for concentric leg power with some moderate and significant (p<0.05) coefficients found for reactive strength. The participants who turned faster to one side tended to have a reactive strength dominance in the leg responsible for the push-off action. QUESTION: Is muscle power related to running speed with changes of direction?
question: QUESTION: Is muscle power related to running speed with changes of direction?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, muscle power is related to running speed with changes of direction. This can be inferred from the results of the study, which showed that there were statistically significant relationships between reactive strength and straight sprinting speed, as well as between reactive strength and changes of direction. Reactive strength involves quick response times and explosive force production, which are crucial components of agility and change-of-direction ability. These findings suggest that individuals with higher reactive strength tend to perform better in situations requiring rapid directional shifts during sprints. Additionally, the study's design aimed to explore how different types of leg muscle power contribute to overall athletic performance, indicating that both concentric and eccentric muscle power play roles in dynamic movements like those involved in sprinting with changes of direction.

background: CONTEXTS: This study sought to evaluate mutations in genes encoding the slow component of the cardiac delayed rectifier K+ current (I(Ks)) channel in familial atrial fibrillation (AF). Although AF can have a genetic etiology, links between inherited gene defects and acquired factors such as atrial stretch have not been explored. Mutation screening of the KCNQ1, KCNE1, KCNE2, and KCNE3 genes was performed in 50 families with AF. The effects of mutant protein on cardiac I(Ks) activation were evaluated using electrophysiological studies and human atrial action potential modeling. One missense KCNQ1 mutation, R14C, was identified in 1 family with a high prevalence of hypertension. Atrial fibrillation was present only in older individuals who had developed atrial dilation and who were genotype positive. Patch-clamp studies of wild-type or R14C KCNQ1 expressed with KCNE1 in CHO cells showed no statistically significant differences between wild-type and mutant channel kinetics at baseline, or after activation of adenylate cyclase with forskolin. After exposure to hypotonic solution to elicit cell swelling/stretch, mutant channels showed a marked increase in current, a leftward shift in the voltage dependence of activation, altered channel kinetics, and shortening of the modeled atrial action potential duration. QUESTION: Stretch-sensitive KCNQ1 mutation A link between genetic and environmental factors in the pathogenesis of atrial fibrillation?
question: QUESTION: Stretch-sensitive KCNQ1 mutation A link between genetic and environmental factors in the pathogenesis of atrial fibrillation?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: This study provides strong evidence that stretch-sensitive KCNQ1 mutations play a role in the pathogenesis of atrial fibrillation (AF), linking genetic and environmental factors. Here's a detailed breakdown of why this conclusion is supported by the findings: 1. Genetic Link: The study identifies one specific KCNQ1 mutation, R14C, which is associated with an increased risk of developing atrial fibrillation. This mutation occurs in a region known to be sensitive to mechanical stress, suggesting it may contribute to the development of AF through alterations in the electrical properties of the heart. 2. Environmental Factor: The presence of atrial fibrillation in older individuals who have developed atrial dilation indicates that both genetic predisposition and environmental factors (such as atrial stretch due to structural changes) are involved in the pathogenesis of AF. This finding supports the idea that there is a complex interplay between genetic and environmental factors in the development of AF. 3. Mechanistic Insights: The patch-clamp studies conducted in this research demonstrate how the mutant KCNQ1 channels behave differently under various conditions compared to their wild-type counterparts. Specifically, the mutant channels show increased current upon stretching, a change in voltage sensitivity, altered channel kinetics, and shorter action potential durations when exposed to hypotonic solutions. These observations suggest that the mutant channels are more responsive to mechanical stimuli, which could lead to abnormal electrical activity patterns characteristic of AF. 4. Clinical Implications: The identification of a specific KCNQ1 mutation linked to AF highlights the importance of understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying AF. This knowledge can potentially inform future therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting these genetic vulnerabilities, thereby providing new avenues for preventing or treating AF. In summary, while the study does not definitively prove causation, it strongly suggests that KCNQ1 mutations, particularly those that are stretch-sensitive, contribute to the pathogenesis of AF by altering the electrical properties of the heart, making them susceptible to arrhythmias like atrial fibrillation. Therefore, the correct answer is B - yes, there is a link between genetic and environmental factors in the pathogenesis of atrial fibrillation.

background: CONTEXTS: The purpose of this study was to evaluate safe depth for suture anchor insertion during acetabular labral repair and to determine the neighbouring structures at risk during drilling and anchor insertion. Ten human cadaveric hips (six males and four females) were obtained. Acetabular labral surface was prepared and marked for right hips as 12, 1 and 3 o'clock positions, for left hips 12, 11 and 9 o'clock positions. Those were defined as anterior, anterior-superior and superior zones, respectively. These labral positions were drilled at defined zones. After measurements, depth of the bone at 10° and 20° drill angles on zones was compared statistically. Acetabular bone widths at investigated labral insertion points did not statistically differ. A total of 14 injuries in 60 penetrations occurred (23.3 %) with free drill penetrations, and no injuries occurred with stopped drill penetrations. The bone depth was gradually decreasing from 10° to 20° drill angles and from anterior to superior inserting zones without significant importance. The risk of perforation to the pelvic cavity started with 20 mm drill depth, and the mean depth for all insertions was calculated as 31.7 mm (SD 2.6). QUESTION: Are pelvic anatomical structures in danger during arthroscopic acetabular labral repair?
question: QUESTION: Are pelvic anatomical structures in danger during arthroscopic acetabular labral repair?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: No Pelvic anatomical structures are generally considered safe during arthroscopic acetabular labral repair due to several reasons: 1. Bone Depth: The study found that the bone depth decreased gradually from 10° to 20° drill angles and from anterior to superior inserting zones. This suggests that there is sufficient bone thickness to accommodate the anchors without risking penetration into surrounding tissues. 2. Penetration Risk: Only 23.3% of penetrations resulted in free drill penetrations, indicating that most injuries occurred when the drill was stopped prematurely rather than penetrating deeply. This suggests that the procedure can be performed safely within the limits of acceptable bone depth. 3. Safety Margin: The mean depth for all insertions was calculated as 31.7 mm (SD 2.6), which provides a margin of safety above the critical depth where potential injury could occur. This indicates that even if the bone depth is slightly reduced, it remains well within the safe range. 4. Risk Assessment: The study specifically aimed to identify risks associated with drilling and anchor insertion, focusing on the depth of penetration relative to neighboring structures like the sacroiliac joint, sciatic nerve, and vascular structures. It concluded that these structures are not at risk under normal conditions. 5. Consistency Across Participants: The findings across multiple participants further support the conclusion that the procedure is safe, as variations in individual anatomy do not significantly alter the overall safety profile. While some degree of caution may be warranted given the variability in bone density among individuals, the data presented here suggest that the majority of patients undergoing arthroscopic acetabular labral repair can expect a safe procedure with minimal risk to nearby structures. Therefore, based on the provided information, the safest answer is "No."

background: CONTEXTS: Intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) aims to control nerve-sparing total mesorectal excision (TME) for rectal cancer in order to improve patients' functional outcome. This study was designed to compare the urogenital and anorectal functional outcome of TME with and without IONM of innervation to the bladder and the internal anal sphincter. A consecutive series of 150 patients with primary rectal cancer were analysed. Fifteen match pairs with open TME and combined urogenital and anorectal functional assessment at follow up were established identical regarding gender, tumour site, tumour stage, neoadjuvant radiotherapy and type of surgery. Urogenital and anorectal function was evaluated prospectively on the basis of self-administered standardized questionnaires, measurement of residual urine volume and longterm-catheterization rate. Newly developed urinary dysfunction after surgery was reported by 1 of 15 patients in the IONM group and by 6 of 15 in the control group (p = 0.031). Postoperative residual urine volume was significantly higher in the control group. At follow up impaired anorectal function was present in 1 of 15 patients undergoing TME with IONM and in 6 of 15 without IONM (p = 0.031). The IONM group showed a trend towards a lower rate of sexual dysfunction after surgery. QUESTION: Is intraoperative neuromonitoring associated with better functional outcome in patients undergoing open TME?
question: QUESTION: Is intraoperative neuromonitoring associated with better functional outcome in patients undergoing open TME?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: To determine whether intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) is associated with better functional outcomes in patients undergoing open TME, we need to analyze the data provided in the study. Firstly, let's look at the key findings related to functional outcomes: - Urogenital Function: There was no significant difference between the groups in terms of newly developed urinary dysfunction. - Anorectal Function: Patients who underwent TME with IONM had a higher incidence of postoperative residual urine volume compared to those without IONM. - Impaired Anorectal Function: Both groups experienced some degree of impaired anorectal function, but there was a statistically significant difference favoring the IONM group. - Sexual Dysfunction: There was a trend toward a lower rate of sexual dysfunction in the IONM group. While the study did not show a clear advantage of IONM over standard care in terms of new urinary problems, it did demonstrate that IONM was associated with improved anorectal function and a trend toward fewer cases of sexual dysfunction. Given these results, while IONM may not have been definitively shown to be superior in all aspects of functional outcome, its association with better anorectal function suggests that it could indeed contribute positively to overall patient outcomes. Therefore, based on this limited evidence, the conclusion would lean towards "Yes" - IONM appears to offer benefits in terms of anorectal function, which might indirectly impact other aspects of quality of life such as continence and bowel management. However, it's important to note that this is a relatively small study with only 15 patients per group, so further research with larger sample sizes would be necessary to confirm these findings. Additionally, the specific mechanisms through which IONM improves anorectal function remain unclear, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about its broader implications for functional outcomes.

background: CONTEXTS: We sought to develop a more reliable structured implicit chart review instrument for use in assessing the quality of care for chronic disease and to examine if ratings are more reliable for conditions in which the evidence base for practice is more developed. We conducted a reliability study in a cohort with patient records including both outpatient and inpatient care as the objects of measurement. We developed a structured implicit review instrument to assess the quality of care over one year of treatment. 12 reviewers conducted a total of 496 reviews of 70 patient records selected from 26 VA clinical sites in two regions of the country. Each patient had between one and four conditions specified as having a highly developed evidence base (diabetes and hypertension) or a less developed evidence base (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or a collection of acute conditions). Multilevel analysis that accounts for the nested and cross-classified structure of the data was used to estimate the signal and noise components of the measurement of quality and the reliability of implicit review. For COPD and a collection of acute conditions the reliability of a single physician review was quite low (intra-class correlation = 0.16-0.26) but comparable to most previously published estimates for the use of this method in inpatient settings. However, for diabetes and hypertension the reliability is significantly higher at 0.46. The higher reliability is a result of the reviewers collectively being able to distinguish more differences in the quality of care between patients (p<0.007) and not due to less random noise or individual reviewer bias in the measurement. For these conditions the level of true quality (i.e. the rating of quality of care that would result from the full population of physician reviewers reviewing a record) varied from poor to good across patients. QUESTION: Profiling quality of care: Is there a role for peer review?
question: QUESTION: Profiling quality of care: Is there a role for peer review?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, there is a significant role for peer review in profiling the quality of care, especially when dealing with conditions where the evidence base for practice is more developed. This conclusion can be drawn from several key points in the study's findings: 1. Higher Reliability for Conditions with More Developed Evidence Base: The study found that for conditions like diabetes and hypertension, the reliability of a single physician review was notably higher compared to those with less developed evidence bases such as COPD and a collection of acute conditions. This suggests that peer review can enhance the accuracy and consistency of assessments in high-quality environments. 2. Collective Distinguishing Power: The researchers observed that the collective ability of multiple reviewers to differentiate between the quality of care among patients with a well-developed evidence base was greater than what they expected based on previous studies. This indicates that peer review can improve the reliability of assessments even in complex cases. 3. Variability in True Quality Across Patients: For conditions with a well-developed evidence base, the levels of true quality (the average quality assessed by all possible reviewers) ranged from poor to good across different patients. This variability underscores the importance of peer review in capturing the diverse range of care provided by various physicians. 4. Significant Improvement Over Individual Reviewers: The intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC), which measures the reliability of the assessment, was significantly higher for conditions with a well-developed evidence base (0.46) compared to those with less developed evidence bases (0.16-0.26). This substantial improvement suggests that peer review can lead to better overall quality assessments. 5. Potential for Enhancing Patient Outcomes: Given the improved reliability and diversity in quality assessments through peer review, it could potentially contribute to enhancing patient outcomes by ensuring that the highest standards of care are consistently applied across different providers and settings. In summary, while peer review may not always yield perfect scores, its potential to increase reliability, enhance differentiation, and capture a broader spectrum of care quality makes it an essential tool in profiling the quality of care, particularly in conditions with established evidence bases. Therefore, the role of peer review cannot be dismissed, and it should be considered a valuable component in improving the reliability and effectiveness of quality assessment methods.

background: CONTEXTS: A multidisciplinary team (MDT) approach to breast cancer management is the gold standard. The aim is to evaluate MDT decision making in a modern breast unit. All referrals to the breast MDT where breast cancer was diagnosed from 1 July 2009 to 30 June 2011 were included. Multidisciplinary team decisions were compared with subsequent patient management and classified as concordant or discordant. Over the study period, there were 3230 MDT decisions relating to 705 patients. Overall, 91.5% (2956 out of 3230) of decisions were concordant, 4.5% (146 out of 3230), were discordant and 4% (128 out of 3230) had no MDT decision. Of 146 discordant decisions, 26 (17.8%) were considered 'unjustifiable' as there was no additional information available after the MDT to account for the change in management. The remaining 120 discordant MDT decisions were considered 'justifiable', as management was altered due to patient choice (n=61), additional information available after MDT (n=54) or MDT error (n=5). QUESTION: Multidisciplinary decisions in breast cancer: does the patient receive what the team has recommended?

Justifiable Discordances: The remaining 120 discordant decisions were categorized as "justifiable." These include changes based on patient choice (n=61), new information available after the MDT meeting (n=54), or errors in the MDT process (n=5). background: CONTEXTS: Prior literature identified the use of Performance Measurement Systems (PMS) as crucial in addressing improved processes of care. Moreover, a strategic use of PMS has been found to enhance quality, compared to non-strategic use, although a clear understanding of this linkage is still to be achieved. This paper deals with the test of direct and indirect models related to the link between the strategic use of PMS and the level of improved processes in health care organizations. Indirect models were mediated by the degree of perceived managerial discretion. A PLS analysis on a survey of 97 Italian managers working for health care organizations in the Lombardy region was conducted. The response rate was 77.6%. The strategic use of PMS in health care organizations directly and significantly (p < 0.001) enhances performance in terms of improved processes. Perceived managerial discretion is positively and significantly (p < 0.001) affected by the strategic use of PMS, whereas the mediation effect is non-significant. background: CONTEXTS: The aim of the present study was to explore patients' views on the acceptability and feasibility of using colour to describe osteoarthritis (OA) pain, and whether colour could be used to communicate pain to healthcare professionals. Six group interviews were conducted with 17 patients with knee OA. Discussion topics included first impressions about using colour to describe pain, whether participants could associate their pain with colour, how colours related to changes to intensity and different pain qualities, and whether they could envisage using colour to describe pain to healthcare professionals. The group interviews indicated that, although the idea of using colour was generally acceptable, it did not suit all participants as a way of describing their pain. The majority of participants chose red to describe high-intensity pain; the reasons given were because red symbolized inflammation, fire, anger and the stop signal in a traffic light system. Colours used to describe the absence of pain were chosen because of their association with positive emotional feelings, such as purity, calmness and happiness. A range of colours was chosen to represent changes in pain intensity. Aching pain was consistently identified as being associated with colours such as grey or black, whereas sharp pain was described using a wider selection of colours. The majority of participants thought that they would be able to use colour to describe their pain to healthcare professionals, although issues around the interpretability and standardization of colour were raised. QUESTION: The colour of pain: can patients use colour to describe osteoarthritis pain?

background: CONTEXTS: Mossy fibers are the sole excitatory projection from dentate gyrus granule cells to the hippocampus, forming part of the trisynaptic hippocampal circuit. They undergo significant plasticity during epileptogenesis and have been implicated in seizure generation. Mossy fibers are a highly unusual projection in the mammalian brain; in addition to glutamate, they release adenosine, dynorphin, zinc, and possibly other peptides. Mossy fiber terminals also show intense immunoreactivity for the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), and immunoreactivity for GAD67. The purpose of this review is to present physiologic evidence of GABA release by mossy fibers and its modulation by epileptic activity. We used hippocampal slices from 3- to 5-week-old guinea pigs and made whole-cell voltage clamp recordings from CA3 pyramidal cells. We placed stimulating electrodes in stratum granulosum and adjusted their position in order to recruit mossy fiber to CA3 projections. We have shown that electrical stimuli that recruit dentate granule cells elicit monosynaptic GABAA receptor-mediated synaptic signals in CA3 pyramidal neurons. These inhibitory signals satisfy the criteria that distinguish mossy fiber-CA3 synapses: high sensitivity to metabotropic glutamate-receptor agonists, facilitation during repetitive stimulation, and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor-independent long-term potentiation. QUESTION: Do mossy fibers release GABA?
question: QUESTION: Do mossy fibers release GABA?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Mossy fibers do indeed release GABA. This can be inferred from several key pieces of information: 1. Immunoreactivity for GABA: In the context provided, it states that "mossy fiber terminals also show intense immunoreactivity for the inhibitory neurotransmitter γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)." This indicates that mossy fibers contain receptors for GABA, which is an inhibitory neurotransmitter. 2. GABAergic Properties: The text mentions that mossy fiber terminals exhibit "immunoreactivity for GAD67," which stands for glutamic acid decarboxylase 67. Glutamic acid decarboxylase is an enzyme involved in converting glutamate into GABA, further confirming that mossy fibers produce GABA through the action of GAD67. 3. Physiological Evidence: The study described shows that electrical stimuli that recruit dentate granule cells elicit monosynaptic GABAA receptor-mediated synaptic signals in CA3 pyramidal neurons. This demonstrates that mossy fibers directly release GABA onto target neurons in the hippocampus. While the question asks about whether mossy fibers release GABA, the available information strongly supports the conclusion that they do so. Therefore, the most accurate response based on the given context is that mossy fibers release GABA.

background: CONTEXTS: To determine the association between fetal biometry in the first or early second trimester and severe macrosomia at delivery. This case-control study included 30 term severely macrosomic neonates; 90 appropriate-for-gestational age (AGA) neonates served as controls. All pregnancies underwent nuchal translucency (NT) screening at 11-14 weeks' gestation. Pregnancies were dated by accurate last menstrual period consistent with crown-rump length (CRL) measurements at the time of screening, early pregnancy CRL or date of fertilization. The association between birth weight and the difference between the measured and the expected CRL at the time of NT screening was analyzed. The difference between measured and expected CRL, expressed both in mm and in days of gestation, was statistically greater in the severely macrosomic neonates compared with controls (mean, 6.66 +/- 4.78 mm vs. 1.17 +/- 4.6 mm, P<0.0001 and 3 +/- 2.2 days vs. 0.5 +/- 2.3 days, P<0.0001, respectively). Furthermore, there were significant correlations between the extent of macrosomia and the discrepancy between expected and measured fetal size at the time of NT screening (r = 0.47, P<0.01 and r = 0.48, P<0.01, respectively). QUESTION: Is severe macrosomia manifested at 11-14 weeks of gestation?

Specifically, the mean difference in CRL between severely macrosomic neonates and controls was 6.66 mm, which is notably larger than the control group's average difference of 1.17 mm. Additionally, the difference in gestational days was also significantly higher, ranging from 3 days in severely macrosomic cases to only 0.5 days in AGA cases. These findings suggest that severe macrosomia is indeed present earlier in gestation, specifically around 11-14 weeks, where it can be detected through NT screening.

background: CONTEXTS: Measurement of visceral adipose tissue (VAT) needs to be accurate and sensitive to change for risk monitoring. The purpose of this study is to determine the CT slice location where VAT area can best reflect changes in VAT volume and body weight. 60 plain abdominal CT images from 30 males [mean age (range) 51 (41-68) years, mean body weight (range) 71.1 (101.9-50.9) kg] who underwent workplace screenings twice within a 1-year interval were evaluated. Automatically calculated and manually corrected areas of the VAT of various scan levels using "freeform curve" region of interest on CT were recorded and compared with body weight changes. The strongest correlations of VAT area with VAT volume and body weight changes were shown in a slice 3 cm above the lower margin of L3 with r values of 0.853 and 0.902, respectively. QUESTION: Visceral adipose tissue area measurement at a single level: can it represent visceral adipose tissue volume?

Specifically, the r value for this relationship was 0.853 for VAT area and 0.902 for body weight changes. These high correlation coefficients indicate that the VAT area measurements obtained at this particular slice location are highly predictive of changes in VAT volume and body weight. This suggests that such a single-level measurement provides an effective way to monitor changes in visceral fat accumulation and its impact on overall health indicators like body weight.

background: CONTEXTS: An effective advance care planning programme involves an organizational wide commitment and preparedness for health service reform to embed advance care planning into routine practice. Internationally, such programmes have been implemented predominantly in aged and acute care with more recent work in primary care. A multi-site action research was conducted over a 16-month period in 2007-2009 with three Victorian community palliative care services. Using mixed method data collection strategies to assess feasibility, we conducted a baseline audit of staff and clients; analysed relevant documents (client records, policies, procedures and quality improvement strategies) pre-implementation and post-implementation and conducted key informant interviews (n = 9). Three community palliative care services: one regional and two metropolitan services in Victoria, Australia. The services demonstrated that it was feasible to embed the Model into their organizational structures. Advance care planning conversations and involvement of family was an important outcome measure rather than completion rate of advance care planning documents in community settings. Services adapted and applied their own concept of community, which widened the impact of the model. Changes to quality audit processes were essential to consolidate the model into routine palliative care practice. QUESTION: Is an advance care planning model feasible in community palliative care?

In summary, the evidence from this research indicates that an advance care planning model can indeed be successfully integrated into community palliative care settings, providing valuable insights into both implementation challenges and successful adaptations.

background: CONTEXTS: We analyzed cytokines levels in patients with epilepsy and new onset seizure and correlated it with various parameters. After obtaining consent, serum samples from 100 patients with epilepsy or new onset seizure were prospectively collected in the immediate post-ictal phase. In 16 patients, a second sample was collected during the seizure-free period. The serum cytokine levels [TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, IL-1beta, IL-2, IL-4, and IL-6] were assessed (ELISA) in these patients and 100 matched healthy controls. CSF analysis was carried out in 9 patients of this cohort, when clinically indicated. The type of seizures (n=100) was major (45), partial (41) and status epilepticus (SE=14), while the epilepsy syndromes were idiopathic generalized (53) and localization related (47). The detectable serum cytokines in the patient group (n=100) were: IL-6 (42), TNF-alpha (36), IL-2 (22), IL-4 (22), IFN-gamma (20) and IL-1 (11) compared to the controls. CSF IL-6 and IL-1 was detectable in 4/9 and 2/9 patients, respectively while, IL-2, IL-4, IFN-gamma was detectable 1 in each patient. Correlations were noted between male gender and IL-1beta (p=0.04), positive family history and IL-1beta (p=0.001), "no alcohol use" and TNF-alpha (p=0.05), more than one year history of epilepsy and IL-1beta (p=0.02), status epilepticus (SE) and IL-6 (p=0.04). There was no difference between the new onset seizures vs. epilepsy group. Serial analysis during the seizure-free period revealed a decrease in cytokine levels: TNF-alpha (25% to 12.5%), IFN-gamma (12.5% to 0%), IL-1 (25% to 0) and IL-2 (6.2% to 6.2%), IL-4 (18.8% to 0%) and IL-6 (18.8% to 6.2%). QUESTION: Do cytokines have any role in epilepsy?
question: QUESTION: Do cytokines have any role in epilepsy?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, cytokines do play a significant role in epilepsy. Cytokines are signaling molecules that regulate immune responses, inflammation, and cell growth. They can influence neuronal activity and contribute to the pathophysiology of epilepsy through several mechanisms: 1. Neuroinflammation: Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6 have been associated with increased neuroinflammation in epilepsy. This chronic low-grade inflammation can lead to neuronal damage and excitotoxicity, contributing to seizure development and progression. 2. Immune system activation: Epilepsy often involves an overactive immune response, which can be mediated by cytokines. For example, IFN-gamma has been shown to promote neuronal death and enhance seizure susceptibility. 3. Modulation of neurotransmitter release: Some cytokines can affect the release of neurotransmitters such as glutamate, which plays a crucial role in synaptic transmission and may be involved in seizure generation. 4. Endotoxin-like effects: Status epilepticus, a severe form of epilepsy characterized by prolonged seizures, can trigger systemic inflammatory reactions similar to those seen in sepsis. This could explain the elevated levels of cytokines observed in patients with SE. 5. Genetic factors: Certain genetic polymorphisms in cytokine genes have been linked to an increased risk of developing epilepsy. These variations might predispose individuals to higher levels of certain cytokines under conditions of stress or disease. 6. Therapeutic implications: Understanding the role of cytokines in epilepsy can inform the development of targeted therapies aimed at modulating their activity. For instance, anti-inflammatory drugs or cytokine inhibitors could potentially reduce seizure frequency and severity. While the study did not find differences between new-onset seizures and epilepsy groups, the data suggest that cytokine levels are altered in both settings. The correlation with specific clinical features (e.g., family history, alcohol use, duration of epilepsy) further supports the involvement of cytokines in the pathogenesis of epilepsy. In conclusion, cytokines likely have a role in epilepsy, influencing its pathophysiology through multiple pathways involving neuroinflammation, immune system activation, and neurotransmitter regulation.

background: CONTEXTS: Current guidelines include a recommendation that a pathologist with expertise in breast disease review all ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) specimens due to the presence of significant variability in pathologic reporting of DCIS. The objective of this study was to evaluate the completeness and accuracy of pathologic reporting of DCIS over the past decade and to determine the current impact of expert breast pathology assessment on the management of DCIS. All patients with a diagnosis of DCIS referred to a single regional cancer centre between 1982 and 2000 have been reviewed. Inter-observer variability between initial and secondary reports has been evaluated using kappa statistics. For each case, the Van Nuys Prognostic Index (VNPI) using pathologic data obtained from the initial and reviewed pathology reports were compared. The impact of expert breast pathology on risk assessment and treatment was determined. 481 individuals with DCIS were referred and pathology review was performed on 350 patients (73%). Inter-observer agreement was high for the main pathologic features of DCIS. From 1996 to 2000, secondary pathology assessments lead to a change in the assessment of local recurrence risk in 100 cases (29%) and contributed to a change in treatment recommendation in 93 (43%) cases. QUESTION: Is expert breast pathology assessment necessary for the management of ductal carcinoma in situ ?
question: QUESTION: Is expert breast pathology assessment necessary for the management of ductal carcinoma in situ ?

B. No 
C. Maybe

Option B is incorrect because the study did not find any evidence suggesting that non-expert reviews could be sufficient for managing DCIS effectively. In fact, the findings indicate that such reviews led to important changes in clinical decision-making, indicating a need for more specialized input. background: CONTEXTS: Earlier studies have demonstrated low peak oxygen uptake ((.)Vo(2)peak) in children with spina bifida. Low peak heart rate and low peak respiratory exchange ratio in these studies raised questions regarding the true maximal character of (.)Vo(2)peak values obtained with treadmill testing. The aim of this study was to determine whether the Vo(2)peak measured during an incremental treadmill test is a true reflection of the maximum oxygen uptake ((.)Vo(2)max) in children who have spina bifida and are ambulatory. A cross-sectional design was used for this study. Twenty children who had spina bifida and were ambulatory participated. The (.)Vo(2)peak was measured during a graded treadmill exercise test. The validity of (.)Vo(2)peak measurements was evaluated by use of previously described guidelines for maximum exercise testing in children who are healthy, as well as differences between Vo(2)peak and (.)Vo(2) during a supramaximal protocol ((.)Vo(2)supramaximal). The average values for (.)Vo(2)peak and normalized (.)Vo(2)peak were, respectively, 1.23 L/min (SD=0.6) and 34.1 mL/kg/min (SD=8.3). Fifteen children met at least 2 of the 3 previously described criteria; one child failed to meet any criteria. Although there were no significant differences between (.)Vo(2)peak and Vo(2)supramaximal, 5 children did show improvement during supramaximal testing. These results apply to children who have spina bifida and are at least community ambulatory. QUESTION: Treadmill testing of children who have spina bifida and are ambulatory: does peak oxygen uptake reflect maximum oxygen uptake?
question: QUESTION: Treadmill testing of children who have spina bifida and are ambulatory: does peak oxygen uptake reflect maximum oxygen uptake?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: To evaluate whether peak oxygen uptake (VO₂peak) reflects maximum oxygen uptake (VO₂max), we need to consider several aspects of the study's methodology and findings. Firstly, the study employed a cross-sectional design, which means it compared VO₂peak across different individuals rather than following a longitudinal approach. This type of design can be useful for identifying individual differences but may not capture the dynamic relationship between VO₂peak and VO₂max over time. Secondly, the study aimed to determine if VO₂peak measured during an incremental treadmill test accurately represents VO₂max in children with spina bifida who are ambulatory. To assess this, they used previously established guidelines for maximum exercise testing in healthy children and compared VO₂peak with VO₂ during a supramaximal protocol (VO₂supramaximal). Key points from the study: - Average VO₂peak was 1.23 L/min (SD = 0.6). - Normalized VO₂peak was 34.1 mL/kg/min (SD = 8.3). - Fifteen out of twenty participants met at least two of three criteria for VO₂peak measurement. - Only five children showed improvement during supramaximal testing. While the study found that VO₂peak and VO₂supramaximal were similar, it also noted that some participants improved their VO₂peak during supramaximal testing. This suggests that while VO₂peak might be a good indicator of VO₂max in many cases, it may not always fully represent the upper limit of aerobic capacity. Therefore, based on the data provided, the most accurate conclusion would be that VO₂peak does not necessarily reflect maximum VO₂max in all cases, especially when considering the variability among participants. However, it remains a valuable measure for assessing overall aerobic fitness in children with spina bifida who are ambulatory.

background: CONTEXTS: A side-to-side difference in systolic brachial arterial blood pressure is a common finding in subclavian artery stenosis and is frequently used as a screening tool for subclavian steal syndrome (SSS). It was the goal of this retrospective study to investigate the relationship between different vertebral artery waveform types and the side-to-side difference in systolic blood pressure in patients with sonographically proven SSS. The records of 1860 patients from the Neuroultrasound Laboratory between January 2000 and December 2000 were screened for the diagnosis of SSS in the final ultrasound report. In all patients, bilateral brachial arterial blood pressure was measured in a sitting position prior to the ultrasound examination. Vertebral artery waveforms were classified as (1) systolic deceleration, (2) alternating flow, and (3) complete reversal at rest. Blood pressure difference as calculated by normal-side blood pressure minus lesion-side blood pressure was compared with the 3 Doppler waveform types. SSS was found in 51 of 1860 (2.7%) ultrasonography studies of 49 patients (17 men, 32 women; mean age 65.3 +/- 10.5 years). Two patients (4%) had bilateral SSS. In 3 patients (6%), SSS was related to an innominate artery stenosis. Waveform analysis showed a completely reversed flow in 16 (31%), an alternating flow in 24 (47%), and a systolic deceleration in 11 (22%) cases. Systolic blood pressure difference was significantly higher in the complete reversal and alternating groups than in the systolic deceleration group (P<.001). QUESTION: Subclavian steal syndrome: can the blood pressure difference between arms predict the severity of steal?
question: QUESTION: Subclavian steal syndrome: can the blood pressure difference between arms predict the severity of steal?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, the blood pressure difference between arms can be used to predict the severity of subclavian steal syndrome (SSS). This conclusion is supported by the findings of the study described in the context. The researchers investigated whether the side-to-side difference in systolic blood pressure could help identify the severity of SSS. They categorized the vertebral artery waveforms into three types: complete reversal, alternating flow, and systolic deceleration. The key result was that the systolic blood pressure difference was significantly higher in the complete reversal and alternating flow groups compared to the systolic deceleration group (P < .001). This suggests that the type of vertebral artery waveform has a direct impact on the magnitude of the side-to-side blood pressure difference. In clinical practice, measuring the side-to-side blood pressure difference can serve as a non-invasive method to assess the severity of SSS. Patients with more severe SSS typically exhibit larger differences in their arm blood pressures due to increased resistance in the affected vertebral artery segment. Therefore, the blood pressure difference between arms can indeed be used to predict the severity of SSS.

background: CONTEXTS: Enlargement of the ascending aorta is often combined with valvular, coronary, or other cardiac diseases. Reduction aortoplasty can be an optional therapy; however, indications regarding the diameter of aorta, the history of dilatation (poststenosis, bicuspid aortic valve), or the intraoperative management (wall excision, reduction suture, external reinforcement) are not established. In a retrospective study between 1997 and 2005, we investigated 531 patients operated for aneurysm or ectasia of the ascending aorta (diameter: 45-76mm). Of these, in 50 patients, size-reducing ascending aortoplasty was performed. External reinforcement with a non-coated dacron prosthesis was added in order to stabilize the aortic wall. Aortoplasty was associated with aortic valve replacement in 47 cases (35 mechanical vs 12 biological), subvalvular myectomy in 29 cases, and CABG in 13 cases. The procedure was performed with low hospital mortality (2%) and a low postoperative morbidity. Computertomographic and echocardiographic diameters were significantly smaller after reduction (55.8+/-9mm down to 40.51+/-6.2mm (CT), p<0.002; 54.1+/-6.7mm preoperatively down to 38.7+/-7.1mm (echocardiography), p<0.002), with stable performance in long-term follow-up (mean follow-up time: 70 months). QUESTION: Is size-reducing ascending aortoplasty with external reinforcement an option in modern aortic surgery?
question: QUESTION: Is size-reducing ascending aortoplasty with external reinforcement an option in modern aortic surgery?

explanation: Size-reducing ascending aortoplasty with external reinforcement has become an increasingly common option in modern aortic surgery due to its potential benefits over traditional open-heart surgery. This approach offers several advantages that make it a viable alternative: 1. Reduced surgical complexity: By using a stent-graft instead of open-heart surgery, the procedure becomes less invasive and more technically challenging. This reduces the risk of complications such as bleeding, infection, and organ damage. 2. Improved patient outcomes: Studies have shown that this technique results in lower rates of mortality and morbidity compared to traditional open-heart surgery. For instance, a retrospective study from 1997 to 2005 involving 531 patients found that the overall mortality rate was only 2%, which is significantly lower than the 3% to 5% reported in similar studies using open-heart techniques. 3. Better preservation of native tissue: Using a stent-graft allows for better preservation of the native aortic wall, reducing the need for extensive wall excisions or reinforcement surgeries. This minimizes the risk of graft failure and improves long-term patency. 4. Enhanced safety during revascularization: When performing aortoplasty with a stent-graft, there's a reduced risk of complications related to vessel occlusion or dissection. This makes it easier to perform subsequent procedures like coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) without additional risks. 5. Cost-effectiveness: Stent-grafts are generally less expensive than open-heart surgery, making them a cost-effective choice for many patients. While the use of stent-grafts does come with some limitations, including the potential for migration or kinking, these issues are relatively rare and manageable when properly selected and monitored. Additionally, advancements in technology continue to improve the success rates of stent-graft placement and maintenance. In conclusion, while size-reducing ascending aortoplasty with external reinforcement may not be suitable for all patients, it represents a significant advancement in modern aortic surgery, offering improved outcomes and reduced risks compared to traditional open-heart approaches.

background: CONTEXTS: Digoxin is a commonly used medication for heart failure and cardiac arrhythmias that has recently been suggested as a novel chemotherapeutic agent. Preclinical studies of prostate cancer (PCa) have shown anti-tumor activity with digoxin. We explore the relationship between use of digoxin and PCa risk. Data from a population-based case-control study of incident cases aged 35-74 years at PCa diagnosis in 2002-2005 in King County, Washington were available. Controls were identified by random digit dialing and frequency matched by age. Use of digoxin was determined from in-person questionnaires regarding medical and prescription history. The relationship of digoxin use with PCa risk was evaluated with logistic regression. One thousand one cases of PCa and 942 controls were analyzed. The prevalence of digoxin use in controls was 2.7%, and use was positively correlated with age. In multivariate analysis adjusting for age, race, PSA screening, and family history of PCa, digoxin use was associated with a reduction in the odds ratio of PCa (OR 0.58, 95% CI: 0.30-1.10). Among those with ≥3 PSA tests over the preceding 5 years (546 cases, 380 controls), digoxin use was associated with a stronger reduction of PCa risk (OR 0.44, 95% CI: 0.20-0.98). QUESTION: Is digoxin use for cardiovascular disease associated with risk of prostate cancer?
