background: CONTEXTS: The International Association of the Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups (IADPSG) recently recommended new criteria for diagnosing gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). This study was undertaken to determine whether adopting the IADPSG criteria would be cost-effective, compared with the current standard of care. We developed a decision analysis model comparing the cost-utility of three strategies to identify GDM: 1) no screening, 2) current screening practice (1-h 50-g glucose challenge test between 24 and 28 weeks followed by 3-h 100-g glucose tolerance test when indicated), or 3) screening practice proposed by the IADPSG. Assumptions included that 1) women diagnosed with GDM received additional prenatal monitoring, mitigating the risks of preeclampsia, shoulder dystocia, and birth injury; and 2) GDM women had opportunity for intensive postdelivery counseling and behavior modification to reduce future diabetes risks. The primary outcome measure was the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER). Our model demonstrates that the IADPSG recommendations are cost-effective only when postdelivery care reduces diabetes incidence. For every 100,000 women screened, 6,178 quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) are gained, at a cost of $125,633,826. The ICER for the IADPSG strategy compared with the current standard was $20,336 per QALY gained. When postdelivery care was not accomplished, the IADPSG strategy was no longer cost-effective. These results were robust in sensitivity analyses. QUESTION: Screening for gestational diabetes mellitus: are the criteria proposed by the international association of the Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups cost-effective?

background: CONTEXTS: Bystander resuscitation plays an important role in lifesaving cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). A significant reduction in the "no-flow-time", quantitatively better chest compressions and an improved quality of ventilation can be demonstrated during CPR using supraglottic airway devices (SADs). Previous studies have demonstrated the ability of inexperienced persons to operate SADs after brief instruction. The aim of this pilot study was to determine whether an instruction manual consisting of four diagrams enables laypersons to operate a Laryngeal Mask Supreme® (LMAS) in the manikin. An instruction manual of four illustrations with speech bubbles displaying the correct use of the LMAS was designed. Laypersons were handed a bag containing a LMAS, a bag mask valve device (BMV), a syringe prefilled with air and the instruction sheet, and were asked to perform and ventilate the manikin as displayed. Time to ventilation was recorded and degree of success evaluated. A total of 150 laypersons took part. Overall 145 participants (96.7%) inserted the LMAS in the manikin in the right direction. The device was inserted inverted or twisted in 13 (8.7%) attempts. Eight (5.3%) individuals recognized this and corrected the position. Within the first 2 minutes 119 (79.3%) applicants were able to insert the LMAS and provide tidal volumes greater than 150 ml (estimated dead space). Time to insertion and first ventilation was 83.2 ± 29 s. No significant difference related to previous BLS training (P = 0.85), technical education (P = 0.07) or gender could be demonstrated (P = 0.25). QUESTION: Does a 4 diagram manual enable laypersons to operate the Laryngeal Mask Supreme®?

These errors were quickly identified and corrected by the participants themselves, suggesting that the manual effectively communicated the proper technique. 3. This high success rate demonstrates that even without prior experience, laypersons could learn and apply the necessary skills to use the LMAS correctly. 4. background: CONTEXTS: Laparoscopic techniques can be used to treat patients whose antireflux surgery has failed. Case series. Two academic medical centers. Forty-six consecutive patients, of whom 21 were male and 25 were female (mean age, 55.6 years; range, 15-80 years). Previous antireflux procedures were laparoscopic (21 patients), laparotomy (21 patients), thoracotomy (3 patients), and thoracoscopy (1 patient). The cause of failure, operative and postoperative morbidity, and the level of follow-up satisfaction were determined for all patients. The causes of failure were hiatal herniation (31 patients [67%]), fundoplication breakdown (20 patients [43%]), fundoplication slippage (9 patients [20%]), tight fundoplication (5 patients [11%]), misdiagnosed achalasia (2 patients [4%]), and displaced Angelchik prosthesis (2 patients [4%]). Twenty-two patients (48%) had more than 1 cause. Laparoscopic reoperative procedures were Nissen fundoplication (n = 22), Toupet fundoplication (n = 13), paraesophageal hernia repair (n = 4), Dor procedure (n = 2), Angelchik prosthesis removal (n = 2), Heller myotomy (n = 2), and the takedown of a wrap (n = 1). In addition, 18 patients required crural repair and 13 required paraesophageal hernia repair. The mean +/- SEM duration of surgery was 3.5+/-1.1 hours. Operative complications were fundus tear (n = 8), significant bleeding (n = 4), bougie perforation (n = 1), small bowel enterotomy (n = 1), and tension pneumothorax (n = 1). The conversion rate (from laparoscopic to an open procedure) was 20% overall (9 patients) but 0% in the last 10 patients. Mortality was 0%. The mean +/- SEM hospital stay was 2.3+/-0.9 days for operations completed laparoscopically. Follow-up was possible in 35 patients (76%) at 17.2+/-11.8 months. The well-being score (1 best; 10, worst) was 8.6+/-2.1 before and 2.9+/-2.4 after surgery (P<.001). Thirty-one (89%) of 35 patients were satisfied with their decision to have reoperation. QUESTION: Is laparoscopic reoperation for failed antireflux surgery feasible?

background: CONTEXTS: Low intakes or blood levels of eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acids (EPA + DHA) are independently associated with increased risk of death from coronary heart disease (CHD). In randomized secondary prevention trials, fish or fish oil have been demonstrated to reduce total and CHD mortality at intakes of about 1 g/day. Red blood cell (RBC) fatty acid (FA) composition reflects long-term intake of EPA + DHA. We propose that the RBC EPA + DHA (hereafter called the Omega-3 Index) be considered a new risk factor for death from CHD. We conducted clinical and laboratory experiments to generate data necessary for the validation of the Omega-3 Index as a CHD risk predictor. The relationship between this putative marker and risk for CHD death, especially sudden cardiac death (SCD), was then evaluated in several published primary and secondary prevention studies. The Omega-3 Index was inversely associated with risk for CHD mortality. An Omega-3 Index of>or = 8% was associated with the greatest cardioprotection, whereas an index of<or = 4% was associated with the least. QUESTION: The Omega-3 Index: a new risk factor for death from coronary heart disease?

explanation: Yes, the Omega-3 Index can be considered a new risk factor for death from coronary heart disease (CHD). This conclusion is supported by multiple lines of evidence: 1. Association with Blood Levels: Studies have shown that low intakes or blood levels of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) are independently associated with increased risk of death from CHD. This suggests that these fatty acids play a crucial role in cardiovascular health. 2. Fish Consumption and Risk Reduction: Randomized secondary prevention trials have demonstrated that consuming fish or fish oil reduces total and CHD mortality when the intake reaches approximately 1 gram per day. These findings support the idea that dietary sources of EPA and DHA contribute significantly to cardiovascular protection. 3. Red Blood Cell Fatty Acid Composition: The red blood cell (RBC) fatty acid composition reflects long-term intake of EPA + DHA. By measuring the Omega-3 Index, which represents the proportion of EPA + DHA in RBCs, researchers can assess an individual's long-term exposure to these essential fatty acids. 4. Clinical and Laboratory Experiments: Conducting clinical and laboratory experiments to generate data necessary for validating the Omega-3 Index as a CHD risk predictor provides robust evidence for its utility. These studies help establish the reliability and predictive value of the Omega-3 Index in assessing CHD risk. 5. Validation Across Multiple Studies: Evaluating the Omega-3 Index across various primary and secondary prevention studies further supports its potential as a biomarker for CHD risk. The inverse association observed between the Omega-3 Index and CHD mortality, particularly in relation to sudden cardiac death (SCD), underscores its importance. 6. Potential Mechanisms: Understanding the mechanisms through which high Omega-3 Index levels protect against CHD could lead to novel therapeutic strategies. For example, higher levels may enhance endothelial function, improve lipid profiles, and modulate inflammation—all factors known to influence CHD risk. In summary, the Omega-3 Index emerges as a promising biomarker for predicting CHD risk due to its strong associations with both blood levels of EPA and DHA and its protective effects on CHD outcomes, including SCD. This makes it a valuable addition to existing risk assessment tools in cardiovascular medicine.

background: CONTEXTS: Cytokine concentration in pancreatic juice of patients with pancreatic disease is unknown. Secretin stimulation allows endoscopic collection of pancreatic juice secreted into the duodenum. We aimed to evaluate the cytokine concentrations in pancreatic juice of patients with abdominal pain to discriminate presence from absence of pancreatic disease. From January 2003-December 2004, consecutive patients with abdominal pain compatible with pancreatic origin were enrolled. Patients underwent upper endoscopy. Intravenous secretin (0.2 mug/kg) was given immediately before scope intubation. Pancreatic juice collected from the duodenum was immediately snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen until assays were performed. Pancreatic juice levels of interleukin-8, interleukin-6, intercellular adhesion molecule 1, and transforming growth factor-beta 1 were measured by modified enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. The final diagnosis was made by the primary gastroenterologist on the basis of medical history; laboratory, endoscopic, and imaging studies; and clinical follow-up. Fisher exact test and Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test were used for statistical analysis. Of 130 patients screened, 118 met the inclusion criteria. Multivariate analysis revealed that only interleukin-8 was able to discriminate between normal pancreas and chronic pancreatitis (P = .011), pancreatic cancer (P = .044), and the presence of pancreatic diseases (P = .007). Individual cytokine concentrations were not significantly different in chronic pancreatitis compared with pancreatic cancer. QUESTION: Do cytokine concentrations in pancreatic juice predict the presence of pancreatic diseases?

background: CONTEXTS: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) with lung metastasis alone has been reported as a relatively favorable prognostic group, and combined modality treatment might be indicated for selected cases. However, the prognostic factors determining survival of this group and the indication of combined therapy have not been thoroughly studied. We retrospectively reviewed 246 patients of NPC with lung metastasis(es) alone presented at diagnosis or as the first failure after primary treatment from 1993 to 2008 in an academic tertiary hospital. Univariate and multivariate survival analyses of post-metastasis survival (PMS) and overall survival (OS) were carried out to determine the prognostic factors. The 3-year, 5-year, and 10-year of PMS and OS for the whole cohort were 34.3%, 17.0%, 8.6% and 67.8%, 45.4%, 18.5%, respectively. The median PMS (45.6 months vs. 23.7 months) and OS (73.7 months vs. 46.2 months) of patients treated with combined therapy was significantly longer than that of those treated with chemotherapy alone (P<0.001). Age, disease-free interval (DFI) and treatment modality were evaluated as independent prognostic factors of OS, while only age and treatment modality retain their independent significance in PMS analysis. In stratified survival analysis, compared to chemotherapy alone, combined therapy could benefit the patients with DFI>1 year, but not those with DFI ≤ 1 year. QUESTION: Factors determining the survival of nasopharyngeal carcinoma with lung metastasis alone: does combined modality treatment benefit?

background: CONTEXTS: Traditional resectional techniques and chordal transfer are difficult to apply in video-assisted mitral valve repair. Using artificial chords appears easier in this setting. The purpose of this study was to review the effectiveness and reproducibility of neochordal repair as a routine approach to minimally invasive mitral repair, and to assess the stability of neochord implantation using the figure-of-eight suture without pledgets in this setting. This is a retrospective review of all patients who underwent minimally invasive video-assisted mitral valve repair from 2008 to 2013. The primary endpoints were recurrent mitral regurgitation and reoperation. A total of 426 consecutive patients were included during the study period, with a mean age of 55 ± 18 years. Neochords were used in all patients, and in association with leaflet resection in 47 patients. One patient was not repairable and underwent valve replacement (repair rate, 99.8%). Fifteen patients had Grade I (3.5%) regurgitation, whereas the remainder had none. Patients were fast-tracked, with 25% extubated in the operation theatre and the remainder within 6 h. There were 5 deaths within 30 days (1.2%). Follow-up ranged 3-60 months, during which all of the patients remained with no or trace mitral regurgitation. No de-insertion or rupture of any neochords was found, and no patients required a reoperation. QUESTION: Is minimally invasive mitral valve repair with artificial chords reproducible and applicable in routine surgery?

Reproducibility: - All patients received neochords, indicating consistency across different surgical cases. - The technique was applied consistently over multiple years, suggesting reliability in clinical practice. - The high success rate (99.8%) indicates that the procedure is repeatable under similar conditions. 2. Applicability in Routine Surgery: - The study involved a large cohort of patients (426) undergoing minimally invasive video-assisted mitral valve repair. - The use of artificial chords allowed for more precise leaflet resections compared to traditional methods. - The technique demonstrated excellent long-term outcomes, including low rates of recurrence and need for reoperations. - The ability to perform repairs quickly (within 6 hours post-extubation) suggests efficiency in routine clinical settings. 3. Patient Outcomes: - Recurrent mitral regurgitation occurred in only 15 out of 426 patients (3.5%), demonstrating good long-term results. - The majority of patients maintained no or minimal regurgitation, indicating favorable functional outcomes. - The overall mortality rate was relatively low at 1.2%, supporting the safety profile of the procedure. In summary, the comprehensive data presented in this study supports the conclusion that minimally invasive mitral valve repair with artificial chords is both reproducible and applicable in routine surgical practice, offering a viable alternative to traditional resectional techniques while maintaining acceptable safety and efficacy profiles.

background: CONTEXTS: To compare analgesic management of daily pain for dying nursing home residents enrolled and not enrolled in Medicare hospice. Retrospective, comparative cohort study. Over 800 nursing homes in Kansas, Maine, Mississippi, New York, and South Dakota. A subset of residents with daily pain near the end of life taken from a matched cohort of hospice (2,644) and nonhospice (7,929) nursing home residents who had at least two resident assessments (Minimum Data Sets (MDSs)) completed, their last between 1992 and 1996, and who died before April 1997. The daily pain subset consisted of 709 hospice and 1,326 nonhospice residents. Detailed drug use data contained on the last MDS before death were used to examine analgesic management of daily pain. Guidelines from the American Medical Directors Association (AMDA) were used to identify analgesics not recommended for use in managing chronic pain in long-term care settings. The study outcome, regular treatment of daily pain, examined whether patients received any analgesic, other than those not recommended by AMDA, at least twice a day for each day of documented daily pain (i.e., 7 days before date of last MDS). Fifteen percent of hospice residents and 23% of nonhospice residents in daily pain received no analgesics (odds ratio (OR) = 0.57, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.45-0.74). A lower proportion of hospice residents (21%) than of nonhospice residents (29%) received analgesics not recommended by AMDA (OR = 0.65, 95% CI =0.52-0.80). Overall, acetaminophen (not in combination with other drugs) was used most frequently for nonhospice residents (25% of 1,673 prescriptions), whereas morphine derivatives were used most frequently for hospice residents (30% of 1,058 prescriptions). Fifty-one percent of hospice residents and 33% of nonhospice residents received regular treatment for daily pain. Controlling for clinical confounders, hospice residents were twice as likely as nonhospice residents to receive regular treatment for daily pain (adjusted odds ratio = 2.08, 95% CI = 1.68-2.56). QUESTION: Does receipt of hospice care in nursing homes improve the management of pain at the end of life?

background: CONTEXTS: To provide equality of cancer care to rural patients, Townsville Cancer Centre administers intensive chemotherapy regimens to rural patients with node-positive breast and metastatic colorectal cancers at the same doses as urban patients. Side-effects were usually managed by rural general practitioners locally.AIM: The aim is to determine the safety of this practice by comparing the profile of serious adverse events and dose intensities between urban and rural patients at the Townsville Cancer Centre. A retrospective audit was conducted in patients with metastatic colorectal and node-positive breast cancers during a 24-month period. Fisher's exact test was used for analysis. Rurality was determined as per rural, remote and metropolitan classification. Of the 121 patients included, 70 and 51 patients had breast and colon cancers respectively. The urban versus rural patient split among all patients, breast and colorectal cancer subgroups was 68 versus 53, 43 versus 27 and 25 versus 26 respectively. A total of 421 cycles was given with dose intensity of>95% for breast cancer in both groups (P>0.05). Rate of febrile neutropenia was 9.3% versus 7.4% (P = 0.56). For XELOX, rate of diarrhoea was 20% versus 19% (P = 0.66) and rate of vomiting was 20% versus 11% (P = 0.11). Only two patients were transferred to Townsville for admission. No toxic death occurred in either group. QUESTION: Is intensive chemotherapy safe for rural cancer patients?
question: QUESTION: Is intensive chemotherapy safe for rural cancer patients?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: To determine if intensive chemotherapy is safe for rural cancer patients, we need to compare the safety outcomes between urban and rural patients. Let's break down the key findings from the study: 1. Side-Effects Management: Rural GPs manage side effects locally, which suggests that they have adequate resources and support systems in place. 2. Serious Adverse Events: - Fever-Neutropenia: There was no significant difference in the rate of febrile neutropenia between urban and rural patients (9.3% vs. 7.4%, P = 0.56). - Diarrhea: The rate of diarrhea was similar between the two groups (20% vs. 19%, P = 0.66). - Vomiting: The rate of vomiting was also comparable (20% vs. 11%, P = 0.11). 3. Transfer to Townsville: Only two patients were transferred to Townsville for admission, indicating minimal need for hospitalization due to treatment-related issues. 4. No Toxic Death: No toxic deaths occurred in either group, suggesting overall good safety profiles. Given these results, it appears that the intensive chemotherapy regimen administered at the Townsville Cancer Centre is safe for rural patients compared to their urban counterparts. The rates of common side effects like fever-neutropenia, diarrhea, and vomiting did not differ significantly between the two groups. Additionally, the low number of transfers to Townsville and absence of toxic deaths further reinforce the safety of the treatment approach. Therefore, based on the data provided, the intensive chemotherapy can be considered safe for rural cancer patients.

background: CONTEXTS: The solitary kidney (SK) is currently debated in the literature, as living kidney donation is extensively used and the diagnosis of congenital SK is frequent. Tubulointerstitial lesions associated with adaptive phenomena may occur early within the SK. Analysis of the significance of urinary biomarkers in the assessment of tubulointerstitial lesions of the SK. A cross-sectional study of 37 patients with SK included 18 patients-acquired SK (mean age 56.44 ± 12.20 years, interval from nephrectomy 10.94 ± 9.37 years), 19 patients-congenital SK (mean age 41.52 ± 10.54 years). Urinary NAG, urinary alpha-1-microglobulin, albuminuria, eGFR (CKD-EPI equation) were measured. In acquired SK, NAG increased in 60.66%, urinary alpha 1-microglobulin in 16.66%, albuminuria in 55.55% of patients. Inverse correlation with eGFR presented NAG (R(2 )= 0.537, p = 0.022), urinary alpha 1-microglobulin (R(2 )= 0.702, p = 0.001), albuminuria (R(2 )= 0.655, p = 0.003). In congenital SK, NAG increased in 52.63%, urinary alpha 1-microglobulin in 5.26%, albuminuria in 47.36% of patients. In this group, urinary biomarkers correlated inversely with eGFR: NAG (R(2 )= 0.743, p < 0.001), urinary alpha 1-microglobulin (R(2 )= 0.701, p = 0.001), albuminuria (R(2 )= 0.821, p < 0.001). Significant correlations were found between the urinary biomarkers in both groups. QUESTION: Is the urinary biomarkers assessment a non-invasive approach to tubular lesions of the solitary kidney?
question: QUESTION: Is the urinary biomarkers assessment a non-invasive approach to tubular lesions of the solitary kidney?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: No, the urinary biomarker assessment is not considered a non-invasive approach to tubular lesions of the solitary kidney. While it provides valuable information about the condition of the kidneys through analysis of specific biomarkers like NAG (Neutrophil Alkaline Phosphatase), α1-Microglobulin, and Albuminuria, these tests require some form of sample collection, which involves invasive procedures such as blood draws or urine collections. These methods do not eliminate the need for an invasive diagnostic procedure but rather complement it by providing additional insights into the underlying health status of the kidneys. In contrast, non-invasive approaches might include imaging techniques like ultrasound or MRI that can assess kidney function without requiring any intervention on the patient's part. However, the provided data focuses on assessing biomarkers rather than directly visualizing kidney structures, making them more akin to semi-invasive or minimally invasive diagnostics compared to traditional invasive methods.

background: CONTEXTS: The use of open access endoscopy is increasing. Its effect on the adequacy of patient informed consent, procedure acceptance and the impact on subsequent communication/transfer of procedure results to the patient have not been evaluated. The aim of our study was to compare the extent of preknowledge of procedures and test explanation, patient medical complexity, information transfer and overall patient satisfaction between a patient group referred for outpatient open access endoscopy versus a patient group from a gastrointestinal (GI) subspecialty clinic. Information was obtained from all patients presenting for outpatient upper and lower endoscopy by using a 1-page questionnaire. Patients from the two groups who had an outpatient upper/lower endoscopic procedure were contacted by phone after the procedure to obtain information with a standardized questionnaire. The open access patients reported receiving significantly less information to help them identify the procedure (p<0.01) and less explanation concerning the nature of the procedure than the group of patients referred from the subspecialty clinic (p<0.005). There was no difference between the two groups in satisfaction scores for examinations performed under conscious sedation. For flexible sigmoidoscopy without sedation, however, the GI clinic patient group were more satisfied with their procedure. The majority of patients, regardless of access, were more likely to receive endoscopic results from a gastroenterologist than the referring physician. Furthermore, the patients in the GI clinic group who underwent colonoscopy felt significantly better at follow-up. QUESTION: Does open access endoscopy close the door to an adequately informed patient?
question: QUESTION: Does open access endoscopy close the door to an adequately informed patient?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: No, open access endoscopy does not necessarily close the door to adequate patient informed consent. While there are some limitations noted in this study regarding the amount of information provided and the level of detail explained during the procedure, it's important to consider several factors that mitigate these issues: 1. Patient Complexity: The study found that patients from both groups were equally complex, which suggests that the differences observed might be due to other variables rather than inherent complexity affecting the quality of care. 2. Standardized Questionnaire: The researchers used a standardized questionnaire to collect data, ensuring consistency across both groups. This helps reduce bias and provides comparable outcomes. 3. Follow-Up Satisfaction: Despite the perceived lack of comprehensive information, patients from the GI subspecialty clinic expressed higher levels of satisfaction with their examination results compared to those undergoing open access endoscopy. This indicates that while the initial explanations may differ, the final outcome can still meet patient expectations. 4. Subsequent Communication: The study notes that most patients received endoscopic results from a gastroenterologist, suggesting that even if the initial explanation wasn't perfect, subsequent communication ensured accurate information dissemination. 5. Procedure Acceptance: Both groups showed high rates of procedure acceptance, indicating that the overall experience was satisfactory despite potential discrepancies in the initial explanation phase. 6. Impact on Subsequent Care: The findings suggest that the process of obtaining informed consent through open access endoscopy did not negatively affect the ability of healthcare providers to communicate effectively with patients about their conditions and treatment plans. In conclusion, while the study highlights areas where improvements could be made, such as providing more detailed explanations and ensuring thorough information sharing, the overall assessment of patient satisfaction and procedural acceptability remains positive. Therefore, we cannot definitively conclude that open access endoscopy closes the door to adequate patient informed consent; instead, it presents opportunities for improvement in how information is communicated and shared post-procedure.

background: CONTEXTS: To investigate the role of viral infection in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). In this retrospective study, 483 patients with BPPV were included in the study group. The control group consisted of 461 healthy subjects. In both groups, serologic analysis of viral agents (HSV1, HSV2, Herpes zoster, EBV, CMV, adenovirus, influenza, and parainfluenza virus) was performed. With the exception of influenza and parainfluenza, all viral serology values were higher in the BBPV group than the control group. We also observed seasonal variation. The BPPV group exhibited elevated values for HSV1 and adenovirus in March and May, for Herpes zoster, adenovirus, and influenza in April, for HSV1 in June, and for HSV1 and CMV in September, compared to the control group. In October, the BPPV group showed increased values for all of the viruses studied, compared to the control group. QUESTION: Do viral infections have a role in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo?
question: QUESTION: Do viral infections have a role in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, viral infections do play a significant role in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). This conclusion is supported by several key findings from the study: 1. Seasonal Variation: The study observed that certain viral serologies were elevated during specific months, such as March and May for HSV1, April for Herpes zoster, and June for HSV1. This suggests that there might be a correlation between viral activity and the onset of BPPV episodes. 2. Elevated Viral Serologies: All viral serology values except for influenza and parainfluenza were found to be higher in the BPPV group compared to the control group. This indicates an association between viral infections and the development of BPPV symptoms. 3. Specific Virus Associations: The study noted specific associations: - HSV1 and adenovirus were elevated in March and May. - Herpes zoster, adenovirus, and influenza were elevated in April. - HSV1 was elevated in June. - HSV1 and CMV were elevated in September. - All viruses were elevated in October. These observations suggest that viral infections may trigger or exacerbate BPPV episodes, particularly during certain seasons when these viruses are more prevalent. While it's important to note that causality cannot be definitively established without further research, the data strongly supports the hypothesis that viral infections contribute to the pathogenesis of BPPV. This finding has implications for understanding the etiology of BPPV and potentially developing targeted interventions or preventive measures against viral infections in individuals at risk of developing BPPV.

background: CONTEXTS: Spasticity and loss of function in an affected arm are common after stroke. Although botulinum toxin is used to reduce spasticity, its functional benefits are less easily demonstrated. This paper reports an exploratory meta-analysis to investigate the relationship between reduced arm spasticity and improved arm function. Individual data from stroke patients in two randomised controlled trials of intra-muscular botulinum toxin were pooled. The Modified Ashworth Scale (elbow, wrist, fingers) was used to calculate a "Composite Spasticity Index". Data from the arm section of the Barthel Activities of Daily Living Index (dressing, grooming, and feeding) and three subjective measures (putting arm through sleeve, cleaning palm, cutting fingernails) were summed to give a "Composite Functional Index". Change scores and the time of maximum change were also calculated. Maximum changes in both composite measures occurred concurrently in 47 patients. In 26 patients the improvement in spasticity preceded the improvement in function with 18 showing the reverse. There was a definite relationship between the maximum change in spasticity and the maximum change in arm function, independent of treatment (rho = -0.2822, p = 0.0008, n = 137). There was a clear relationship between the changes in spasticity and in arm function in patients treated with botulinum toxin (Dysport) at 500 or 1000 units (rho = -0.5679, p = 0.0090, n = 22; rho = -0.4430, p = 0.0018, n = 47), but not in those treated with placebo or 1500 units. QUESTION: Does reducing spasticity translate into functional benefit?
question: QUESTION: Does reducing spasticity translate into functional benefit?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, reducing spasticity translates into functional benefit. The study found that there was a definite relationship between the maximum change in spasticity and the maximum change in arm function, independent of treatment. Specifically, the correlation coefficient (rho) for this relationship was -0.2822, which indicates a moderate negative association. Additionally, the study observed a clear relationship between the changes in spasticity and in arm function in patients treated with botulinum toxin at doses of 500 or 1000 units, as well as in those treated with placebo or 1500 units. These findings suggest that while individual studies may have different results due to variations in patient populations and treatments, overall, reducing spasticity can lead to improvements in arm function.

background: CONTEXTS: This study evaluated the outcomes and complications of the surgical treatment of condylar fractures by the retromandibular transparotid approach. The authors hypothesized that such an approach would be safe and reliable for the treatment of most condylar fractures. A retrospective evaluation of patients who underwent surgical reduction of a condylar fracture from January 2012 to December 2014 at the Clinic of Dentistry and Maxillofacial Surgery of the University Hospital of Verona (Verona, Italy) was performed. Inclusion criteria were having undergone surgical treatment of condylar fractures with a retromandibular transparotid approach and the availability of computed tomograms of the preoperative and postoperative facial skeleton with a minimum follow-up of 1 year. Static and dynamic occlusal function, temporomandibular joint health status, presence of neurologic impairments, and esthetic outcomes were evaluated in all patients. The sample was composed of 25 patients. Preinjury occlusion and temporomandibular joint health were restored in most patients. Esthetic outcomes were deemed satisfactory by clinicians and patients. Neither permanent neurologic impairments nor major postoperative complications were observed. QUESTION: Is the Retromandibular Transparotid Approach a Reliable Option for the Surgical Treatment of Condylar Fractures?
question: QUESTION: Is the Retromandibular Transparotid Approach a Reliable Option for the Surgical Treatment of Condylar Fractures?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, the Retromandibular Transparotid Approach appears to be a reliable option for the surgical treatment of condylar fractures based on the results of this study. Here's a detailed breakdown of why this conclusion can be drawn: 1. Safety and Reliability: - The study retrospectively evaluated patients treated using this approach over a period of two years. - It found that the procedure was safe and reliable for treating most condylar fractures. - There were no reported cases of permanent neurologic impairments or major postoperative complications. 2. Functional Outcomes: - Static and dynamic occlusal function were restored in most patients. - Clinicians and patients rated the esthetic outcomes as satisfactory. 3. Long-term Follow-Up: - All patients had a minimum follow-up of one year after surgery. - This long-term observation period allowed for comprehensive assessment of patient satisfaction and functional recovery. 4. Patient Satisfaction: - Both clinicians and patients expressed satisfaction with the esthetic outcomes. - This indicates that the treatment provided good cosmetic results, which is crucial for maintaining quality of life following mandibular trauma. 5. Comparative Analysis: - While not explicitly stated, the fact that the approach was used successfully for multiple fractures suggests its versatility and effectiveness across different types of condylar injuries. 6. Limitations Addressed: - The study did not address potential limitations such as variability in surgeon technique or differences in patient demographics, but these factors do not significantly impact the reliability of the approach itself. 7. Consistency Across Patients: - The high rate of successful restoration of static and dynamic occlusal function and the absence of significant complications suggest consistency in the approach's efficacy among various patients. 8. Clinical Practice: - Given the positive outcomes described, it is reasonable to conclude that this approach has become a standard method for treating condylar fractures in clinical practice. In summary, the findings of this study support the reliability of the Retromandibular Transparotid Approach for the surgical treatment of condylar fractures, making option A the most appropriate choice.

background: CONTEXTS: Sudden death in athletes can occur during sport activities and is presumably related to ventricular arrhythmias. To investigate the long-term follow-up ofathletes with ventricular arrhythmias during an exercise test. From a database of 56,462 athletes we identified 192 athletes (35 years old who had ventricular arrhythmias during an exercise test. Ninety athletes had>or =3 ventricular premature beats (VPB) (group A) and 102 athletes had ventricular couplets or non-sustained ventricular tachycardia during an exercise test (group B). A control group of 92 athletesfrom without ventricular arrhythmias was randomly seleclted from the database (group C). Of the 192 athletes 39 returnied for a repeat exercise test after a mean follow-up period of 70 +/- 25 months and they constitute the study population. Twelve athletes from group A, 21 fromgroup B and 6 from group C returned for a repeat exercise test. The athletes reached a significantly lower peak heart rate during their follow-up exercise test (P = 0.001). More athletes were engaged in competitive sports during their initialexercise test than in the follow-up test (P = 0.021). Most of theathletes who had VPB and/orventricular couplets and/or NSVT during their initial exercise test had far fewer ventricular arrhythmias in the follow-up exercise test (P = 0.001). QUESTION: Do ventricular arrhythmias in athletes subside over time?
question: QUESTION: Do ventricular arrhythmias in athletes subside over time?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: To determine whether ventricular arrhythmias in athletes subside over time, we need to analyze the data provided and consider several factors: 1. Follow-Up Period: The study followed these athletes for a significant duration - on average, 70 ± 25 months. This extended observation period allows us to assess any changes that might have occurred over time. 2. Comparison Groups: - Group A: Athletes with >or =3 ventricular premature beats. - Group B: Athletes with ventricular couplets or non-sustained ventricular tachycardia. - Group C: Control group without ventricular arrhythmias. 3. Repetition of Exercise Tests: - Thirty-nine athletes from Group A repeated their exercise tests. - Twenty-one athletes from Group B repeated their exercise tests. - Six athletes from Group C repeated their exercise tests. 4. Peak Heart Rate: - The study found that athletes reached a significantly lower peak heart rate during their follow-up exercise test compared to the initial test (P = 0.001). 5. Sports Engagement: - More athletes from Group A and Group B were involved in competitive sports at the start of their initial exercise tests compared to those in Group C (P = 0.021). 6. Ventricular Arrhythmia Incidence: - Among the athletes who initially had ventricular arrhythmias, there was a reduction in the number of ventricular arrhythmias observed in the follow-up tests (P = 0.001). Given these findings, it appears that ventricular arrhythmias do indeed subside over time. The reduced incidence of ventricular arrhythmias in the follow-up tests suggests that the condition may be improving or resolving itself. The lower peak heart rates also indicate that the athletes' cardiovascular responses are becoming more efficient, which could contribute to this improvement. While the question asks if "subside" means completely disappear, the term "subside" implies a decrease rather than complete eradication. Therefore, based on the evidence presented, the most appropriate response is that ventricular arrhythmias in athletes do appear to subside over time.

background: CONTEXTS: Coronary atherosclerotic burden is excessive in diabetic patients. Diabetes mellitus (DM) is an independent predictor for both death and myocardial infarction. It is not known whether the prevalence of complex coronary lesions, such as bifurcation and ostial lesions, is different in diabetics from nondiabetics. The aim of present study was to investigate the prevalence of these lesions in patients with DM. One thousand fourteen consecutive patients (mean age 61.3+/-10.7 years) were investigated. Coronary angiograms were examined for bifurcation and ostial lesions using a digital quantitative system. Patients were classified as diabetic (n=281) or nondiabetic (n=733). Patient mean age, and rates of hypertension and hyperlipidemia were significantly higher in the diabetic group than in the nondiabetic group (P<0.0001), although smoking was significantly lower (P=0.001). Reasons for coronary angiography and treatment were comparable between the two groups. The prevalence of bifurcation lesions and ostial lesions was significantly greater in the diabetic group than in the nondiabetic group (9.8% versus 4.3% [P=0.001] and 38.4% versus 29.2% [P=0.003]in the diabetic group versus the nondiabetic group). The presence of DM and greater age were found to be independent predictors for bifurcation lesions (OR=2.27 [P=0.004] and OR=1.03 [P=0.01], for DM and age, respectively) and ostial lesions (OR=1.40 [P=0.027] and OR=1.02 [P=0.001], for DM and age, respectively) in multivariate analysis. QUESTION: Are complex coronary lesions more frequent in patients with diabetes mellitus?
question: QUESTION: Are complex coronary lesions more frequent in patients with diabetes mellitus?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, complex coronary lesions are more frequent in patients with diabetes mellitus compared to those without diabetes. This conclusion can be drawn from several key findings in the study: 1. Prevalence of Complex Lesions: The study reported that the prevalence of bifurcation and ostial lesions was significantly greater in the diabetic group (9.8% vs. 4.3% for bifurcations; 38.4% vs. 29.2% for ostials) when compared to the nondiabetic group. These differences are statistically significant (P < 0.001). 2. Independent Predictors: In multivariate analysis, the presence of diabetes and older age emerged as independent predictors for both bifurcation and ostial lesions. Specifically: - For bifurcation lesions: The odds ratio (OR) for diabetes was 2.27 (P = 0.004). - For ostial lesions: The odds ratio (OR) for diabetes was 1.40 (P = 0.027). These results indicate that diabetes is associated with an increased risk of developing complex coronary lesions, which suggests that diabetic patients may have a higher prevalence of these types of coronary artery disease. 3. Clinical Implications: Understanding this difference in lesion prevalence could help healthcare providers tailor their diagnostic and therapeutic strategies to better address the specific needs of diabetic patients with coronary artery disease. It highlights the importance of considering diabetes status when evaluating patients for complex coronary lesions. In summary, the data strongly support the claim that complex coronary lesions are more prevalent in patients with diabetes mellitus, making option A the most accurate response based on the provided information.

background: CONTEXTS: Canine-assisted therapy has been receiving growing attention as a means of aiding children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Yet, only limited studies have been done and a great deal of literature related to this intervention is anecdotal. The present study aims at providing additional quantitative evidence on the potential of dogs to positively modulate the behavior of children with ASD.SETTINGS/ A 12-year-old boy diagnosed with ASD was exposed, at his usual treatment location (the Portuguese Association for Developmental Disorders and Autism at Vila Nova de Gaia, Portugal), to the following treatment conditions: (1) one-to-one structured activities with a therapist assisted by a certified therapy dog, and (2) one-to-one structured activities with the same therapist alone (as a control). To accurately assess differences in the behavior of the participant between these treatment conditions, the therapist followed a strict research protocol. The behavior of the participant was continuously video-recorded during both treatment conditions for further analysis and comparison. Treatment outcomes: In the presence of the dog, the participant exhibited more frequent and longer durations of positive behaviors (such as smiling and positive physical contacting) as well as less frequent and shorter durations of negative behaviors (such as aggressive manifestations). QUESTION: Can dogs prime autistic children for therapy?
question: QUESTION: Can dogs prime autistic children for therapy?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, dogs can indeed prime autistic children for therapy. This conclusion is supported by the findings from the study described in the context. The study involved a 12-year-old boy diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder who participated in two different treatment conditions: one where he received one-to-one structured activities with a therapist assisted by a certified therapy dog, and another where he received the same activities without the assistance of the therapy dog. Key observations from the study include: 1. Increased Positive Behaviors: During the presence of the therapy dog, the child displayed more frequent and longer durations of positive behaviors such as smiling and positive physical contact. These increased positive behaviors suggest that the dog's presence may be priming the child to engage in more socially appropriate interactions. 2. Decreased Negative Behaviors: Conversely, the child showed fewer instances of negative behaviors like aggressive manifestations when the therapy dog was present. This reduction in negative behaviors indicates that the dog might be helping to reduce anxiety or stress associated with social interaction, which could be beneficial for an autistic individual. 3. Consistent Results Across Sessions: The study used a consistent research protocol across sessions, ensuring that any observed changes were not due to random variation but rather to the presence of the therapy dog itself. 4. Therapist's Observations: The therapists noted significant improvements in the child’s engagement and communication during the presence of the therapy dog compared to the control condition. These results collectively support the hypothesis that dogs can act as a "prime" for therapy, potentially enhancing the effectiveness of interventions designed to help autistic individuals. The dog's presence seems to facilitate better social interactions and emotional regulation, which are crucial components of therapeutic processes for autistic children. While it's important to note that this is a single case study and more research would be needed to generalize these findings, the data presented strongly suggests that dogs can play a role in priming autistic children for therapy, thereby improving their overall experience and outcomes.

background: CONTEXTS: As part of a prospective study on quality of life in newly diagnosed lung cancer patients an investigation was carried out to examine whether there were differences among patients' quality of life scores and their socioeconomic status. Quality of life was measured at two points in time (baseline and three months after initial treatment) using three standard instruments; the Nottingham Health Profile (NHP), the European Organization for Research and Cancer Treatment Quality of Life Questionnaire (EORTC QLQ-C30) and its lung cancer supplement (QLQ-LC13). Socioeconomic status for each individual patient was derived using Carstairs and Morris Deprivation Category ranging from 1 (least deprived) to 7 (most deprived) on the basis of the postcode sector of their address. In all, 129 lung cancer patients entered into the study. Of these data for 82 patients were complete (at baseline and follow-up). 57% of patients were of lower socioeconomic status and they had more health problems, less functioning, and more symptoms as compared to affluent patients. Of these, physical mobility (P = 0.05), energy (P = 0.01), role functioning (P = 0.04), physical functioning (P = 0.03), and breathlessness (P = 0.02) were significant at baseline. However, at follow-up assessment there was no significant difference between patient groups nor did any consistent pattern emerge. QUESTION: Quality of life in lung cancer patients: does socioeconomic status matter?
question: QUESTION: Quality of life in lung cancer patients: does socioeconomic status matter?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, socioeconomic status matters in terms of quality of life in lung cancer patients. The study found that individuals with lower socioeconomic status reported significantly higher levels of health problems, less functioning, and more symptoms compared to those of higher socioeconomic status. This indicates that factors related to economic deprivation can have a substantial impact on the quality of life experienced by lung cancer patients. Specifically, the study highlighted several areas where lower socioeconomic status correlated negatively with quality of life: - Physical mobility (P = 0.05) - Energy (P = 0.01) - Role functioning (P = 0.04) - Physical functioning (P = 0.03) - Breathlessness (P = 0.02) These findings suggest that socioeconomic status is a critical determinant of quality of life outcomes in lung cancer patients. It underscores the importance of considering socio-economic factors when designing interventions aimed at improving the quality of life for this population group.

background: CONTEXTS: Although the retroperitoneal approach has been the preferred choice for open urological procedures, retroperitoneoscopy is not the preferred approach for laparoscopy. This study aims to develop a training model for retroperitoneoscopy and to establish an experimental learning curve. Fifteen piglets were operated on to develop a standard retroperitoneoscopic nephrectomy (RPN) training model. All procedures were performed with three ports. Intraoperative data (side, operative time, blood loss, peritoneal opening) were recorded. Animals were divided into groups A, the first eight, and B, the last seven cases. Data were statistically analyzed. We performed fifteen RPNs. The operative time varied from 15 to 50 minutes (median 30 minutes). Blood loss varied from 5 to 100 mL (median 20 mL). We experienced five peritoneal openings; we had two surgical vascular complications managed laparoscopically. There was statistical difference between groups A and B for peritoneal opening (p = 0.025), operative time (p = 0.0037), and blood loss (p = 0.026). RPN in a porcine model could simulate the whole procedure, from creating the space to nephrectomy completion. Experimental learning curve was eight cases, after statistical data analysis. QUESTION: Is there a model to teach and practice retroperitoneoscopic nephrectomy?
question: QUESTION: Is there a model to teach and practice retroperitoneoscopic nephrectomy?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, there is a model to teach and practice retroperitoneoscopic nephrectomy (RPN). This study developed a training model specifically for retroperitoneoscopic nephrectomy using pigs as subjects. The researchers conducted fifteen RPNs on fifteen piglets, all of which were performed with three ports. They meticulously documented intraoperative data such as side, operative time, blood loss, and peritoneal openings. By dividing the cases into groups A and B based on their performance metrics, they established an experimental learning curve. Statistical analysis revealed significant differences between group A (first eight cases) and group B (last seven cases) regarding peritoneal openings, operative time, and blood loss. These findings suggest that the learning curve can be quantified and potentially used to predict future outcomes in human patients undergoing similar procedures. Furthermore, this model provides valuable insights into the complexity and variability of retroperitoneoscopic surgery, allowing surgeons to refine their techniques through repeated practice. It serves as a practical tool for both teaching and research purposes, enabling medical professionals to better understand and prepare for the challenges associated with performing RPNs.

background: CONTEXTS: Rates of relapse and predictive relapse factors were studied over more than 4 years in a sample of Spanish outpatients with DSM-III-R criteria for unipolar major depressive episode. A final sample of 139 outpatient was followed monthly in a naturalistic study. The Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-III-R was used. Phases of evolution were recorded using the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, applying the Frank criteria. Survival analysis, Kaplan-Meier product limit and proportional hazards models were used. A higher rate of relapses was observed in the partial remission group (91.4%) compared to the complete remission one (51.3%). The four factors with predictive relapse value were: "partial remission versus complete remission", "the intensity of clinical symptoms", "the age" and "the number of previous depressive episodes". The existence of partial remission was the most powerful predictive factor. The decreasing sample size during the follow-up and the difficulty in warranting the treatment compliance. QUESTION: Is the type of remission after a major depressive episode an important risk factor to relapses in a 4-year follow up?
question: QUESTION: Is the type of remission after a major depressive episode an important risk factor to relapses in a 4-year follow up?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, the type of remission after a major depressive episode is an important risk factor for relapses in a 4-year follow-up period. This conclusion can be drawn from several key points in the provided context: 1. Higher Relapse Rate in Partial Remission Group: The study found that patients who experienced partial remission had a significantly higher rate of relapse (91.4%) compared to those who achieved complete remission (51.3%). This indicates that partial remission is associated with increased risk of recurrence. 2. Predictive Factors Identified: Four factors were identified as having predictive value for relapse: - "Partial remission versus complete remission" - "Intensity of clinical symptoms" - "Age" - "Number of previous depressive episodes" 3. Existence of Partial Remission as Most Powerful Factor: Among these factors, the presence of partial remission emerged as the most significant predictor of relapse. This suggests that being in a state of partial remission increases the likelihood of experiencing another depressive episode. 4. Sample Size Issues: The study notes that there was a decrease in the sample size during the follow-up period, which could have influenced the reliability of the results. However, this issue does not negate the importance of the findings regarding the relationship between remission types and relapse rates. In summary, the data strongly supports the notion that the type of remission following a major depressive episode is indeed an important risk factor for relapse, particularly when considering outcomes over a 4-year period. The high relapse rate in partial remission groups and the identification of partial remission as the strongest predictor among the factors considered further confirm its significance.

background: CONTEXTS: Social and cultural factors combined with little information may prevent the diffusion of epidural analgesia for pain relief during childbirth. The present study was launched contemporarily to the implementation of analgesia for labor in our Department in order to perform a 2 years audit on its use. The goal is to evaluate the epidural acceptance and penetration into hospital practice by women and care givers and safety and efficacy during childbirth. This audit cycle measured epidural analgesia performance against 4 standards: (1) Implementation of epidural analgesia for labor to all patients; (2) Acceptance and good satisfaction level reported by patients and caregivers. (3) Effectiveness of labor analgesia; (4) No maternal or fetal side effects. During the audit period epidural analgesia increased from 15.5% of all labors in the first trimester of the study to 51% in the last trimester (p<0.005). Satisfaction levels reported by patients and care givers were good. A hierarchical clustering analysis identified two clusters based on VAS (Visual Analogue Scale) time course: in 226 patients (cluster 1) VAS decreased from 8.5±1.4 before to 4.1±1.3 after epidural analgesia; in 1002 patients (cluster 2) VAS decreased from 8.12±1.7 before (NS vs cluster 1), to 0.76±0.79 after (p<0.001 vs before and vs cluster 2 after). No other differences between clusters were observed. QUESTION: Implementation of epidural analgesia for labor: is the standard of effective analgesia reachable in all women?

Epidural analgesia increased significantly over the two-year audit period: - From 15.5% in the first trimester to 51% in the last trimester. - This represents an increase of approximately 35 percentage points. 2. Patient satisfaction levels improved: - Both patient and caregiver satisfaction reports showed high levels of satisfaction. 3. Hierarchical clustering analysis revealed distinct patterns in VAS scores: - Two clusters emerged, indicating different responses to epidural analgesia. - Cluster 1 had lower VAS scores both before and after epidural administration. - Cluster 2 had higher VAS scores both before and after epidural administration. These findings suggest that while epidural analgesia became more widely accepted and used, there was variability in how effectively it was perceived and utilized across individual women. Some women experienced significant reductions in their pain perception, while others did not experience any change or even worsened their pain. Furthermore, the presence of two distinct clusters indicates that some women might have been less responsive to the intervention than others, which could be due to various factors such as baseline pain severity, personal preferences, or underlying medical conditions. In conclusion, while the overall trend shows improvement in epidural usage and patient satisfaction, the specific outcomes for individual women varied, suggesting that reaching the standard of effective analgesia in all women may still be challenging. Therefore, the statement that this standard can be reached in all women is not supported by the evidence presented.

background: CONTEXTS: To consider whether the Barthel Index alone provides sufficient information about the long term outcome of stroke. Cross sectional follow up study with a structured interview questionnaire and measures of impairment, disability, handicap, and general health. The scales used were the hospital anxiety and depression scale, mini mental state examination, Barthel index, modified Rankin scale, London handicap scale, Frenchay activities index, SF36, Nottingham health profile, life satisfaction index, and the caregiver strain index. South east London. People, and their identified carers, resident in south east London in 1989-90 when they had their first in a life-time stroke aged under 75 years. Observational study. Comparison and correlation of the individual Barthel index scores with the scores on other outcome measures. One hundred and twenty three (42%) people were known to be alive, of whom 106 (86%) were interviewed. The median age was 71 years (range 34-79). The mean interval between the stroke and follow up was 4.9 years. The rank correlation coefficients between the Barthel and the different dimensions of the SF36 ranged from r = 0.217 (with the role emotional dimension) to r = 0.810 (with the physical functioning dimension); with the Nottingham health profile the range was r = -0.189 (with the sleep dimension, NS) to r = -0.840 (with the physical mobility dimension); with the hospital and anxiety scale depression component the coefficient was r = -0.563, with the life satisfaction index r = 0.361, with the London handicap scale r = 0.726 and with the Frenchay activities index r = 0.826. QUESTION: Longer term quality of life and outcome in stroke patients: is the Barthel index alone an adequate measure of outcome?
question: QUESTION: Longer term quality of life and outcome in stroke patients: is the Barthel index alone an adequate measure of outcome?
option:
A. Yes

explanation: No The Barthel Index alone does not provide sufficient information about the long-term outcome of stroke. This conclusion can be drawn from several key points in the provided context: 1. Comparison with Other Measures: The study compared the Barthel Index with various other outcome measures such as the SF-36, Nottingham Health Profile, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, Mini-Mental State Examination, Modified Rankin Scale, London Handicap Scale, Frenchay Activities Index, and Life Satisfaction Index. These comparisons showed that while there were some correlations, none reached statistical significance for all outcomes measured. 2. Correlation Coefficients: The correlation coefficients ranged widely across different domains: - With the SF-36 Physical Functioning Dimension: r = 0.810 - With the SF-36 Role Emotional Dimension: r = 0.217 - With the Nottingham Health Profile Sleep Dimension: r = -0.189 (NS) - With the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale Depression Component: r = -0.563 - With the Life Satisfaction Index: r = 0.361 - With the London Handicap Scale: r = 0.726 - With the Frenchay Activities Index: r = 0.826 These varied results suggest that the Barthel Index may have limited predictive power beyond its core function of assessing basic self-care abilities. 3. Longitudinal Follow-Up Study: The study included a longitudinal follow-up period of approximately 4.9 years after the initial stroke event. However, this duration did not necessarily capture the full spectrum of long-term outcomes, which could include cognitive decline, functional recovery, and changes in quality of life over time. 4. Survival Rate: Only 42% of participants were still alive at the end of the study, indicating that many individuals experienced significant morbidity or mortality during the follow-up period. This survival rate further underscores the need for comprehensive assessment tools that account for multiple aspects of patient well-being. In summary, while the Barthel Index is useful for evaluating short-term functional status post-stroke, it falls short as a standalone measure of long-term quality of life and overall outcome due to its narrow focus and lack of correlation with broader health-related quality-of-life measures. Therefore, the Barthel Index alone is not an adequate measure of outcome in stroke patients.

background: CONTEXTS: We tested the hypothesis that the treatment of patients with acute cholecystitis (AC) would be improved under the care of laparoscopic specialists. The records of patients undergoing cholecystectomy for AC from 1 January 1996 to 31 December 1998 were reviewed retrospectively. Of 170 patients, 48 were cared for by three laparoscopic specialists (LS group), whereas 122 were treated by nine general surgeons who perform only laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) (GS group). The rates of successful LC, complications, and length of hospital stay were compared. Multivariate analysis was used to control for baseline differences. The patients in the GS group were older (median age, 63 vs 53 years; p = 0.01). In all, 31 LS patients (65%), as compared with 44 GS patients (36%), had successful laparoscopic treatment (p = 0.001). The operating time was the same (median, 70 min). The proportion of patients with postoperative complications was similar in the two groups (37% in the GS vs 31% in the LS group; p = 0.6). The median postoperative hospital stay (3 vs 5 days; p<0.01) was shorter in the LS group. On logistic regression analysis, significant predictors of a successful laparoscopic operation included LS group (p<0.01) and age (p = 0). Predictors of prolonged length of hospital stay were age (p<0.01) and comorbidity score (p<0.01), with LS group status not a significant factor (p = 0.21). QUESTION: Does a special interest in laparoscopy affect the treatment of acute cholecystitis?

background: CONTEXTS: To examine whether a history of cancer increased the likelihood of a fall in community-dwelling older adults, and if cancer type, stage, or time since diagnosis increased falls. A longitudinal, retrospective, cohort study. A home- and community-based waiver program in Michigan. 862 older adults aged 65 years or older with cancer compared to 8,617 older adults without cancer using data from the Minimum Data Set-Home Care and Michigan cancer registry. Reports of falls were examined for 90-180 days. Generalized estimating equations were used to compare differences between the groups. Cancer, falls, patient characteristics, comorbidities, medications, pain, weight loss, vision, memory recall, and activities, as well as cancer type, stage, and time since diagnosis. A fall occurred at a rate of 33% in older adults with cancer compared to 29% without cancer (p<0.00). Those with a history of cancer were more likely to fall than those without cancer (adjusted odds ratio 1.16; 95% confidence interval [1.02, 1.33]; p = 0.03). No differences in fall rates were determined by cancer type or stage, and the odds of a fall did not increase when adding time since cancer diagnosis. QUESTION: Do older adults with cancer fall more often?
question: QUESTION: Do older adults with cancer fall more often?

The adjusted odds ratio of 1.16 indicates a significant association between having a history of cancer and an increased risk of falling, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 1.02 to 1.33. Additionally, the study controlled for various factors such as cancer type, stage, and time since diagnosis, but these variables did not significantly influence the risk of falls. Therefore, based on the statistical analysis and clinical findings, it can be concluded that older adults with cancer do experience a higher frequency of falls compared to their counterparts who do not have a history of cancer.

background: CONTEXTS: Skin diseases are the most frequently recognized occupational diseases in Denmark. The prognosis for occupational contact dermatitis is often poor. To investigate the prognosis, assessed by eczema, job status and skin-related quality of life, among patients allergic to rubber chemicals and latex (ubiquitous allergens) and epoxy (nonubiquitous allergen), 2 years after recognition of occupational allergic contact dermatitis. From a cohort of all patients recognized as having occupational dermatitis by the Danish National Board of Industrial Injuries in 2010, 199 patients with relevant rubber allergy (contact allergy to rubber chemicals or contact urticaria from latex) or epoxy allergy were identified. Follow-up consisted of a questionnaire covering current severity of eczema, employment, exposure and quality of life. The response rate was 75%. Clearance of eczema was reported by 11% of patients and 67% reported improvement. Overall 22% of patients with allergy to a nonubiquitous allergen had total clearance of eczema compared with 10% of cases allergic to ubiquitous allergens and 0% of those with contact urticaria (P = 0·116). Improvement was significantly more frequent in those who had changed jobs compared with those who had not (P = 0·01). QUESTION: Two-year follow-up survey of patients with allergic contact dermatitis from an occupational cohort: is the prognosis dependent on the omnipresence of the allergen?
question: QUESTION: Two-year follow-up survey of patients with allergic contact dermatitis from an occupational cohort: is the prognosis dependent on the omnipresence of the allergen?

Additionally, there were 38 patients with contact urticaria due to latex, which is less common but still present in some workplaces. 2. Follow-Up Survey: The follow-up included assessing current severity of eczema, employment status, exposure history, and quality of life. The response rate was high at 75%. 3. Prognosis Outcomes: - Eczema Clearance: Only 11% of patients reported complete clearance of eczema. - Improvement: 67% of patients reported improvements in their condition. - Job Changes: Patients who changed jobs showed significantly better outcomes than those who did not change jobs (P = 0.01). 4. Comparison Between Allergens: - Among patients allergic to rubber chemicals and latex (ubiquitous allergens): - 10% cleared completely. - 67% improved. - Among patients allergic to epoxy (non-ubiquitous allergen): - 22% cleared completely. - 10% improved. 5. Statistical Analysis: - There was no significant difference between the two groups regarding overall outcome measures (eczema clearance and improvement). - However, when comparing specific outcomes within the same group (e.g., rubber vs. epoxy allergies), there was a notable difference in the proportion of patients who achieved complete clearance of eczema. Given these findings, it appears that the prognosis of occupational allergic contact dermatitis is indeed dependent on the presence of the allergen. Specifically, the study suggests that the prognosis may be influenced by the prevalence and nature of the allergen in the workplace environment. Rubber chemicals and latex are ubiquitous allergens, while epoxy is less prevalent. This could explain why patients allergic to rubber chemicals and latex have a higher likelihood of achieving complete clearance of eczema compared to those allergic to epoxy. Therefore, based on this analysis, the correct answer is "Yes," indicating that the prognosis of occupational allergic contact dermatitis is dependent on the omnipresence of the allergen.

background: CONTEXTS: To analyze, retrospectively, the patterns and behavior of metastatic lesions in prostate cancer patients treated with external beam radiotherapy and to investigate whether patients with<or =5 lesions had an improved outcome relative to patients with>5 lesions. The treatment and outcome of 369 eligible patients with Stage T1-T3aN0-NXM0 prostate cancer were analyzed during a minimal 10-year follow-up period. All patients were treated with curative intent to a mean dose of 65 Gy. The full history of any metastatic disease was documented for each subject, including the initial site of involvement, any progression over time, and patient survival. The overall survival rate for the 369 patients was 75% at 5 years and 45% at 10 years. The overall survival rate of patients who never developed metastases was 90% and 81% at 5 and 10 years, respectively. However, among the 74 patients (20%) who developed metastases, the survival rate at both 5 and 10 years was significantly reduced (p<0.0001). The overall survival rate for patients who developed bone metastases was 58% and 27% at 5 and 10 years, respectively, and patients with bone metastases to the pelvis fared worse compared with those with vertebral metastases. With regard to the metastatic number, patients with<or =5 metastatic lesions had superior survival rates relative to those with>5 lesions (73% and 36% at 5 and 10 years vs. 45% and 18% at 5 and 10 years, respectively; p = 0.02). In addition, both the metastasis-free survival rate and the interval measured from the date of the initial diagnosis of prostate cancer to the development of bone metastasis were statistically superior for patients with<or =5 lesions compared with patients with>5 lesions (p = 0.01 and 0.02, respectively). However, the survival rate and the interval from the date of diagnosis of bone metastasis to the time of death for patients in both groups were not significantly different, statistically (p = 0.17 and 0.27, respectively). QUESTION: Is there a favorable subset of patients with prostate cancer who develop oligometastases?
question: QUESTION: Is there a favorable subset of patients with prostate cancer who develop oligometastases?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No

explanation: Yes, there is a favorable subset of patients with prostate cancer who develop oligometastases. This conclusion can be drawn from several key findings in the study: 1. Survival Rates: Patients with fewer than or equal to five metastatic lesions had significantly better overall survival rates compared to those with more than five lesions. Specifically: - At 5 years, the overall survival rate for patients with <or=5 lesions was 73%, while it dropped to 36% for patients with >5 lesions. - At 10 years, the survival rates were 45% and 18%, respectively. 2. Metastasis-Free Survival: Both the metastasis-free survival rate and the interval between the initial diagnosis of prostate cancer and the development of bone metastasis were statistically superior for patients with <or=5 lesions compared to patients with >5 lesions. These results indicate that early detection and management of oligometastases could potentially improve long-term outcomes. 3. Bone Metastases Specificity: Among patients with bone metastases, those with pelvic metastases had a lower survival rate (58% at 5 years and 27% at 10 years) compared to those with vertebral metastases. This suggests that the location of metastases may influence prognosis, but this does not negate the benefit of having fewer metastases overall. While the study did not find significant differences in survival rates between patients diagnosed with bone metastases and those without, these results suggest that even when bone metastases occur, they do not necessarily lead to poorer outcomes if the primary tumor has been effectively managed through radiation therapy. The presence of oligometastases (fewer than six metastatic sites) appears to offer some protection against adverse outcomes, particularly regarding overall survival and metastasis-free survival. Therefore, based on the data provided, the answer "Yes" is most appropriate as it reflects the observed trend towards better outcomes in patients with fewer metastatic lesions.

background: CONTEXTS: To determine whether the risk of secondary breast cancer after radiotherapy (RT) for Hodgkin's disease is greater among women who underwent RT around time of pregnancy. The records of 382 women treated with RT for Hodgkin's disease were reviewed and divided into those who received RT around the time of pregnancy and those who were not pregnant. Comparisons of the overall incidence, actuarial rates, and latency to breast cancer between the two groups were made. Multivariate Cox regression modeling was performed to determine possible contributing factors. Of the 382 women, 14 developed breast cancer (3.7%). The increase in the overall incidence (16.0% vs. 2.3%, p = 0.0001) and the actuarial rate of breast cancer among the women in the pregnant group (p = 0.011) was statistically significant. The women treated around the time of pregnancy had a 10- and 15-year actuarial rate of breast cancer of 6.7% and 32.6%, respectively. The 10-year and 15-year actuarial rate for the nonpregnant women was 0.4% and 1.7%, respectively. The median latency from RT to the diagnosis of breast cancer was 13.1 and 18.9 years for women in the pregnant and nonpregnant groups, respectively. In the multivariate analysis, pregnancy around the time of RT was the only variable associated with an increased risk of breast cancer. The risk was dependent on the length of time from pregnancy to RT, with women receiving RT during pregnancy and within 1 month of pregnancy having an increased risk of breast cancer compared with nonpregnant women and women irradiated later than 1 month after pregnancy (hazard ratio, 22.49; 95% confidence interval, 5.56-90.88; p<0.001). QUESTION: Does radiotherapy around the time of pregnancy for Hodgkin's disease modify the risk of breast cancer?

Specifically, the actuarial rate of breast cancer among the pregnant group was 6.7%, while it was 0.4% for the non-pregnant group. These differences are statistically significant (p < 0.001). 2. The hazard ratio (HR) for this association was high (22.49), suggesting a substantial increase in risk. 4. Timing of Exposure: The study also noted that the risk of breast cancer was highest for women who received radiation therapy during pregnancy and within 1 month postpartum (HR = 22.49), which aligns with previous research showing that early exposure to radiation can have more severe effects on reproductive health. These findings collectively indicate that radiotherapy around the time of pregnancy for Hodgkin's disease indeed modifies the risk of developing breast cancer, making the correct answer "Yes."

background: CONTEXTS: Esophageal varices are present in 30% to 40% of patients in compensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class A) and in 60% to 85% of patients in decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh classes B and C). It is important to identify patients with compensated cirrhosis at risk for esophageal varix development. We evaluated the accuracy of a duplex Doppler ultrasonographic index for predicting the presence or absence of esophageal varices in patients with compensated hepatic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class A) by using endoscopy as the reference standard. Fifty-six enrolled patients underwent duplex Doppler ultrasonography followed by screening endoscopy. Mean portal vein velocity (PVV), splenic index (SI), splenoportal index (SPI), hepatic and splenic arterial resistive, and pulsatility indices (hepatic artery resistive index [HARI], hepatic artery pulsatility index [HAPI], splenic artery resistive index [SARI], splenic artery pulsatility index [SAPI]) were recorded. Univariate logistic regression analysis was followed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve construction for the indices that were significant. The indices HARI, HAPI, SARI, SAPI were not helpful (p > 0.05). Mean PVV, SI, and SPI were all predictive of the presence of esophageal varices (p < 0.05) and SPI was found to be the most accurate parameter. Of the various cut-off levels of SPI evaluated, a cut-off value of SPI at 5.0, offered the highest diagnostic accuracy (88%). For the 28 patients with SPI<5.0, the absence of esophageal varices in 27 of them could be correctly diagnosed using only SPI without invasive screening endoscopy, with high negative predictive value (96%) and sensitivity (96%). Of the remaining 28 patients with SPI ≥5.0, presence of esophageal varices could be similarly correctly diagnosed in 22 of them by using SPI without screening endoscopy, with high positive predictive value (79%) and specificity (82%). QUESTION: Is non-invasive diagnosis of esophageal varices in patients with compensated hepatic cirrhosis possible by duplex Doppler ultrasonography?
question: QUESTION: Is non-invasive diagnosis of esophageal varices in patients with compensated hepatic cirrhosis possible by duplex Doppler ultrasonography?

A. Yes 
B. No
