background: CONTEXTS: Stock et al. (Eur Respir J 25:47-53, 2005) recently estimated asthma prevalence in Germany using claims data on prescriptions and hospital diagnoses and found high prevalence peaks in infants. Our objective was to critically assess and discuss various aspects of identifying children with asthma using prescription data. We replicated the selection procedure of Stock et al. using data on 290,919 children aged 0-17 years insured in the Gmünder ErsatzKasse (GEK) in 2005. Asthma prevalence was also estimated in a sample of 17,641 children aged 0-17 years participating in the German Health Interview and Examination Survey for Children and Adolescents (KiGGS) from 2003 to 2006. In children aged 0-4 years insured in the GEK, prevalences were found to range from 11.7 to 17.7% for boys and from 7.2 to 11.1% for girls when the criteria of Stock et al. were applied. A steady decline in prevalences was observed in older age groups. Asthma prevalence estimated in the KiGGS data showed a quite different distribution. In the age group 0-4 years, prevalences were found to range from 0 to 2.6% in boys and from 0 to 1.0% in girls; in children>4 years, prevalences were found to increase with increasing age. QUESTION: Prescriptions as a proxy for asthma in children: a good choice?
question: QUESTION: Prescriptions as a proxy for asthma in children: a good choice?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Prescriptions as a proxy for asthma in children can be considered a reasonable choice under certain conditions, but it has limitations that should be acknowledged. The primary advantage of using prescription data is its ability to capture the actual use of medications, which may reflect the presence of symptoms and need for treatment. However, there are several factors to consider before relying solely on this method: 1. Underreporting: Not all cases of asthma will necessarily result in an asthma-related prescription being written. Some individuals might not seek medical attention or have their condition documented accurately, leading to underreporting. 2. Overreporting: Conversely, some individuals who do not actually have asthma might receive prescriptions due to other respiratory issues or allergies, potentially overestimating the true prevalence. 3. Temporal Variability: Prescription patterns can vary significantly depending on seasonal changes, medication availability, and patient compliance. This temporal variability makes it challenging to generalize across populations without additional context. 4. Age-Specific Patterns: As mentioned in the question, the prevalence estimates varied significantly based on age. For example, in younger children, the prevalence was higher than expected, while in older children, it increased with age. These differences highlight the importance of considering age-specific trends rather than generalizing across all ages. 5. Quality of Data: The quality of the data used in both studies (claims data vs. health interview survey) could influence the results. Claims data might suffer from inaccuracies if not properly validated, whereas health interviews provide more direct information about symptomatology and diagnosis. In conclusion, while prescriptions can serve as a useful proxy for assessing asthma prevalence in children, they must be interpreted carefully given the inherent limitations and potential biases associated with such data sources. A combination of multiple methods, including clinical assessments and longitudinal studies, would likely provide a more comprehensive understanding of asthma prevalence in children.

background: CONTEXTS: Combining various antiretroviral agents into one single dosage form has been a strategy to reduce pill burden and enhance medication adherence among human immunodeficiency virus /AIDS (HIV/AIDS) patients. This is a cost-utility study from a health care system's perspective comparing coformulated fixed dose (FXD) strategy versus multiple free dose combination (FRC) in antiretroviral therapy. The Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) was used to identify HIV/AIDS patients with ≥2 active antiretroviral medications. Patients on FXD were matched in 1:1 ratio with the FRC group using propensity scores. All medical costs excluding those paid by patients and families were included. Utility was measured using SF-6D scores from the SF-12 questionnaire. Incremental cost-utility ratios (ICURs) were calculated using the mean annual estimates. A cost-effectiveness acceptability curve was determined using a Monte Carlo probabilistic simulation technique. Nine FXD antiretroviral formulations approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration by 2005 was included in this study. One hundred seventy HIV/AIDS patients with ≥2 antiretroviral agents were identified from the MEPS database, of which 53% (n=92) were on FXD formulation. On matching, 70 patients from FXD had a match from the FRC group. No differences in sociodemographic and health status variables were observed between the matched groups. The mean annual cost was $15,766.15 for FXD patients and $11,875.21 for FRC patients. The mean utility gained by using FXD over FRC was 0.085; however, this difference was not statistically significant. The ICUR for the FXD treatment over FRC treatment was $45,540.49/quality-adjusted life years (QALYs). Probabilistic sensitivity analysis showed FXD to dominate FRC (>50% probability of being cost-effective) above the $40,000 threshold. QUESTION: Does combining antiretroviral agents in a single dosage form enhance quality of life of HIV/AIDS patients?
question: QUESTION: Does combining antiretroviral agents in a single dosage form enhance quality of life of HIV/AIDS patients?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: No, combining antiretroviral agents in a single dosage form does not enhance the quality of life of HIV/AIDS patients as indicated by the results of this study. Here’s a detailed breakdown of why this conclusion can be drawn: 1. Utility Measurement: The study measures utility using SF-6D scores from the SF-12 questionnaire. Utility represents an individual's subjective well-being or quality of life. In this case, the mean utility gain when switching from FRC to FXD was only 0.085, indicating that there was no substantial improvement in quality of life due to the combined dosing regimen. 2. Cost-Effectiveness Analysis: The incremental cost-utility ratio (ICUR) for the FXD treatment over FRC treatment was calculated at $45,540.49 per QALY gained. This high ICUR suggests that while the FXD regimen may have some benefits, it also comes with significantly higher healthcare costs compared to the FRC regimen. Therefore, the overall benefit-to-cost ratio is unfavorable, implying that the improved quality of life achieved through the FXD regimen is outweighed by its increased financial burden. 3. Propensity Score Matching: Despite attempting to control for potential confounders such as sociodemographic and health status variables, the study still found no statistical significance in the utility gains between the two groups. This further supports the notion that the combined dosing regimen did not improve the quality of life of HIV/AIDS patients. In summary, although the study aimed to compare the effectiveness of different antiretroviral regimens, the lack of significant improvements in quality of life and the high associated costs suggest that combining antiretroviral agents in a single dosage form does not enhance the quality of life of HIV/AIDS patients.

background: CONTEXTS: Although desflurane is commonly used to control surgically induced hypertension, its effects on left ventricular (LV) function have not been investigated in this clinical situation. The purpose of the present study was to evaluate the LV function response to desflurane, when used to control intraoperative hypertension. In 50 patients, scheduled for vascular surgery, anesthesia was induced with sufentanil 0.5 microg/kg, midazolam 0.3 mg/kg and atracurium 0.5 mg/kg. After tracheal intubation, anesthesia was maintained with increments of drugs with controlled ventilation (N2O/O2=60/40%) until the start of surgery. A 5 Mhz transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) probe was inserted after intubation. Pulmonary artery catheter and TEE measurements were obtained after induction (to)(control value), at surgical incision (t1) if it was associated with an increase in systolic arterial pressure (SAP) greater than 140 mmHg (hypertension) and after control of hemodynamic parameters by administration of desflurane (return of systolic arterial pressure to within 20% of the control value) (t2) in a fresh gas flow of 31/ min. Sixteen patients developed hypertension at surgical incision. SAP was controlled by desflurane in all 16 patients. Afterload assessed by systemic vascular resistance index (SVRI), end-systolic wall-stress (ESWS) and left-ventricular stroke work index (LVSWI) increased with incision until the hypertension returned to post-induction values with mean end-tidal concentration of 5.1+/-0.7% desflurane. No change in heart rate, cardiac index, mean pulmonary arterial pressure, stroke volume, end-diastolic and end-systolic cross-sectional areas, fractional area change and left ventricular circumferential fiber shortening was noted when desflurane was added to restore blood pressure. QUESTION: Does desflurane alter left ventricular function when used to control surgical stimulation during aortic surgery?
question: QUESTION: Does desflurane alter left ventricular function when used to control surgical stimulation during aortic surgery?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: No, desflurane does not alter left ventricular function when used to control surgical stimulation during aortic surgery. This conclusion can be drawn from several key points: 1. Effectiveness of Desflurane: The primary goal of using desflurane as an anesthetic agent is to manage intraoperative hypertension. In this study, desflurane successfully controlled hypertension in all 16 patients who experienced it during their surgeries. This indicates that desflurane's ability to reduce blood pressure without affecting myocardial performance aligns well with its intended use. 2. Cardiac Parameters: During the period when desflurane was administered to control hypertension, no significant changes were observed in any cardiac parameters such as heart rate, cardiac index, mean pulmonary arterial pressure, stroke volume, end-diastolic and end-systolic cross-sectional areas, fractional area change, or left ventricular circumferential fiber shortening. These findings suggest that desflurane did not induce adverse effects on the heart muscle itself. 3. Left Ventricular Function Assessment: The study specifically measured left ventricular function through various indices including systemic vascular resistance index (SVRI), end-systolic wall stress (ESWS), and left-ventricular stroke work index (LVSWI). Despite these assessments showing increases in load (SVRI) and strain (ESWS) due to the surgical incision, there was no corresponding increase in left ventricular dysfunction indicated by changes in other parameters like heart rate, cardiac output, or regional wall motion abnormalities. 4. Controlled Conditions: The authors controlled for factors that could influence left ventricular function, such as preload, afterload, and contractility, which remained stable throughout the intervention. This further supports the notion that the observed changes in SVRI and ESWS were primarily driven by the surgical incision rather than by the pharmacological manipulation of desflurane. In summary, while desflurane may affect the mechanical properties of the heart (as evidenced by increased SVRI and ESWS), it does not appear to cause structural damage or functional impairment of the left ventricle under the conditions studied here. Therefore, based on the data provided, we can conclude that desflurane does not alter left ventricular function when used to control surgical stimulation during aortic surgery.

background: CONTEXTS: The aim of this study was to assess the efficacy of ureteroscopy for lower ureteric stones without the use of fluoroscopy. Between June 2001 and January 2005, a total of 110 patients with a mean age of 33.5 years (range 12-65) suffering from of lower ureteral calculi (below the upper margin of the sacroiliac joint) prospectively underwent ureteroscopic removal. Retrograde pyelography was avoided, and no safety guidewire was placed. Whenever required, the ureteric meatus was dilated with a ureteric balloon under direct vision. Double-J stent placement was done with the aid of ureteroscopy. A fluoroscope was kept standby. The patients had a postoperative X-ray of the kidney-ureter-bladder region to document the stone clearance. The mean stone size was 8.7 mm (range 6-15). Complete clearance without the use of fluoroscopy was achieved in 99 patients (94.2%). Fluoroscopy was required in 6 patients (4%) for calcified stricture (n = 1), duplex system (n = 1), narrow and tortuous meatus causing difficulty in passing the 5-Fr balloon dilator (n = 3), and confirmation of spontaneous passage of the stone (n = 1). Of the 13 patients who required balloon dilatation it was successfully achieved without fluoroscopy. Double-J stenting was done due to mucosal ulceration (n = 3), polypoid reaction (n = 2), and perforation (n = 1). All these patients had correct placement of the stent, as confirmed by X-ray of the kidney-ureter-bladder region postoperatively. QUESTION: Is fluoroscopy essential for retrieval of lower ureteric stones?
question: QUESTION: Is fluoroscopy essential for retrieval of lower ureteric stones?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: No, fluoroscopy is not essential for the retrieval of lower ureteric stones using ureteroscopy. This conclusion can be drawn based on several key points from the study's findings: 1. Success Rate Without Fluoroscopy: In 99 out of 110 cases (94.2%), complete clearance of the stones was achieved without the use of fluoroscopy. This high success rate indicates that fluoroscopy is not necessary for successful stone removal in most cases. 2. Fluoroscopy Required Only in Specific Cases: - Calcified Stricture: One patient needed fluoroscopy for a calcified stricture. - Duplex System: Another patient required fluoroscopy for a duplex system. - Narrow and Tortuous Meatus: Three patients required fluoroscopy because of difficulties in passing the 5-Fr balloon dilator. - Confirmation of Spontaneous Passage: One patient required fluoroscopy to confirm spontaneous passage of the stone. These specific instances where fluoroscopy was used were either complications related to the procedure itself or confirming natural outcomes rather than being essential steps in the overall process of stone removal. 3. Balloon Dilatation Success: For the 13 patients who required balloon dilation, all were able to achieve successful dilation without the need for fluoroscopy. This further supports the idea that fluoroscopy is not strictly necessary for this step. 4. Double-J Stent Placement: While double-J stents were placed in some cases, they were correctly positioned in all but one case, which confirms their effectiveness without the need for fluoroscopy. In summary, the data strongly suggests that fluoroscopy is not a critical component of the ureteroscopy procedure for lower ureteric stones. It serves more as an auxiliary tool when necessary to address complications or ensure proper placement of devices like balloons or stents, but its necessity is significantly reduced compared to traditional fluoroscopic procedures.

background: CONTEXTS: Recent studies have found a choroidal thickening in amblyopic eyes and suggested that there might be a relationship between the choroid and amblyopia. The present study aimed to evaluate the effect of a six-month treatment of amblyopia on choroidal thickness in anisometropic hyperopic amblyopic children. Thirty-two anisometropic hyperopic children with unilateral amblyopia were included in this prospective study. Subfoveal choroidal thickness was measured as the distance between the retinal pigment epithelium and the chorioscleral edge, by using spectral domain enhanced depth imaging optical coherence tomography. The treatment of amblyopia was performed based on the full correction of the refractive error with eyeglasses, a refractive adaptation phase and occlusion by patching the fellow eye. The mean visual acuity of the amblyopic eyes significantly increased from 0.35 ± 0.3 to 0.16 ± 0.2 logMAR after the treatment (p < 0.001). The mean initial choroidal thickness was significantly higher in the amblyopic eyes than in the fellow eyes (p = 0.019). There were no significant differences between the pre- and post-treatment mean choroidal thickness in the amblyopic eyes (p = 0.428) and in the fellow eyes (p = 0.343). The mean choroidal thickness was still higher in the amblyopic eyes than in the fellow eyes after the treatment (p = 0.006). QUESTION: Does the treatment of amblyopia normalise subfoveal choroidal thickness in amblyopic children?
question: QUESTION: Does the treatment of amblyopia normalise subfoveal choroidal thickness in amblyopic children?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, the treatment of amblyopia normalizes subfoveal choroidal thickness in amblyopic children. This conclusion is supported by several key findings from the study: 1. Visual Acuity Improvement: - The mean visual acuity of the amblyopic eyes significantly improved from 0.35 ± 0.3 to 0.16 ± 0.2 logMAR after the treatment. - This improvement suggests that the treatment effectively reduced the impact of amblyopia on vision, which could indirectly affect choroidal thickness. 2. Initial Choroidal Thickness Differences: - The mean initial choroidal thickness was significantly higher in the amblyopic eyes compared to the fellow eyes (p = 0.019). - This difference indicates that the choroidal tissue may be thicker in amblyopic eyes due to various factors such as decreased blood flow, inflammation, or other structural changes associated with amblyopia. 3. Post-Treatment Changes: - After the treatment period of six months, the mean choroidal thickness remained higher in the amblyopic eyes than in the fellow eyes (p = 0.006). - However, it's important to note that the overall choroidal thickness normalized, suggesting that the treatment had a positive effect on reducing choroidal thickness. 4. Statistical Analysis: - The statistical analysis showed no significant differences between the pre- and post-treatment mean choroidal thickness in both groups (amblyopic and fellow eyes), indicating that the treatment did not cause any adverse effects on choroidal thickness. - The p-values for these comparisons being greater than 0.05 suggest that the observed differences were not statistically significant. In summary, while the initial choroidal thickness was higher in amblyopic eyes, the treatment successfully reduced this thickness over time, leading to normalization. Therefore, the treatment of amblyopia does indeed normalize subfoveal choroidal thickness in amblyopic children.

background: CONTEXTS: Most staging systems for soft tissue sarcoma are based on histologic malignancy-grade, tumor size and tumor depth. These factors are generally dichotomized, size at 5 cm. We believe it is unlikely that tumor depth per se should influence a tumor's metastatic capability. Therefore we hypothesized that the unfavourable prognostic importance of depth could be explained by the close association between size and depth, deep-seated tumors on average being larger than the superficial ones. When tumor size is dichotomized, this effect should be most pronounced in the large size (>5 cm) group in which the size span is larger. We analyzed the associations between tumor size and depth and the prognostic importance of grade, size and depth in a population-based series of 490 adult patients with soft tissue sarcoma of the extremity or trunk wall with complete, 4.5 years minimum, follow-up. Multivariate analysis showed no major prognostic effect of tumor depth when grade and size were taken into account. The mean size of small tumors was the same whether superficial or deep but the mean size of large and deep-seated tumors were one third larger than that of large but superficial tumors. Tumor depth influenced the prognosis in the subset of high-grade and large tumors. In this subset deep-seated tumors had poorer survival rate than superficial tumors, which could be explained by the larger mean size of the deep-seated tumors. QUESTION: Should tumor depth be included in prognostication of soft tissue sarcoma?
question: QUESTION: Should tumor depth be included in prognostication of soft tissue sarcoma?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, tumor depth should be included in the prognostication of soft tissue sarcoma. This conclusion is supported by several key findings from the study described: 1. No Major Prognostic Effect of Tumor Depth: The multivariate analysis did not show any significant prognostic effect of tumor depth when grade and size were taken into account. This suggests that while tumor depth may have some impact, it does not significantly contribute to predicting overall survival independently of other factors like grade and size. 2. Association Between Size and Depth: The study found that deep-seated tumors tended to be larger than superficial tumors, regardless of their grade. This indicates that tumor size can be an important factor influencing prognosis, especially in larger tumors (≥5 cm). 3. Prognosis in High-Grade and Large Tumors: Among high-grade and large tumors, deep-seated tumors had worse survival rates compared to superficial tumors. This finding supports the idea that tumor depth might play a role in prognosis, particularly among more aggressive tumors. 4. Larger Mean Size of Deep-Seated Tumors: The mean size of deep-seated tumors was approximately one-third larger than that of large but superficial tumors. This difference in size could explain the observed differences in prognosis, as deeper tumors tend to be larger and thus potentially more challenging to treat. Given these points, including tumor depth in prognostic models would help capture the additional information provided by this variable, thereby improving the accuracy of predictions. However, it's crucial to note that the inclusion of tumor depth alone might still miss other important prognostic factors such as grade and size, which together provide a comprehensive picture of the patient's risk profile.

background: CONTEXTS: This study investigated associations between the performance of dental students in each of the three components of the selection procedure [academic average, Undergraduate Medicine and Health Sciences Admission Test (UMAT) and structured interview], socio-demographic characteristics and their academic success in an undergraduate dental surgery programme. Longitudinal review of admissions data relating to students entering dental education at the University of Otago, New Zealand, between 2004 and 2009 was compared with academic performance throughout the dental programme. After controlling for variables, pre-admission academic average, UMAT scores and interview performance did not predict performance as a dental student. Class place in second year, however, was a strong predictor of class place in final year. Multivariate analysis demonstrated that the best predictors of higher class placement in the final year were New Zealand European ethnicity and domestic (rather than international) student status. Other socio-demographic characteristics were not associated with performance. These interim findings provide a sound base for the ongoing study. QUESTION: Does performance in selection processes predict performance as a dental student?
question: QUESTION: Does performance in selection processes predict performance as a dental student?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: This study investigates the association between various factors related to dental student selection procedures and their subsequent academic performance during an undergraduate dental surgery program. The key finding from this research is that none of the selected factors—such as academic average, UMAT scores, and structured interview performance—predicts the performance of dental students once they have entered the program. 1. Academic Average: - The study found no significant relationship between the academic average before admission and the final year's performance. 2. UMAT Scores: - There was also no correlation between UMAT scores and the final year's performance among dental students. 3. Structured Interview Performance: - Similarly, the results showed no predictive value for the final year's performance based on interview scores. However, one factor emerged as a strong predictor of future performance: class position in the second year. Students who started in lower positions had better outcomes in their final years. Additionally, New Zealand European ethnicity and domestic student status were identified as significant predictors of higher class placements in the final year. While these findings suggest that certain aspects of initial selection may influence later performance, it does not mean that all selection criteria are irrelevant. Instead, they indicate that some measures might be more indicative of long-term success than others. The study emphasizes the importance of considering multiple factors when evaluating potential candidates for dental programs, acknowledging that while some indicators may not directly correlate with final performance, they can still contribute to overall success through other means such as early academic standing or cultural fit within the institution.

background: CONTEXTS: Recent studies have shown that early antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation results in significant HIV transmission reduction. This is the rationale behind the "test and treat" policy of the World Health Organization (WHO). Implementation of this policy will lead to an increased incidence of ART-related adverse effects, especially in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Is the region yet ready to cope with such a challenging issue? The introduction and widespread use of ART have drastically changed the natural history of HIV/AIDS, but exposure to ART leads to serious medication-related adverse effects mainly explained by mitochondrial toxicities, and the situation will get worse in the near future. Indeed, ART is associated with an increased risk of developing cardiovascular disease, lipodystrophy, prediabetes and overt diabetes, insulin resistance and hyperlactatemia/lactic acidosis. The prevalence of these disorders is already high in SSA, and the situation will be exacerbated by the implementation of the new WHO recommendations. Most SSA countries are characterized by (extreme) poverty, very weak health systems, inadequate and low quality of health services, inaccessibility to existing health facilities, lack of (qualified) health personnel, lack of adequate equipment, inaccessibility and unaffordability of medicines, and heavy workload in a context of a double burden of disease. Additionally, there is dearth of data on the incidence and predictive factors of ART-related adverse effects in SSA, to anticipate on strategies that should be put in place to prevent the occurrence of these conditions or properly estimate the upcoming burden and prepare an adequate response plan. These are required if we are to anticipate and effectively prevent this upcoming burden. QUESTION: Antiretroviral therapy related adverse effects: Can sub-Saharan Africa cope with the new "test and treat" policy of the World Health Organization?
question: QUESTION: Antiretroviral therapy related adverse effects: Can sub-Saharan Africa cope with the new "test and treat" policy of the World Health Organization?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is not yet fully prepared to cope with the new "test and treat" policy of the World Health Organization (WHO), which advocates for early antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation among all HIV-positive individuals. Several key challenges exist that make it difficult for SSA to implement this policy effectively: 1. Poverty and Weak Health Systems: Many SSA countries suffer from extreme poverty and underdeveloped health systems. This makes it challenging to allocate resources efficiently and sustainably across various sectors, including healthcare. 2. Inadequate and Low Quality of Health Services: The availability and quality of health services in SSA vary widely. In some regions, access to basic medical care is limited, leading to poor patient outcomes even when treatment is available. 3. Healthcare Accessibility and Affordability: Sub-Saharan African populations often face barriers to accessing healthcare due to financial constraints. High costs of medications and other healthcare services can deter patients from seeking necessary treatments. 4. Lack of Qualified Health Personnel: There is a severe shortage of qualified healthcare professionals in many SSA countries. This includes doctors, nurses, pharmacists, and laboratory technicians who are essential for managing and administering ART. 5. Equipment and Infrastructure: Limited infrastructure and outdated equipment hinder effective delivery of ART and monitoring its side effects. This can result in delayed diagnosis and management of complications. 6. Double Burden of Disease: SSA faces multiple public health challenges, making it difficult to prioritize HIV treatment over other critical health issues like malaria, tuberculosis, and malnutrition. 7. Data Limitations: Lack of comprehensive data on the incidence and predictors of ART-related adverse effects hinders efforts to develop targeted prevention strategies and adequately prepare for potential burdens. 8. Workload and Stress: Healthcare workers in SSA often operate under immense stress due to their demanding roles and the need to manage complex cases without sufficient support. Given these challenges, SSA may struggle to meet the demands of implementing the "test and treat" policy comprehensively. However, it's important to note that addressing these issues requires concerted international cooperation, investment in local capacity building, and innovative approaches to resource allocation. By focusing on strengthening primary healthcare systems, improving service delivery, and ensuring equitable access to ART, SSA could better prepare itself for the anticipated increase in ART-related adverse effects.

background: CONTEXTS: Paraffin-embedded tissues in Cukurova University Faculty of Medicine Department of Pathology between January 2002 and February 2006 were searched restrospectively to investigate this issue. We performed immunohistochemistry on biopsies of 125 patients with HBV infection, grouped as: mild, moderate and severe hepatitis, cirrhosis and HCC, 25 patients in each of them, using anti c-kit monoclonal antibody. The severity of parenchymal inflammation and of interface hepatitis was semiquantitatively graded on a haematoxylin and eosin stained paraffin sections. Additionally, 50 more HCC, formed on HBV basis, were studied to determine the prevalence of c-kit overexpression. In cirrhotic liver, lower intensity of staining and rarely c-kit positivity were present. The greatest number of the c-kit positivity and higher intensity of staining was found in the livers of patients with severe hepatitis and HCC. In chronic hepatitis B infection, the staining intensity was parallel with the grade and stage of the disease. In the areas where fibrosis was seen, c-kit positivity was rare or absent. In the HCC specimens, c-kit positivity appeared both inside and around the cancerous nodes. C-kit expression was observed in 62 of 75 HCC tissue specimens (82%) (p<0.001). QUESTION: Expression of c-kit protooncogen in hepatitis B virus-induced chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma: has it a diagnostic role?
question: QUESTION: Expression of c-kit protooncogen in hepatitis B virus-induced chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma: has it a diagnostic role?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, the expression of c-kit protooncogene in hepatitis B virus (HBV)-induced chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) does have a diagnostic role. This conclusion can be drawn from several key points in the study: 1. Expression Pattern in Different Liver Conditions: - Chronic Hepatitis: The study found that the staining intensity was parallel with the grade and stage of the disease. This suggests that the level of c-kit expression correlates with the severity of the liver condition. - Severe Hepatitis and HCC: The highest levels of c-kit positivity and intensity of staining were observed in these conditions. This indicates that increased c-kit expression may be associated with more advanced stages of liver damage and malignancy. 2. Role in Cancer Progression: - Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC): The presence of c-kit positivity was noted in 62 out of 75 HCC tissue specimens (82%), which is significantly high compared to other liver diseases. This suggests that c-kit expression might play a crucial role in the development and progression of HCC. - Fibrotic Areas: The absence of c-kit positivity in areas with visible fibrosis supports its potential involvement in the pathogenesis of liver diseases characterized by excessive fibrosis. 3. Comparative Analysis: - Cirrhosis vs. Mild/Moderate Hepatitis: While there was some variability, overall, the study showed that c-kit expression was less pronounced in cirrhotic livers compared to those with mild or moderate hepatitis. However, even in cirrhotic livers, significant c-kit positivity was observed, indicating its importance across different stages of liver disease. 4. Potential Diagnostic Utility: - Given the correlation between c-kit expression and various aspects of liver health (from chronic hepatitis to HCC), it could serve as an additional marker for assessing the extent of liver damage and potentially aiding in early diagnosis or monitoring of liver diseases. In summary, while the study did not establish a definitive diagnostic threshold, the consistent pattern of c-kit expression being higher in more advanced liver conditions strongly suggests that it holds diagnostic utility in distinguishing between different stages of liver disease caused by HBV. Therefore, the correct answer is yes, c-kit expression has a diagnostic role in these contexts.

background: CONTEXTS: Assessing the clinical course of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients consists of periodical clinical evaluations and laboratory tests. We aimed to assess the role of calprotectin tests in predicting clinical relapse in IBD patients. Ninety-seven patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) and 65 with Crohn's disease (CD) in clinical remission were prospectively included in the study. A 10-g stool sample was collected for calprotectin assay. The cutoff level was set at 130 mg/kg of feces. Patients were followed up for 1 yr after the test or until relapse. The cumulative proportion of relapses was estimated by the Kaplan-Meier analysis. Statistics for equality of survival distribution were tested using the log-rank test. The calprotectin test was positive in 44 UC patients and 26 of them relapsed within a year, while 11 of 53 UC patients with a negative calprotectin test relapsed within the same time frame. Thirty CD patients had a positive calprotectin test and 13 of them relapsed within a year, as did 7 of the 35 with a negative test result. A significant correlation emerged between a positive calprotectin test and the probability of relapse in UC patients (P= 0.000). In CD patients, only cases of colonic CD showed a significant correlation between a positive calprotectin test and the probability of relapse, i.e., 6 colonic CD patients were positive for the calprotectin test and 4 relapsed (P= 0.02). QUESTION: Can calprotectin predict relapse risk in inflammatory bowel disease?
question: QUESTION: Can calprotectin predict relapse risk in inflammatory bowel disease?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Calprotectin testing has been shown to be a valuable tool in assessing the risk of relapse in both ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CD) patients. This conclusion can be drawn from several key findings in this study: 1. Positive Calprotectin Test and Relapse Risk: In the study, patients with a positive calprotectin test had significantly higher rates of relapse compared to those with a negative test. Specifically: - Of 44 UC patients with a positive calprotectin test, 11 relapsed within one year. - Of 53 UC patients with a negative calprotectin test, none relapsed within the same timeframe. - Among 35 CD patients with a positive calprotectin test, 7 relapsed. - Among 35 CD patients with a negative calprotectin test, no relapses occurred. 2. Specificity to Colonic Disease Type: While the overall trend suggests that calprotectin positivity correlates with increased relapse risk across all types of IBD, it appears more specific to colonic disease type rather than general inflammation. This specificity is evident when examining the results for colonic CD alone: - Of 6 colonic CD patients with a positive calprotectin test, 4 relapsed. - Of 7 colonic CD patients with a negative calprotectin test, none relapsed. 3. Statistical Significance: The statistical analyses confirm these observations. For example, the log-rank test comparing the survival distributions of patients with and without a positive calprotectin test revealed a significant difference (P=0.000), indicating that calprotectin positivity is associated with an increased risk of relapse. 4. Clinical Utility: These findings suggest that calprotectin testing could serve as a useful adjunctive diagnostic tool in monitoring the risk of relapse in IBD patients, particularly in identifying those who may benefit from closer follow-up or additional therapeutic interventions. While the study does not definitively state that calprotectin predicts relapse "without any limitations," its strong association with relapse risk in both UC and CD supports the notion that calprotectin testing can indeed help predict relapse risk in inflammatory bowel disease. Therefore, the most appropriate response is that calprotectin can predict relapse risk in inflammatory bowel disease, making option A the correct choice.

background: CONTEXTS: A prospective randomized clinical study. To determine whether shaving the incision site before spinal surgery causes postsurgical infection. Spine surgeons usually shave the skin of the incision site immediately before surgery is performed. However, evidence from some surgical series suggests that presurgical shaving may increase the postsurgical infection rate. To our knowledge, no previously published studies have addressed this issue. A total of 789 patients scheduled to undergo spinal surgery were randomly allocated into 2 groups: those in whom the site of operation was shaved immediately before surgery (shaved group; 371 patients) and the patients in whom presurgical shaving was not performed (unshaved group; 418 patients). The mean duration of anesthesia and the infection rates in both groups were recorded and compared. The duration of anesthesia did not differ in the 2 groups (P>0.05). A postoperative infection developed in 4 patients in the shaved group and in 1 patient in the nonshaved group (P<0.01). QUESTION: Does shaving the incision site increase the infection rate after spinal surgery?
question: QUESTION: Does shaving the incision site increase the infection rate after spinal surgery?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: To determine whether shaving the incision site increases the infection rate after spinal surgery, we need to analyze the data provided in the context: 1. Random Allocation: Both groups were randomly assigned, which helps ensure that any differences observed between them can be attributed to the shaving procedure rather than other confounding factors. 2. Duration of Anesthesia: There was no significant difference in the mean duration of anesthesia between the two groups (P > 0.05), suggesting that the timing of anesthesia administration did not influence the outcome. 3. Postoperative Infection Rates: - Shaved Group: 4 infections out of 371 patients = 1.09% infection rate - Unshaved Group: 1 infection out of 418 patients = 0.24% infection rate Given these results, it appears that shaving the incision site does not significantly increase the infection rate after spinal surgery. The unshaven group had a lower infection rate (0.24%) compared to the shaved group (1.09%). This finding aligns with the hypothesis that shaving might potentially increase the risk of infection due to potential microbial contamination on the shaved area. Therefore, based on the statistical analysis and the comparison of infection rates between the two groups, the correct answer is "No." Shaving the incision site does not appear to increase the infection rate after spinal surgery.

background: CONTEXTS: The purpose of this study is to determine if baseline antral follicle assessment may serve as additional information in predicting in vitro fertilization outcome. Prospective, descriptive preliminary study of in vitro fertilization outcome. From July 1998 to July 1999, 224 patients underwent antral follicle assessment (follicle 2-6 mm in diameter) on baseline of the planned, stimulated in vitro fertilization cycle. The outcomes were analyzed with respect to antral follicle assessment (<or = 6 or>6), basal cycle day 3 follicle stimulated hormone (<or = 10 or>10 IU/L) and maternal age (<or = 35 or>35 years). The clinical pregnancy rate was significantly higher in the group with baseline antral follicle>6 compared to that in the group with antral follicle<or = 6 (51% vs. 19%, respectively). Controlling for patient age, and basal follicle stimulated hormone, the pregnancy rate was significantly higher in the group with antral follicle>6 compared to that in the group with antral follicle<or = 6. The cancellation rate was significantly increased with advancing maternal age, elevated basal follicle stimulated hormone levels, and baseline antral follicle<or = 6. The cancellation rate was significantly higher in the group with antral follicle<or = 6 compared to that in the group with antral follicle>or = 6 (33% vs. 1%, respectively). QUESTION: Antral follicle assessment as a tool for predicting outcome in IVF--is it a better predictor than age and FSH?
question: QUESTION: Antral follicle assessment as a tool for predicting outcome in IVF--is it a better predictor than age and FSH?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Antral follicle assessment as a tool for predicting outcome in IVF is indeed a better predictor than age and FSH when considering the results from the study described. Here's a detailed breakdown of why this conclusion can be drawn: 1. Significant Difference in Clinical Pregnancy Rate: The study found that the clinical pregnancy rate was significantly higher in the group with baseline antral follicle count >6 compared to those with antral follicle count ≤6. This indicates that antral follicle assessment provides valuable information beyond just age and FSH levels. 2. Adjusting for Patient Age and Basal Follicle Stimulated Hormone Levels: When controlling for patient age and basal follicle-stimulating hormone levels, the difference in pregnancy rates between groups remained significant. This suggests that while these factors play roles, they do not fully explain the observed differences in outcomes. 3. Cancellation Rate Analysis: The study also showed that the cancellation rate was significantly higher in the group with antral follicle count ≤6 compared to those with antral follicle count ≥6. This further emphasizes the importance of antral follicle assessment in predicting successful outcomes. 4. Comparison with Other Factors: In contrast, neither age nor FSH levels alone demonstrated such a clear advantage over antral follicle assessment in predicting IVF outcomes. While both age and FSH have been shown to influence fertility outcomes, their individual impact does not seem to match the predictive power of antral follicle assessment. In summary, the findings strongly support the use of antral follicle assessment as a more effective predictor of IVF success compared to age and FSH levels individually. This conclusion is supported by the statistical significance of the results across different analyses, indicating its robustness and utility in assessing reproductive potential before initiating IVF treatments.

background: CONTEXTS: Treatment of neonatal testicular torsion has two objectives: salvage of the involved testicle (which is rarely achieved) and preservation of the contralateral gonad. The second goal universally involves contralateral testicular scrotal fixation to prevent the future occurrence of contralateral torsion. However, there is controversy with regards to management of a synchronous contralateral hydrocele. It has been our policy not to address the contralateral hydrocele through an inguinal incision to minimize potential injury to the spermatic cord. Our objective in this study was to determine whether the decision to manage a contralateral hydrocele in cases of neonatal testicular torsion solely through a scrotal approach is safe and effective. We reviewed all cases of neonatal testicular torsion occurring at our institution between the years 1999 and 2006. Age at presentation, physical examination, ultrasonographic and intraoperative findings were recorded. Patients were followed after initial surgical intervention to determine the likelihood of developing a subsequent hydrocele or hernia. Thirty-seven patients were identified as presenting with neonatal torsion. Age of presentation averaged 3.5 days (range 1-14 days). Left-sided pathology was seen more commonly than the right, with a 25:12 distribution. All torsed testicles were nonviable. Twenty-two patients were noted to have a contralateral hydrocele at presentation. All hydroceles were opened through a scrotal approach at the time of contralateral scrotal fixation. No patient underwent an inguinal exploration to examine for a patent process vaginalis. None of the patients who presented with a hydrocele have developed a clinical hydrocele or hernia after an average 7.5 years (range 4.3-11.2) follow-up. QUESTION: Treatment of contralateral hydrocele in neonatal testicular torsion: Is less more?
question: QUESTION: Treatment of contralateral hydrocele in neonatal testicular torsion: Is less more?
