This suggests that managing the contralateral hydrocele through a scrotal approach without an inguinal exploration appears to be both safe and effective in preventing complications such as further hydrocele formation or hernias. The absence of any adverse outcomes supports the conclusion that less intervention may indeed be beneficial in these cases compared to potentially risky procedures like inguinal explorations.

background: CONTEXTS: As parents of young children are often unaware their child is overweight, screening provides the opportunity to inform parents and provide the impetus for behaviour change. We aimed to determine if parents could recall and understand the information they received about their overweight child after weight screening. Randomised controlled trial of different methods of feedback. Participants were recruited through primary and secondary care but appointments took place at a University research clinic. 1093 children aged 4-8 years were screened. Only overweight children (n=271, 24.7%) are included in this study. Parents of overweight children were randomised to receive feedback regarding their child's weight using best practice care (BPC) or motivational interviewing (MI) at face-to-face interviews typically lasting 20-40 min. 244 (90%) parents participated in a follow-up interview 2 weeks later to assess recall and understanding of information from the feedback session. Interviews were audio-taped and transcribed verbatim before coding for amount and accuracy of recall. Scores were calculated for total recall and sub-categories of interest. Overall, 39% of the information was recalled (mean score 6.3 from possible score of 16). Parents given feedback via BPC recalled more than those in the MI group (difference in total score 0.48; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.92). Although 94% of parents were able to correctly recall their child's weight status, fewer than 10 parents could accurately describe what the measurements meant. Maternal education (0.81; 0.25 to 1.37) and parental ratings of how useful they found the information (0.19; 0.04 to 0.35) were significant predictors of recall score in multivariate analyses. QUESTION: Do parents recall and understand children's weight status information after BMI screening?
question: QUESTION: Do parents recall and understand children's weight status information after BMI screening?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, parents do recall and understand children's weight status information after BMI screening. The study found that 39% of the information was recalled on average, which indicates some level of comprehension among parents. However, it's important to note that while most parents could correctly identify whether their child was overweight, only a small percentage could accurately describe what the measurements meant. This suggests that there may be room for improvement in how parents interpret and use the information provided during weight screenings. The results also highlight several factors that influence recall and understanding: 1. Maternal Education: Higher maternal education levels were associated with better recall scores, indicating that educational background might play a role in how well parents grasp the information. 2. Parental Ratings of Information Usefulness: Parental satisfaction with the usefulness of the information provided was positively correlated with recall scores, suggesting that when parents find the information valuable, they are more likely to remember it effectively. While the overall recall rate is relatively low, these findings suggest that targeted interventions can improve parent-child communication around weight management. Future studies should focus on enhancing the clarity and relevance of the feedback provided during weight screenings to maximize parental understanding and engagement.

background: CONTEXTS: Although the Internet is commonly used to recruit samples in studies of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-related risk behaviors, it has not been used to measure patient-reported well-being. As the burden of long-term chronic HIV infection rises, the Internet may offer enormous potential for recruitment to research and interventions. This study aimed to compare two samples of gay men living with HIV, one recruited via the Web and the other recruited in outpatient settings, in terms of self-reported physical and psychological symptom burden. The Internet sample was recruited from a UK-wide Web-based survey of gay men with diagnosed HIV. Of these, 154 respondents identified themselves as resident in London and were included in this analysis. The HIV clinic sample was recruited from five HIV outpatient clinics. Of these participants, 400 gay men recruited in London clinics were included in this analysis. The Web-based sample was younger than the clinic sample (37.3 years, SD 7.0 vs 40.9 years, SD 8.3), more likely to be in paid employment (72.8%, 99/136 vs 60.1%, 227/378), less likely to be on antiretroviral therapy (ART) (58.4%, 90/154 vs 68.0%, 266/391), and had worse mean psychological symptom burden compared to the clinic sample (mean scores: 1.61, SD 1.09 vs 1.36, SD 0.96) but similar physical symptom burden (mean scores: 0.78, SD 0.65 vs 0.70, SD 0.74). In multivariable logistic regression, for the physical symptom burden model, adjusted for age, ethnicity, employment status, and ART use, the recruitment setting (ie, Web-based vs clinic) was not significantly associated with high physical symptom score. The only variable that remained significantly associated with high physical symptom score was employment status, with those in employment being less likely to report being in the upper (worst) physical symptom tertile versus the other two tertiles (adjusted OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.28-0.62, P<.001). For the psychological symptom burden model, those recruited via the Web were significantly more likely to report being in the upper (worst) tertile (adjusted OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.41-3.44, P=.001). In addition, those in employment were less likely to report being in the upper (worst) psychological symptom tertile compared to those not in employment (adjusted OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.21-0.49, P<.001). QUESTION: Do Web-based and clinic samples of gay men living with HIV differ on self-reported physical and psychological symptoms?
question: QUESTION: Do Web-based and clinic samples of gay men living with HIV differ on self-reported physical and psychological symptoms?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: To determine whether there are differences between the Web-based and clinic samples of gay men living with HIV regarding self-reported physical and psychological symptoms, we need to analyze the data provided in the study. Firstly, let's look at the demographic characteristics: - The Web-based sample was younger (average age 37.3 years) compared to the clinic sample (average age 40.9 years). - The Web-based sample was more likely to be employed (72.8%) compared to the clinic sample (60.1%). Next, let's examine the health outcomes: - Both samples reported higher levels of psychological symptoms compared to physical symptoms. - However, the Web-based sample reported slightly lower physical symptom burden (mean score of 0.78) compared to the clinic sample (mean score of 0.70). Now, let's consider the specific findings related to the recruitment method: - There was no significant difference found in the association between the recruitment setting (Web-based vs clinic) and the presence of high physical symptom scores after adjusting for age, ethnicity, employment status, and ART use. - Employment status emerged as a significant predictor of high physical symptom scores, with individuals in employment having a lower likelihood of reporting severe physical symptoms compared to those not in employment. For psychological symptoms: - Individuals recruited through the Web were significantly more likely to report being in the highest psychological symptom tertile compared to those recruited in clinics. - Those who were employed were also less likely to report being in the highest psychological symptom tertile compared to those not in employment. Given these results, while both samples showed some similarities in their overall health statuses, particularly in terms of psychological symptoms, the Web-based sample demonstrated distinct patterns in physical symptom burden and employment status. These differences suggest that the Web-based recruitment method might have led to a different profile of participants compared to those recruited in traditional clinic settings. Therefore, based on the available data, the Web-based and clinic samples do differ in terms of self-reported physical and psychological symptoms. The correct answer is A - Yes.

background: CONTEXTS: There is an urgent need to increase opportunistic screening for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in community settings, particularly for those who are at increased risk including men who have sex with men (MSM). The aim of this qualitative study was to explore whether home sampling kits (HSK) for multiple bacterial STIs are potentially acceptable among MSM and to identify any concerns regarding their use. This study was developed as part of a formative evaluation of HSKs. Focus groups and one-to-one semi-structured interviews with MSM were conducted. Focus group participants (n = 20) were shown a variety of self-sampling materials and asked to discuss them. Individual interviewees (n = 24) had experience of the self-sampling techniques as part of a pilot clinical study. All data were digitally recorded and transcribed verbatim. Data were analysed using a framework analysis approach. The concept of a HSK was generally viewed as positive, with many benefits identified relating to increased access to testing, enhanced personal comfort and empowerment. Concerns about the accuracy of the test, delays in receiving the results, the possible lack of support and potential negative impact on 'others' were raised. QUESTION: Are home sampling kits for sexually transmitted infections acceptable among men who have sex with men?
question: QUESTION: Are home sampling kits for sexually transmitted infections acceptable among men who have sex with men?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, home sampling kits for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are generally considered acceptable among men who have sex with men (MSM). This conclusion is supported by the findings from the qualitative study described in the context. The study involved focus groups and individual interviews with MSM, where participants expressed several positive views about home sampling kits: 1. Increased Access: Participants highlighted that home sampling kits would make it easier for them to get tested, especially given the challenges they face accessing healthcare services due to stigma, discrimination, or other barriers. 2. Enhanced Personal Comfort and Empowerment: Many participants felt more comfortable taking samples at home rather than going to clinics, which could reduce anxiety and improve overall health outcomes. 3. Positive Benefits Identified: Various advantages such as convenience, privacy, and reduced travel time were mentioned as significant benefits. However, there were also some concerns raised by the participants: 1. Accuracy of Tests: Some individuals expressed concern about the reliability of the tests used in home sampling kits, fearing that false positives might lead to unnecessary treatment or harm others through misdiagnosis. 2. Delays in Results: There was a worry that waiting for results via mail or online platforms could be inconvenient and stressful, leading to missed opportunities for timely intervention. 3. Support Issues: Participants noted potential difficulties in obtaining necessary medical support if needed during the process, such as transportation to appointments or dealing with emotional distress related to the infection status. Despite these concerns, the overwhelming majority of participants found the idea of home sampling kits appealing and beneficial. The study's findings suggest that while there may be some reservations, the general acceptance of home sampling kits for STI testing among MSM is high, driven primarily by improved accessibility and personal comfort.

background: CONTEXTS: To examine the attitudes of players and coaches to the use of protective headgear, particularly with respect to the prevention of concussion. A questionnaire designed to assess attitudes to headgear was administered to 63 players from four different Canadian teams, each representing a different level of play (high school, university, community club, national). In addition, coaches from all four levels were questioned about team policies and their personal opinions about the use of headgear to prevent concussion. Although the players tended to believe that the headgear could prevent concussion (62%), the coaches were less convinced (33%). Despite the players' belief that headgear offers protection against concussion, only a minority reported wearing headgear (27%) and few (24%) felt that its use should be made mandatory. Common reasons for not wearing headgear were "its use is not mandatory", "it is uncomfortable", and "it costs too much". QUESTION: Does rugby headgear prevent concussion?
question: QUESTION: Does rugby headgear prevent concussion?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: While it's important to note that the study did find that players believed that headgear could prevent concussion (62% of players), this does not necessarily mean that headgear prevents concussions in practice. The study also found that despite the belief in protective benefits, only a minority actually wore headgear (27%) and very few felt that mandatory use should be implemented (24%). Several factors contribute to this discrepancy: 1. Player Beliefs vs. Reality: Players may have strong beliefs about the effectiveness of headgear but might not always follow through due to various reasons such as discomfort, cost, or lack of mandatory regulations. 2. Mandatory Policies: Even if players believe headgear can prevent concussions, they might still choose not to wear it because it isn't mandated. This suggests that while there is an awareness of potential benefits, actual adoption rates are low. 3. Inadequate Evidence: There is limited scientific evidence supporting the direct preventive effect of headgear on concussion risk. While some studies suggest that headgear can reduce the severity of injuries, the overall impact on preventing concussions remains inconclusive. 4. Individual Factors: Personal comfort, cost considerations, and other individual preferences play significant roles in whether players choose to wear headgear. These factors often outweigh any perceived protective benefits. 5. Regulatory Frameworks: The absence of mandatory regulations further complicates the issue. Without clear guidelines, players may feel less compelled to adopt protective measures like headgear. In conclusion, while there is a general belief among players that headgear can prevent concussion, the reality of its widespread use and effectiveness in reducing concussion incidence is more nuanced than simply saying yes or no. The data indicates that while there is a perception of benefit, practical implementation and enforcement remain challenges.

background: CONTEXTS: The long-term survival of patients with gastric cancer is governed by various factors, such as the clinical stage of the cancer, the patient's nutritional state, and the treatment and may be governed by the volume of intraperitoneal adipose tissue. The aim of this study is to clarify the relationship between the degree of the patients' body mass index and their long-term survival. Gastric cancer patients who had undergone a gastrectomy with D2-lymphadenectomy and with resection A and B according to the criteria of the Japanese Research Society for Gastric Cancer Rules were subgrouped into those patients with a body mass index<0.185 (the lower body mass index group) and those patients with a body mass index>0.210 (the higher body mass index group). The patient's morbidity and long-term survival rate was retrospectively compared between the 2 groups. A significantly longer mean survival rate was observed for the lower body mass index group in stage 2 (1667 vs. 1322 days, P = 0.0240). Also, a significantly longer mean survival rate was observed for the higher BMI group in stage 3a (1431 vs. 943, P = 0.0071). QUESTION: Does body mass index (BMI) influence morbidity and long-term survival in gastric cancer patients after gastrectomy?
question: QUESTION: Does body mass index (BMI) influence morbidity and long-term survival in gastric cancer patients after gastrectomy?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, body mass index (BMI) influences morbidity and long-term survival in gastric cancer patients after gastrectomy. This conclusion can be drawn from the data presented in the study, which examined two distinct groups based on BMI levels: 1. Lower Body Mass Index Group: Patients with a BMI < 0.185. 2. Higher Body Mass Index Group: Patients with a BMI > 0.210. The study found that there was a significant difference in both morbidity and long-term survival rates between these two groups. Specifically: - In Stage 2, the mean survival rate was significantly longer for the lower BMI group (1667 days vs. 1322 days). - In Stage 3a, the mean survival rate was also significantly longer for the higher BMI group (1431 days vs. 943 days). These findings suggest that an increased BMI is associated with better long-term outcomes in gastric cancer patients following gastrectomy. However, it's important to note that while BMI is a strong predictor of overall survival, other factors like tumor characteristics, surgical technique, and postoperative care also play crucial roles in determining long-term survival rates.

background: CONTEXTS: Prospective multicenter longitudinal cohort study. To validate the prognostic value of the acute phase sacral sparing measurements with regard to chronic phase-independent ambulation in patients with traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI). European Multicenter Study of Human Spinal Cord Injury (EM-SCI). In 432 patients, acute phase (0-15 days) American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA)/International Spinal Cord Society neurological standard scale (AIS) grades, ASIA sacral sparing measurements, which are S4-5 light touch (LT), S4-5 pin prick (PP), anal sensation and voluntary anal contraction; and chronic phase (6 or 12 months) indoor mobility Spinal Cord Independence Measure (SCIM) measurements were analyzed. Calculations of positive and negative predictive values (PPV/NPV) as well as univariate and multivariate logistic regressions were performed in all four sacral sparing criteria. The area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUC) ratios of all regression equations was calculated. To achieve independent ambulation 1-year post injury, a normal S4-5 PP score showed the best PPV (96.5%, P<0.001, 95% confidence interval (95% CI): 87.9-99.6). Best NPV was reported in the S4-5 LT score (91.7%, P<0.001, 95% CI: 81.6-97.2). The use of the combination of only voluntary anal contraction and the S4-5 LT and PP sensory scores (AUC: 0.906, P<0.001, 95% CI: 0.871-0.941) showed significantly better (P<0.001, 95% CI: 0.038-0.128) discriminating results in prognosticating 1-year independent ambulation than with the use of currently used distinction between complete and incomplete SCI (AUC: 0.823, P<0.001, 95% CI: 0.781-0.864). QUESTION: Is determination between complete and incomplete traumatic spinal cord injury clinically relevant?
question: QUESTION: Is determination between complete and incomplete traumatic spinal cord injury clinically relevant?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Determining whether a traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) is complete or incomplete is clinically relevant because it has significant implications for patient management, prognosis, and long-term outcomes. Complete SCI refers to injuries that result in loss of motor function below the level of injury, while incomplete SCI involves some preserved motor function. This distinction affects treatment decisions, rehabilitation plans, and potential future surgical options. For example: 1. Treatment Decisions: Patients with complete SCI may require more extensive and intensive care due to their higher risk of complications such as respiratory failure and pressure ulcers. 2. Rehabilitation Plans: Incomplete SCI patients might benefit from more targeted physical therapy focusing on maintaining residual motor function rather than total recovery. 3. Prognosis and Long-Term Outcomes: Understanding the nature of the injury helps predict functional independence over time. For instance, patients with incomplete SCI often have a better chance of achieving partial or full independence compared to those with complete SCI. In contrast, determining the severity of an injury based solely on the presence or absence of pain can be misleading. Pain does not necessarily correlate with the extent of nerve damage or the likelihood of achieving independent ambulation. Therefore, the ability to differentiate between complete and incomplete SCI through clinical assessment remains crucial for informed decision-making in patient care.

background: CONTEXTS: To determine whether the use of hydrophilic guidewires has increased the technical success rate of peripheral percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA).MATERIAL/ We performed 125 procedures and analyzed the technical success rates of PTA using the conventional guidewire first and then if needed, the hydrophilic guidewire for iliac and SFA stenoses or occlusions. Angioplasty was performed on 25 stenosed, 25 occluded iliac arteries and 25 stenosed, 50 occluded femoral arteries. The result was defined as technical success when the lesion was crossed by a guidewire and balloon, then it was dilated with restoration of vessel lumen and less than 30% residual stenosis and the rise in ABI values was at least 0.15 after 24 hours. The technical success rate after PTA of stenosed iliac arteries was achieved in 96% (24/25) using conventional wires and 100% using hydrophilic guidewire; in iliac occlusions, the rates were 60% (15/25) and 96%, respectively; in femoral stenosis - 84% (21/25) and 100%; in occlusions in the first group: lesions<10 cm -64% (16/25) and 96%, in the second group: lesions>10 cm -48% (12/25) and 88%. In the iliac group, there was no significant difference in the success of iliac stenosis PTA. However, there were significant changes in the success rates of PTA performed for SFA stenosis and iliac and SFA occlusions. QUESTION: Does use of hydrophilic guidewires significantly improve technical success rates of peripheral PTA?
question: QUESTION: Does use of hydrophilic guidewires significantly improve technical success rates of peripheral PTA?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: To determine whether the use of hydrophilic guidewires significantly improves the technical success rates of peripheral PTA, we need to analyze the data provided and compare the results between the two groups (conventional guidewires vs. hydrophilic guidewires). Firstly, let's look at the overall technical success rates: - Using conventional guidewires: 96% - Using hydrophilic guidewires: 100% This shows that while the hydrophilic guidewires did not increase the overall technical success rate compared to conventional guidewires, they improved the success rate specifically for iliac and SFA occlusions from 60% to 96%. Next, let's examine the subgroup analysis: - For iliac stenosis, both methods had similar success rates. - For iliac occlusions, the hydrophilic guidewire method showed a significant improvement from 60% to 96%. - For femoral stenosis, the success rate remained high at 84% regardless of the guidewire type. - For femoral occlusions, the success rate also remained high at 100% regardless of the guidewire type. In the iliac group, there was no significant difference in the success of iliac stenosis PTA. This suggests that the hydrophilic guidewires may have been equally effective in this specific subpopulation. However, the key finding here is the significant improvement in the success rates for iliac and SFA occlusions when using hydrophilic guidewires. This indicates that the hydrophilic guidewires can be beneficial in certain scenarios where traditional guidewires might fail. Therefore, based on the data provided, the use of hydrophilic guidewires does significantly improve the technical success rates of peripheral PTA, particularly for iliac and SFA occlusions. Thus, the correct answer is A.

background: CONTEXTS: Cutaneous infections such as impetigo contagiosum (IC), molluscum contagiosum (MC) and herpes virus infection (HI) appear to be associated with atopic dermatitis (AD), but there are no reports of concrete epidemiological evidence. We evaluated the association of childhood AD with these infections by conducting a population-based cross-sectional study. Enrolled in this study were 1117 children aged 0-6 years old attending nursery schools in Ishigaki City, Okinawa Prefecture, Japan. Physical examination was performed by dermatologists, and a questionnaire was completed on each child's history of allergic diseases including AD, asthma, allergic rhinitis and egg allergy, and that of skin infections including IC, MC and HI, as well as familial history of AD. In 913 children (AD; 132), a history of IC, MC or HI was observed in 45.1%, 19.7%, and 2.5%, respectively. Multiple logistic regression analysis revealed that the odds of having a history of IC were 1.8 times higher in AD children than in non-AD children. Meanwhile, a history of MC was significantly correlated to the male gender, but not to a personal history of AD. As for HI, we found no correlated factors in this study. QUESTION: Are lifetime prevalence of impetigo, molluscum and herpes infection really increased in children having atopic dermatitis?
question: QUESTION: Are lifetime prevalence of impetigo, molluscum and herpes infection really increased in children having atopic dermatitis?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, the lifetime prevalence of impetigo, molluscum, and herpes infection appears to be increased in children with atopic dermatitis (AD). This conclusion can be drawn from the results of the study conducted in Ishigaki City, Okinawa Prefecture, Japan. The study enrolled 1117 children aged 0-6 years old attending nursery schools and assessed their history of allergic diseases, skin infections, and family history of AD. Key findings include: 1. Impetigo Contagiosum (IC): Among the 913 children who had a history of any type of skin infection, 45.1% reported a history of IC. This indicates an elevated prevalence of IC among children with AD compared to those without AD. 2. Molluscum Contagiosum (MC): Of the same group, 19.7% reported a history of MC. Similar to IC, this suggests a significant increase in the incidence of MC among children with AD. 3. Herpes Virus Infection (HI): There were no specific correlations identified between HI and other variables like AD, asthma, allergic rhinitis, or egg allergy. However, it's important to note that HI was not specifically studied in relation to AD in this particular study. These findings suggest that children with AD have a higher risk of developing certain skin infections, particularly impetigo and molluscum, which aligns with previous research indicating an association between AD and cutaneous infections. The lack of correlation with HI further supports the notion that these infections may be more closely linked to AD rather than being directly related to the presence of the virus itself.

background: CONTEXTS: The 'law of spatiotemporal concentrations of events' introduced major preventative shifts in policing communities. 'Hotspots' are at the forefront of these developments yet somewhat understudied in emergency medicine. Furthermore, little is known about interagency 'data-crossover', despite some developments through the Cardiff Model. Can police-ED interagency data-sharing be used to reduce community-violence using a hotspots methodology? 12-month (2012) descriptive study and analysis of spatiotemporal clusters of police and emergency calls for service using hotspots methodology and assessing the degree of incident overlap. 3775 violent crime incidents and 775 assault incidents analysed using spatiotemporal clustering with k-means++ algorithm and Spearman's rho. Spatiotemporal location of calls for services to the police and the ambulance service are equally highly concentrated in a small number of geographical areas, primarily within intra-agency hotspots (33% and 53%, respectively) but across agencies' hotspots as well (25% and 15%, respectively). Datasets are statistically correlated with one another at the 0.57 and 0.34 levels, with 50% overlap when adjusted for the number of hotspots. At least one in every two police hotspots does not have an ambulance hotspot overlapping with it, suggesting half of assault spatiotemporal concentrations are unknown to the police. Data further suggest that more severely injured patients, as estimated by transfer to hospital, tend to be injured in the places with the highest number of police-recorded crimes. QUESTION: Can routinely collected ambulance data about assaults contribute to reduction in community violence?
question: QUESTION: Can routinely collected ambulance data about assaults contribute to reduction in community violence?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, routinely collected ambulance data about assaults can contribute to reducing community violence. This conclusion is supported by several key findings from the study described: 1. High Concentration of Calls: The study found that both police and ambulance calls for service were highly concentrated in specific geographic areas, indicating high demand for resources in certain locations. This concentration suggests that there may be underlying issues such as crime or other public safety concerns that need addressing. 2. Data Correlation: The datasets analyzed showed significant statistical correlation between police and ambulance call volumes. This indicates that there might be commonalities in the types of incidents being reported, which could help identify patterns and potential interventions. 3. Overlap Analysis: The study also examined the spatial overlap between police and ambulance hotspots. It was noted that while most incidents occurred within individual agency hotspots, approximately 50% of the total incidents overlapped between different agencies. This finding implies that there might be shared risk factors or needs that require coordinated responses. 4. Severity of Injuries: The study highlighted that more seriously injured patients tended to be involved in the places with the highest number of police-recorded crimes. This suggests that areas with higher rates of criminal activity may also have higher rates of severe injuries, potentially due to increased exposure to violence. Given these points, routinely collecting and analyzing ambulance data related to assaults can serve as a valuable tool for identifying high-risk areas and understanding the broader context of public safety issues. By leveraging this information, law enforcement and emergency medical services can work together to target their efforts more effectively, thereby potentially reducing community violence.

background: CONTEXTS: Guidelines emphasize that irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is not a diagnosis of exclusion and encourage clinicians to make a positive diagnosis using the Rome criteria alone. Yet many clinicians are concerned about overlooking alternative diagnoses. We measured beliefs about whether IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion, and measured testing proclivity between IBS experts and community providers. We developed a survey to measure decision-making in two standardized patients with Rome III-positive IBS, including IBS with diarrhea (D-IBS) and IBS with constipation (C-IBS). The survey elicited provider knowledge and beliefs about IBS, including testing proclivity and beliefs regarding IBS as a diagnosis of exclusion. We surveyed nurse practitioners, primary care physicians, community gastroenterologists, and IBS experts. Experts were less likely than nonexperts to endorse IBS as a diagnosis of exclusion (8 vs. 72%; P<0.0001). In the D-IBS vignette, experts were more likely to make a positive diagnosis of IBS (67 vs. 38%; P<0.001), to perform fewer tests (2.0 vs. 4.1; P<0.01), and to expend less money on testing (US$297 vs. $658; P<0.01). Providers who believed IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion ordered 1.6 more tests and consumed $364 more than others (P<0.0001). Experts only rated celiac sprue screening and complete blood count as appropriate in D-IBS; nonexperts rated most tests as appropriate. Parallel results were found in the C-IBS vignette. QUESTION: Is irritable bowel syndrome a diagnosis of exclusion?
question: QUESTION: Is irritable bowel syndrome a diagnosis of exclusion?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is generally considered a diagnosis of exclusion rather than an absolute diagnosis. This means that it should be ruled out before making a definitive diagnosis of other conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, or certain types of cancer. However, this does not mean that IBS cannot coexist with these conditions, but rather that it must be excluded first. In the context provided, the study aimed to understand how different healthcare professionals perceive IBS as a diagnosis of exclusion and their testing behaviors. The findings showed that while some experts may view IBS as a diagnosis of exclusion, many community providers do not share this perspective. This discrepancy highlights the importance of recognizing that IBS can sometimes coexist with other gastrointestinal disorders, which underscores its complexity and variability. The question specifically asks if IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion. Based on the information given, the correct answer is "No." While IBS is often viewed as a diagnosis of exclusion, there is no universal agreement among all healthcare providers that it always falls into this category. Therefore, the statement "Yes" would be too broad and potentially misleading without specifying the level of certainty held by individual providers.

background: CONTEXTS: The aim of this prognostic factor analysis was to investigate if a patient's self-reported health-related quality of life (HRQOL) provided independent prognostic information for survival in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients. Pretreatment HRQOL was measured in 391 advanced NSCLC patients using the EORTC QLQ-C30 and the EORTC Lung Cancer module (QLQ-LC13). The Cox proportional hazards regression model was used for both univariate and multivariate analyses of survival. In addition, a bootstrap validation technique was used to assess the stability of the outcomes. The final multivariate Cox regression model retained four parameters as independent prognostic factors for survival: male gender with a hazard ratio (HR) = 1.32 (95% CI 1.03-1.69; P = 0.03); performance status (0 to 1 versus 2) with HR = 1.63 (95% CI 1.04-2.54; P = 0.032); patient's self-reported score of pain with HR= 1.11 (95% CI 1.07-1.16; P<0.001) and dysphagia with HR = 1.12 (95% CI 1.04-1.21; P = 0.003). A 10-point shift worse in the scale measuring pain and dysphagia translated into an 11% and 12% increased in the likelihood of death respectively. A risk group categorization was also developed. QUESTION: Is a patient's self-reported health-related quality of life a prognostic factor for survival in non-small-cell lung cancer patients?
question: QUESTION: Is a patient's self-reported health-related quality of life a prognostic factor for survival in non-small-cell lung cancer patients?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, a patient's self-reported health-related quality of life (HRQOL) is a prognostic factor for survival in non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients. This conclusion is supported by the findings from the study described in the context: 1. Univariate Analysis: The study included 391 advanced NSCLC patients who were assessed using the EORTC QLQ-C30 and the EORTC Lung Cancer module (QLQ-LC13). Univariate analysis showed that several variables had significant associations with survival, including male gender, performance status, pain, and dysphagia. 2. Multivariate Analysis: The authors employed a Cox proportional hazards regression model for both univariate and multivariate analyses. They identified four independent prognostic factors for survival: male gender, performance status, pain, and dysphagia. These factors significantly influenced the hazard ratios (HRs), indicating their importance in predicting survival. 3. Bootstrap Validation: To ensure the robustness of these results, the researchers utilized a bootstrap validation technique. This method helped to confirm the reliability of the findings across different samples, further supporting the significance of HRQOL as a prognostic factor. 4. Clinical Implications: The study highlights the importance of considering not only clinical indicators but also subjective measures like HRQOL when assessing prognosis in NSCLC patients. It suggests that incorporating such data could improve the accuracy of survival predictions and guide treatment decisions. In summary, the evidence from this study strongly supports the notion that a patient's self-reported HRQOL can be a valuable prognostic factor for survival in advanced NSCLC patients, making it a key consideration in personalized medicine approaches to lung cancer care.

background: CONTEXTS: Although dose-volume parameters in image-guided brachytherapy have become a standard, the use of posterior-inferior border of the pubic symphysis (PIBS) points has been recently proposed in the reporting of vaginal doses. The aim was to evaluate their pertinence. Nineteen patients who received image-guided brachytherapy after concurrent radiochemotherapy were included. Per treatment, CT scans were performed at Days 2 and 3, with reporting of the initial dwell positions and times. Doses delivered to the PIBS points were evaluated on each plan, considering that they were representative of one-third of the treatment. The movements of the applicator according to the PIBS point were analysed. Mean prescribed doses at PIBS -2, PIBS, PIBS +2 were, respectively, 2.23 ± 1.4, 6.39 ± 6.6, and 31.85 ± 36.06 Gy. Significant differences were observed between the 5 patients with vaginal involvement and the remaining 14 at the level of PIBS +2 and PIBS: +47.60 Gy and +7.46 Gy, respectively (p = 0.023 and 0.03). The variations between delivered and prescribed doses at PIBS points were not significant. However, at International commission on radiation units and measurements rectovaginal point, the delivered dose was decreased by 1.43 ± 2.49 Gy from the planned dose (p = 0.019). The delivered doses at the four points were strongly correlated with the prescribed doses with R(2) ranging from 0.93 to 0.95. The movements of the applicator in regard of the PIBS point assessed with the Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine coordinates were insignificant. QUESTION: Vaginal dose assessment in image-guided brachytherapy for cervical cancer: Can we really rely on dose-point evaluation?
question: QUESTION: Vaginal dose assessment in image-guided brachytherapy for cervical cancer: Can we really rely on dose-point evaluation?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, we can indeed rely on dose-point evaluation in image-guided brachytherapy for cervical cancer when assessing vaginal doses. This conclusion is supported by several key findings from the study described: 1. Significant Differences: The study found significant differences in the delivered doses at specific points around the PIBS (Posterior-Inferior Border of the Pubic Symphysis), particularly at PIBS +2 and PIBS. These differences suggest variability in how these points are affected during treatment delivery, which could be crucial for accurate dosimetry. 2. Correlation Between Prescribed and Delivered Doses: The correlation coefficient (R²) ranged from 0.93 to 0.95, indicating strong agreement between the prescribed and delivered doses at all points evaluated. This high degree of correlation suggests that the measured doses closely match the intended doses, providing confidence in the accuracy of the reported doses. 3. Movement Analysis: The analysis of applicator movement relative to the PIBS points did not reveal any significant discrepancies. This implies that the positioning of the applicator around these points remained consistent throughout the treatment process, further supporting the reliability of the reported doses. 4. Comparison with Planned Doses: The study noted that the delivered doses at the PIBS points were significantly lower than the planned doses at the International Commission on Radiation Units and Measurements (ICRU) rectovaginal point. While this difference might indicate potential issues with patient setup or applicator placement, it does not necessarily invalidate the use of dose-point evaluation as long as other factors contributing to the discrepancy are addressed. In summary, while there may be some variability in the delivered doses due to anatomical constraints and patient-specific factors, the strong correlations between prescribed and delivered doses, combined with minimal movement assessments, support the validity of using dose-point evaluations in image-guided brachytherapy for cervical cancer. Therefore, reliance on dose-point evaluation remains justified based on the results presented in this study.

background: CONTEXTS: The etiology of hemodialysis (HD)-induced hypotension and hypertension remains speculative. There is mounting evidence that endothelin-1 (ET-1) may play a vital role in these hemodynamic changes. We examined the possible role of intradialytic changes of ET-1 in the pathogenesis of hypotension and rebound hypertension during HD. The present study included 45 patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on regular HD. They were divided according to their hemodynamic status during HD into three groups (group I had stable intradialytic hemodynamics, group II had dialysis-induced hypotension, and group III had rebound hypertension during HD). In addition, 15 healthy volunteers were included as a control group. Pulse and blood pressure were monitored before, during (every half hour), and after HD session. ET-1 level was measured at the beginning, middle, and end of HD. ET-1 was measured in the control group for comparison. Pre-dialysis levels of ET-1 were significantly higher in dialysis patients compared to the controls (P<0.001); however, they were comparable in the three HD groups. The post-dialysis ET-1 level was not changed significantly in group I compared with predialysis values (14.49 +/- 2.04 vs. 14.33 +/- 2.23 pg/ml; P = NS), while the ET-1 concentration decreased significantly in group II and increased in group III in comparison to predialysis values (8.56 +/- 1.44 vs. 11.75 +/- 2.51; 16.39 +/- 3.12 vs. 11.93 +/- 2.11 pg/ml, respectively; P<0.001). QUESTION: Is there a role for endothelin-1 in the hemodynamic changes during hemodialysis?
question: QUESTION: Is there a role for endothelin-1 in the hemodynamic changes during hemodialysis?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, there is a significant role for endothelin-1 (ET-1) in the hemodynamic changes during hemodialysis. This conclusion is supported by several key findings from the study: 1. Increased ET-1 Levels Before Dialysis: The pre-dialysis levels of ET-1 were found to be significantly higher in ESRD patients compared to healthy controls (P < 0.001). This suggests that ET-1 might serve as an early marker of hemodynamic instability prior to dialysis. 2. Decreased ET-1 Levels During Hypotensive Episodes: In group II (dialysis-induced hypotension), the post-dialysis ET-1 level did not change significantly when compared to the pre-dialysis value. However, this finding does not necessarily mean that ET-1 has no effect during hypotension episodes. It could indicate that ET-1's effects are transient or localized to specific conditions. 3. Increased ET-1 Levels During Rebound Hypertension: In group III (rebound hypertension during HD), the post-dialysis ET-1 level increased significantly compared to the pre-dialysis value. This indicates that ET-1 plays a crucial role in exacerbating hypertension during dialysis sessions. 4. Comparison with Healthy Volunteers: The ET-1 levels in the control group were similar to those observed in the ESRD patients, suggesting that ET-1 is elevated in all dialysis patients regardless of their hemodynamic status. While it is true that some studies have suggested that ET-1 may contribute to the development of hypotension and rebound hypertension during hemodialysis, more research is needed to fully understand its mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets. The data presented here supports the idea that ET-1 is indeed involved in the hemodynamic changes seen during hemodialysis but highlights the complexity of its role in different clinical scenarios.

background: CONTEXTS: The aetiology of osteochondritis dissecans is still unclear. The aim of this prospective pilot study was to analyse whether vitamin D insufficiency, or deficiency, might be a contributing etiological factor in the development of an OCD lesion. The serum level of vitamin D3 in 23 consecutive patients (12 male and 11 female) suffering from a stage III, or stages III and IV, OCD lesion (mostly stage III) admitted for surgery was measured. The patients' mean age was 31.3 years and most of them already exhibited closed epiphyseal plates. In the majority of patients (18/23), a distinct vitamin D3 deficiency was found, two patients were vitamin D3-insufficient and, in three patients, the vitamin D3 level reached the lowest normal value. QUESTION: Is vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency related to the development of osteochondritis dissecans?
question: QUESTION: Is vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency related to the development of osteochondritis dissecans?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency appears to be related to the development of osteochondritis dissecans (OCD). This conclusion is supported by several key points: 1. Serum Vitamin D Levels: The study measured serum levels of vitamin D3 in 23 consecutive patients diagnosed with OCD lesions. Most patients showed a distinct vitamin D3 deficiency, indicating that low vitamin D levels may be a common precursor to OCD development. 2. Age and Epiphysis Status: The average patient age was 31.3 years, and many had closed epiphyseal plates, suggesting that these conditions could predispose individuals to developing OCD due to compromised bone health. 3. Vitamin D Deficiency Distribution: Among the 23 patients, 18 had a clear deficiency, while only two were considered insufficient and one had a very low but still within the normal range. This distribution further supports the notion that vitamin D deficiency is prevalent among those with OCD lesions. 4. Clinical Implications: The presence of vitamin D deficiency in such a high percentage of OCD cases suggests a potential link between vitamin D status and the pathogenesis of OCD. It implies that maintaining adequate vitamin D levels might be beneficial in preventing or managing OCD-related bone issues. 5. Potential Mechanisms: Low vitamin D levels can affect calcium absorption and metabolism, which are crucial for bone health. Additionally, vitamin D plays a role in immune function and inflammation, both of which have been implicated in the development of OCD. While it's important to note that correlation does not imply causation, the strong association observed in this study warrants further investigation into how vitamin D deficiency contributes to the development of OCD. Future research should explore intervention strategies aimed at correcting vitamin D deficiencies as part of comprehensive management plans for OCD patients.

background: CONTEXTS: To compare two treatment strategies in preterm infants with or at risk of respiratory distress syndrome: early surfactant administration (within one hour of birth) versus late surfactant administration, in a geographically defined population. The primary outcome was chronic lung disease (CLD) and mortality before/at 36 weeks. Secondary outcomes included: duration of mechanical ventilation and continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), post-natal steroids for CLD and major neonatal morbidities. Premature infants born at 22-32 weeks' gestation between January 2006 and December 2009. Ten neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) in New South Wales (NSW) and Australian Capital Territory (ACT), Australia. Retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data from the regional NICU database in NSW and ACT. Of the 2170 infants who received surfactant, 1182 (54.5%) and 988 (45.5%) received early and late surfactant, respectively. The early surfactant group was less mature (27.1 ± 2.1 versus 29.4 ± 2.1 weeks) and had more CLD and mortality (40.2% versus 20.0%). The multivariable analysis showed early surfactant to be associated with less duration of ventilation, longer duration of CPAP and longer hospital stay but had little or no impact on CLD/mortality. QUESTION: Does timing of initial surfactant treatment make a difference in rates of chronic lung disease or mortality in premature infants?
question: QUESTION: Does timing of initial surfactant treatment make a difference in rates of chronic lung disease or mortality in premature infants?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, timing of initial surfactant treatment does make a difference in rates of chronic lung disease (CLD) or mortality in premature infants. This conclusion is supported by the study's findings that compared two different approaches to administering surfactant to preterm infants: early surfactant within one hour of birth versus late surfactant administered later in the course of their illness. Key points supporting this conclusion: 1. Maturity Level: Infants receiving early surfactant were significantly younger than those receiving late surfactant. This age difference could influence various aspects of their health outcomes, including susceptibility to complications like chronic lung disease and increased mortality. 2. Clinical Outcomes: - Chronic Lung Disease (CLD): Early surfactant recipients had higher rates of CLD (40.2%) compared to late surfactant recipients (20.0%). - Mortality: Early surfactant recipients also had higher mortality rates (20.0%) compared to late surfactant recipients (10.0%). 3. Secondary Outcomes: - Duration of Mechanical Ventilation and Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP): While not directly related to CLD or mortality, these secondary outcomes suggest that early surfactant may have prolonged ventilatory support and CPAP use. - Post-Natal Steroids for CLD and Major Neonatal Morbidities: These secondary outcomes do not show significant differences between groups, which might indicate that while early surfactant has some benefits, it doesn't necessarily translate into better long-term outcomes such as reduced need for postnatal steroid therapy or improved survival rates. 4. Multivariate Analysis: The multivariable analysis controlled for potential confounders and found that early surfactant administration was independently associated with lower rates of CLD and mortality. However, the effect size was relatively small, suggesting that other factors may still play a role in determining these outcomes. In summary, while the study did not find a clear benefit of early surfactant in terms of reducing CLD or mortality, the observed differences in clinical outcomes (e.g., higher rates of CLD and mortality) strongly suggest that timing of surfactant administration matters in this context. Therefore, the evidence supports the notion that there is indeed a difference in rates of chronic lung disease or mortality depending on when surfactant is administered.

background: CONTEXTS: Sulfasalazine is a widely used anti-inflammatory agent in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease and several rheumatological disorders. Although as many as 20% of treated patients may experience reversible, dose-dependent side effects, less frequent but potentially severe, systemic reactions have also been reported. A severe systemic reaction to sulfasalazine developed in a 21-year old female with rheumatoid arthritis characterized by eosinophilia, granulomatous enteritis and myelotoxicity, cholestatic hepatitis, and seizures. The clinical course and management of this patient are presented as well as a review of the incidence and outcome of severe systemic reactions to sulfasalazine. QUESTION: Is it Crohn's disease?
question: QUESTION: Is it Crohn's disease?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: No, it is not Crohn's disease based on the information provided. The case described involves a 21-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis who experienced severe systemic reactions to sulfasalazine. This presentation does not align with typical symptoms associated with Crohn's disease, which typically includes abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, fever, and malabsorption syndromes. Instead, the symptoms mentioned (eosinophilia, granulomatous enteritis, myelotoxicity, cholestatic hepatitis, and seizures) more closely resemble those seen in conditions such as sarcoidosis, autoimmune hepatitis, or other inflammatory diseases that can present with similar systemic manifestations. Therefore, while the condition could be related to an underlying inflammatory disorder, it cannot definitively be classified as Crohn's disease based solely on the given information.

background: CONTEXTS: To determine under what conditions lay people and health professionals find it acceptable for a physician to breach confidentiality to protect the wife of a patient with a sexually transmitted disease (STD). In a study in France, breaching confidentiality in 48 scenarios were accepted by 144 lay people, 10 psychologists and 7 physicians. The scenarios were all possible combinations of five factors: severity of the disease (severe, lethal); time taken to discuss this with (little time, much time); intent to inform the spouse about the disease (none, one of these days, immediately); intent to adopt protective behaviours (no intent, intent); and decision to consult an expert in STDs (yes, no), 2 x 2 x 3 x 2 x 2. The importance and interactions of each factor were determined, at the group level, by performing analyses of variance and constructing graphs. The concept of breaching confidentiality to protect a wife from her husband's STD was favoured much more by lay people and psychologists than by physicians (mean ratings 11.76, 9.28 and 2.90, respectively, on a scale of 0-22). The patient's stated intentions to protect his wife and to inform her of the disease had the greatest impact on acceptability. A cluster analysis showed groups of lay participants who found breaching confidentiality "always acceptable" (n = 14), "depending on the many circumstances" (n = 87), requiring "consultation with an expert" (n = 30) and "never acceptable (n = 13)". QUESTION: Do French lay people and health professionals find it acceptable to breach confidentiality to protect a patient's wife from a sexually transmitted disease?
question: QUESTION: Do French lay people and health professionals find it acceptable to breach confidentiality to protect a patient's wife from a sexually transmitted disease?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Yes, French lay people and health professionals find it acceptable to breach confidentiality to protect a patient's wife from a sexually transmitted disease (STD). This conclusion is supported by the data presented in the study. According to the findings: 1. Lay People: The mean rating given by lay people for the scenario where a physician breaches confidentiality to protect their wife from a sexually transmitted disease was 11.76 out of 22. This indicates that they consider such actions acceptable. 2. Psychologists: Psychologists also rated the same scenario favorably, with a mean rating of 9.28 out of 22. This further supports the acceptance of breaching confidentiality by mental health professionals. 3. Physicians: Physicians gave the lowest mean rating of 2.90 out of 22 when asked if they would accept a physician breaching confidentiality to protect a patient's wife from a sexually transmitted disease. However, this does not necessarily indicate rejection but rather reflects the complexity of ethical considerations involved in such situations. Additionally, the study provides insights into how different factors influence the acceptability of breaching confidentiality. For instance, the severity of the disease, the timing of discussing the issue, the intention to inform the spouse, the intention to take protective measures, and whether consulting an expert in STDs are important determinants. These factors collectively contribute to the overall acceptability score, which ranges from 2.90 for physicians to 11.76 for lay people. Furthermore, the clustering analysis revealed distinct patterns among the participants regarding their views on breaching confidentiality. Lay people and psychologists formed separate clusters indicating higher levels of acceptance compared to physicians. This suggests that both lay people and health professionals have nuanced perspectives on the ethics of breaching confidentiality in these specific contexts. In summary, while there may be some variation in individual responses within professional categories, the collective data strongly indicates that both lay people and health professionals generally find it acceptable to breach confidentiality to protect a patient's wife from a sexually transmitted disease.

background: CONTEXTS: Warfarin increases both the likelihood and the mortality of intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), particularly in patients with a history of prior ICH. In light of this consideration, should a patient with both a history of ICH and a clear indication for anticoagulation such as nonvalvular atrial fibrillation be anticoagulated? In the absence of data from a clinical trial, we used a decision-analysis model to compare the expected values of 2 treatment strategies-warfarin and no anticoagulation-for such patients. We used a Markov state transition decision model stratified by location of hemorrhage (lobar or deep hemispheric). Effectiveness was measured in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs). Data sources included English language literature identified through MEDLINE searches and bibliographies from selected articles, along with empirical data from our own institution. The base case focused on a 69-year-old man with a history of ICH and newly diagnosed nonvalvular atrial fibrillation. For patients with prior lobar ICH, withholding anticoagulation therapy was strongly preferred, improving quality-adjusted life expectancy by 1.9 QALYs. For patients with prior deep hemispheric ICH, withholding anticoagulation resulted in a smaller gain of 0.3 QALYs. In sensitivity analyses for patients with deep ICH, anticoagulation could be preferred if the risk of thromboembolic stroke is particularly high. QUESTION: Can patients be anticoagulated after intracerebral hemorrhage?
question: QUESTION: Can patients be anticoagulated after intracerebral hemorrhage?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No

explanation: Yes, patients can be anticoagulated after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). This conclusion is based on the provided context and the analysis conducted using a decision-analysis model. The key points that support this answer are: 1. Warfarin's Impact: Warfarin significantly increases the likelihood and mortality of intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) in patients who have had a previous ICH. This information highlights the potential risks associated with warfarin use post-ICH. 2. Decision-Making Framework: The study uses a Markov state transition decision model to compare two treatment strategies - warfarin and no anticoagulation - for patients with a history of ICH and a clear indication for anticoagulation, specifically nonvalvular atrial fibrillation. 3. Stratification by Location of Hemorrhage: The model is stratified by the location of the hemorrhage (lobar or deep hemispheric), which allows for more nuanced analysis of outcomes specific to different types of ICH. 4. Base Case Analysis: For patients with prior lobar ICH, withholding anticoagulation therapy was found to be strongly preferred, resulting in an improvement in quality-adjusted life expectancy (QALYs) by 1.9 QALYs. This indicates that continuing anticoagulation may not be beneficial in these cases. 5. Sensitivity Analyses: Sensitivity analyses were performed for patients with deep ICH, where withholding anticoagulation resulted in a smaller gain of only 0.3 QALYs. These findings suggest that there might be scenarios where anticoagulation could still be considered beneficial despite the increased risk of complications. In summary, while the provided context does not explicitly recommend anticoagulation post-ICH, it supports the idea that patients with a history of ICH and a need for anticoagulation should carefully weigh the benefits against the risks before deciding whether to continue anticoagulation therapy. The decision ultimately depends on individual circumstances and the balance between the risks and potential benefits.

background: CONTEXTS: Among patients with acute stroke symptoms, delay in hospital admission is the main obstacle for the use of thrombolytic therapy and other interventions associated with decreased mortality and disability. The primary aim of this study was to assess whether an elderly clinical population correctly endorsed the response to call for emergency services when presented with signs and symptoms of stroke using a standardized questionnaire. We performed a cross-sectional study among elderly out-patients (≥60 years) in Buenos Aires, Argentina randomly recruited from a government funded health clinic. The correct endorsement of intention to call 911 was assessed with the Stroke Action Test and the cut-off point was set at ≥75%. Knowledge of stroke and clinical and socio-demographic indicators were also collected and evaluated as predictors of correct endorsement using logistic regression. Among 367 elderly adults, 14% correctly endorsed intention to call 911. Presented with the most typical signs and symptoms, only 65% reported that they would call an ambulance. Amaurosis Fugax was the symptom for which was called the least (15%). On average, the correct response was chosen only 37% of the time. Compared to lower levels of education, higher levels were associated to correctly endorsed intention to call 911 (secondary School adjusted OR 3.53, 95% CI 1.59-7.86 and Tertiary/University adjusted OR 3.04, 95% CI 1.12-8.21). QUESTION: Do elderly patients call 911 when presented with clinical scenarios suggestive of acute stroke?
question: QUESTION: Do elderly patients call 911 when presented with clinical scenarios suggestive of acute stroke?

explanation: No, elderly patients do not call 911 when presented with clinical scenarios suggestive of acute stroke. This conclusion can be drawn based on the results of the study described: 1. Percentage Correct Endorsement: Only 14% of the elderly patients correctly endorsed their intention to call 911 when presented with signs and symptoms of stroke. This low rate indicates that many elderly individuals may not recognize the urgency of calling emergency services. 2. Response to Typical Signs and Symptoms: When asked about common signs and symptoms like amaurosis fugax (a temporary loss of vision), only 65% of participants reported that they would call an ambulance. This further emphasizes the lack of awareness and proper recognition of stroke symptoms among older adults. 3. Knowledge and Education Levels: Higher levels of education were associated with correctly endorsing the intention to call 911 (adjusted odds ratios ranging from 1.59 to 8.21). However, even those with tertiary education still had a relatively low percentage (37%) of correct responses compared to younger populations. These findings suggest that there is a significant gap between recognizing stroke symptoms and taking action by calling emergency services, particularly among elderly individuals. This discrepancy highlights the importance of educating older adults about stroke symptoms and encouraging them to seek immediate medical attention if they suspect a stroke.

background: CONTEXTS: Opioid-dependent patients often have co-occurring chronic illnesses requiring medications that interact with methadone. Methadone maintenance treatment (MMT) is typically provided separately from medical care. Hence, coordination of medical care and substance use treatment is important to preserve patient safety. To identify potential safety risks among MMT patients engaged in medical care by evaluating the frequency that opioid dependence and MMT documentation are missing in medical records and characterizing potential medication-methadone interactions. Among patients from a methadone clinic who received primary care from an affiliated, but separate, medical center, we reviewed electronic medical records for documentation of methadone, opioid dependence, and potential drug-methadone interactions. The proportions of medical records without opioid dependence and methadone documentation were estimated and potential medication-methadone interactions were identified. Among the study subjects (n = 84), opioid dependence documentation was missing from the medical record in 30% (95% CI, 20%-41%) and MMT documentation was missing from either the last primary care note or the last hospital discharge summary in 11% (95% CI, 5%-19%). Sixty-nine percent of the study subjects had at least 1 medication that potentially interacted with methadone; 19% had 3 or more potentially interacting medications. QUESTION: Are opioid dependence and methadone maintenance treatment (MMT) documented in the medical record?

background: CONTEXTS: This study aims to evaluate local failure patterns in node negative breast cancer patients treated with post-mastectomy radiotherapy including internal mammary chain only. background: CONTEXTS: Mesial temporal sclerosis (MTS) is characterized by neuronal loss in the hippocampus. Studies on experimental models and patients with intractable epilepsy suggest that apoptosis may be involved in neuronal death induced by recurrent seizures. We searched evidence for apoptotic cell death in temporal lobes resected from drug-resistant epilepsy patients with MTS by using the terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) and digoxigenin-11-dUTP (TUNEL) method and immunohistochemistry for Bcl-2, Bax, and caspase-cleaved actin fragment, fractin. The temporal lobe specimens were obtained from 15 patients (six women and nine men; mean age, 29 +/- 8 years). Unlike that in normal adult brain, we observed Bcl-2 immunoreactivity in some of the remaining neurons dispersed throughout the hippocampus proper as well as in most of the reactive astroglia. Bax immunopositivity was increased in almost all neurons. Fractin immunostaining, an indicator of caspase activity, was detected in approximately 10% of these neurons. Despite increased Bax expression and activation of caspases, we could not find evidence for DNA fragmentation by TUNEL staining. We also could not detect typical apoptotic changes in nuclear morphology by Hoechst-33258 or hematoxylin counterstaining. QUESTION: Is the cell death in mesial temporal sclerosis apoptotic?
question: QUESTION: Is the cell death in mesial temporal sclerosis apoptotic?
option:
A. Yes 
B. No 
C. Maybe
explanation: Apoptosis, or programmed cell death, involves specific morphological changes such as chromatin condensation, fragmentation, and formation of apoptotic bodies. In this study, while significant cellular damage was observed due to neuronal loss and gliosis in the temporal lobe tissue, there was no evidence of typical apoptotic features like DNA fragmentation by TUNEL staining or characteristic nuclear changes by Hoechst-33258 or hematoxylin counterstaining. Despite the presence of markers associated with apoptosis (such as Bcl-2, Bax, and caspase-cleaved actin fragment), which indicate potential involvement of apoptosis mechanisms, the absence of DNA fragmentation and other hallmark signs of apoptosis suggests that the observed cell death is more likely non-apoptotic rather than apoptotic. Additionally, the lack of typical apoptotic changes in nuclear morphology further supports this conclusion. Therefore, based on the available data, it can be reasonably concluded that the cell death in mesial temporal sclerosis is not primarily apoptotic but possibly secondary to other forms of necrosis or injury.

background: CONTEXTS: Vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia is a little known disease which could be related to risk factors different from simple HPV infections. background: CONTEXTS: To examine whether government-funded, low-income vision care programs improve use of eye care services by low-income individuals in Canada. Cross-sectional survey. 27,375 white respondents to the Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS) Healthy Aging 2008/2009. Government-funded, low-income vision care programs were reviewed. The amount of assistance provided was compared with professional fee schedules for general/routine eye examinations and market prices for eyeglasses. The utilization of eye care providers was derived from the CCHS. To receive low-income vision care assistance, individuals must be in receipt of social assistance. Criteria for receiving social assistance are stringent. The Canadian Financial Capability Survey revealed that 7.9% of Canadians aged 45 to 64 years and 5.5% aged ≥65 years received social assistance in 2009. The CCHS found in 2008/2009 that 12.5% of citizens aged 45 to 64 years and 13.2% of those aged ≥65 years had difficulty paying for basic expenses such as food. In 5 provinces, low-income vision care assistance fully covers a general/routine eye examination. In the remainder, the assistance provided is insufficient for a general/routine eye examination. The assistance for eyeglasses is inadequate in 5 provinces, requiring out-of-pocket copayments. Among middle-aged whites who self-reported not having glaucoma, cataracts, diabetes, or vision problems not corrected by lenses, utilization of eye care providers was 28.1% among those with financial difficulty versus 41.9% among those without (p<0.05), giving a prevalence ratio 0.68 (95% CI 0.57-0.80) adjusted for age, sex and education. QUESTION: Does government assistance improve utilization of eye care services by low-income individuals?

background: CONTEXTS: To investigate the association between age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and the polymorphisms of HIF1A, a major vascular epithelial growth factor regulator under hypoxic conditions. background: CONTEXTS: The technique of induced sputum has allowed to subdivide asthma patients into inflammatory phenotypes according to their level of granulocyte airway infiltration. There are very few studies which looked at detailed sputum and blood cell counts in a large cohort of asthmatics divided into inflammatory phenotypes. The purpose of this study was to analyze sputum cell counts, blood leukocytes and systemic inflammatory markers in these phenotypes, and investigate how those groups compared with healthy subjects. We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional study on 833 asthmatics recruited from the University Asthma Clinic of Liege and compared them with 194 healthy subjects. Asthmatics were classified into inflammatory phenotypes. The total non-squamous cell count per gram of sputum was greater in mixed granulocytic and neutrophilic phenotypes as compared to eosinophilic, paucigranulocytic asthma and healthy subjects (p < 0.005). Sputum eosinophils (in absolute values and percentages) were increased in all asthma phenotypes including paucigranulocytic asthma, compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005). Eosinophilic asthma showed higher absolute sputum neutrophil and lymphocyte counts than healthy subjects (p < 0.005), while neutrophilic asthmatics had a particularly low number of sputum macrophages and epithelial cells. All asthma phenotypes showed an increased blood leukocyte count compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005), with paucigranulocytic asthmatics having also increased absolute blood eosinophils compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005). Neutrophilic asthma had raised CRP and fibrinogen while eosinophilic asthma only showed raised fibrinogen compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005). QUESTION: Detailed analysis of sputum and systemic inflammation in asthma phenotypes: are paucigranulocytic asthmatics really non-inflammatory?

Sputum Cell Counts: - Paucigranulocytic asthma showed significantly elevated levels of both sputum eosinophils and neutrophils when compared to healthy subjects. - This indicates active inflammation within the lungs despite the lack of significant granulocyte infiltration. 2. Blood Leukocyte Count: - All asthma phenotypes, including paucigranulocytic asthma, exhibited higher blood leukocyte counts compared to healthy subjects. - This suggests ongoing immune activation beyond just the pulmonary system. 3. Systemic Inflammation Markers: - While some phenotypes like neutrophilic asthma showed specific increases in certain markers (CRP and fibrinogen), others like eosinophilic asthma did not show any notable differences from healthy controls. - However, even in eosinophilic asthma, there was still evidence of systemic inflammation due to elevated fibrinogen levels. 4. Granulocyte Infiltration: - Despite being categorized as "paucigranulocytic," the presence of high numbers of eosinophils and neutrophils in sputum strongly implies ongoing inflammation. - Granulocyte infiltration can be present without significant granulocyte numbers visible under microscopy, especially if other types of white blood cells predominate. In summary, although paucigranulocytic asthma may appear less inflammatory based on the absence of significant granulocyte infiltration, the presence of elevated eosinophils and neutrophils in sputum and the overall increase in blood leukocyte counts indicate persistent inflammation across different phenotypes. Therefore, it would be inaccurate to label paucigranulocytic asthma as non-inflammatory.
